Coldhearted, indeed.

Aspiring Los Angeles-area rapper ColdheartedAC was arrested Wednesday and charged with allegedly participating in an $8.1 million stolen-check scheme spanning southern California.

The 31-year-old Quartz Hill artist, whose real name is Ada William Obayuwana and who also performs under the name AC, was federally indicted alongside two others, Albert Tai Vu, 28, of Westminster, and Cassandra Marie Murrillo, 31, of San Diego, the Department of Justice announced Friday.

The 25-count federal indictment alleges the trio obtained more than 50 stolen U.S. Treasury checks and hundreds of checks belonging to individuals and businesses, then cashed or attempted to cash them.

Between April 2022 and December 2023, the defendants allegedly targeted checks containing tax refunds, Social Security payments and veterans’ benefits. Investigators say they forged endorsements, altered names and addresses and used fake business documents to impersonate people and companies connected to the checks.

open image in gallery L.A.-area rapper ColdheartedAC, whose Instagram post is shown here, and two others face bank fraud charges in an alleged $8.1 million stolen-check scheme ( Department of Justice )

The alleged scheme stretched across Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties, where the defendants allegedly opened bank accounts to deposit the stolen checks and move the money.

Obayuwana allegedly attempted to cash at least three Treasury tax-refund checks worth a combined $382,109 and successfully cashed one, withdrawing $229,109, according to federal prosecutors.

He is accused of carrying more than 100 stolen or fraudulent checks worth over $6.1 million in his car when authorities found them in Oceanside in December 2023. Among the checks were 48 Treasury checks worth about $2.56 million, including tax refunds and federal benefit payments. Investigators allege eight of those checks had already been cashed for around $1.7 million.

The rapper has more htan 338,000 Instagram followers and more than 3,000 YouTube subscribers. He often showcases his lavish lifestyle online, including lots of jewelry and a photo with boxing legend Floyd Mayweather.

Co-defendant Albert Tai Vu allegedly attempted to cash at least six Treasury checks totaling $2.15 million and successfully cashed two tax-refund checks worth $772,159. He also allegedly cashed two $250,000 cashier’s checks at an Anaheim bank, using proceeds from one to purchase a Range Rover and money from the other to pay Murrillo, who was also charged in the alleged scheme.

open image in gallery ColdheartedAC allegedly tried to cash $382,109 in Treasury checks and was later found with more than 100 fraudulent checks worth over $6.1 million ( DOJ )

Murrillo allegedly attempted to cash two checks totaling $60,193 and successfully cashed one worth $31,405.

Obayuwana remains in federal custody and faces nine counts of bank fraud, three counts of delivering stolen Treasury checks and one count of aggravated identity theft.

Vu, who was arrested Thursday, faces bank fraud, money-laundering, stolen check and identity theft charges.

Murillo, who is expected to surrender to federal authorities in Los Angeles on Monday, faces an additional charge of delivering stolen Treasury checks.

If convicted, the defendants could face up to 30 years in federal prison for each bank fraud count, up to 10 years for each counterfeit Treasury check and money laundering count, plus a mandatory additional two-year sentence for each aggravated identity theft count, according to the Justice Department.

A man who initially lied to police by claiming his girlfriend was killed in a hit-and-run has been jailed over her death.

Matthew DuPlessis, 35, was given a sentence of nine years and three months’ imprisonment at Chester Crown Court on Friday, Cheshire Constabulary said.

He had admitted at an earlier hearing to perverting the course of justice and causing death by careless driving while unfit through drugs.

Police said DuPlessis and his partner Charlotte Dodd, also 35, had travelled to Blackpool on September 23 2023, before neighbours overheard them arguing later that night.

The couple left Ms Dodd’s home together at 1.30am and continued their argument as they drove around Congleton in DuPlessis’s van.

While on Padbury Lane, Congleton, Ms Dodd exited the van while it was still moving, striking the carriageway and suffering fatal injuries, according to the force.

open image in gallery Charlotte Dodd was 35 when she died on September 23 2023 ( PA )

A passerby stopped his car when he saw her in the road with DuPlessis sat on a grass verge behind her.

The defendant, of Richard Darrock Way in Crewe, told the man there had been a hit and run, police said.

DCI Dave Hutcheon, of the major investigation team, said: “DuPlessis told multiple witnesses at the scene including his own parents, members of the public, paramedics and police at the scene that he and Charlotte were walking along Padgbury Lane having been out drinking and that Charlotte was dancing in the carriageway.”

The officer said DuPlessis had told people that a dark coloured vehicle had struck his girlfriend and fled the scene while he had his back turned.

“We launched a fail to stop investigation at the scene, and the defendant was treated as a witness and later allowed to leave with his parents,” DCI Hutcheon said.

However, an officer attending the scene had recognised DuPlessis’s name and that he drove a white van similar to one that was parked there.

In 2024, the defendant admitted driving with excess cocaine in his body in relation to the incident and was disqualified from driving for three years.

Meanwhile, the investigation into Ms Dodd’s death continued and DuPlessis admitted to police that she had repeatedly threatened to jump out of the vehicle, but did not.

He refused to say how she came to leave the van, police said, but CCTV along Padgbury Lane showed the driver door shut with an interior light on, indicating that the passenger door was open.

DuPlessis told police Ms Dodd had opened the passenger door as she wanted to get out, the force said.

The video showed the van continuing a further 195 metres at an average speed of 19mph.

Forensic analysis found the van was over the centre line of the carriage line as the defendant went to turn left into Arnside Avenue and Ms Dodd left the vehicle at that junction.

Following sentencing Ms Dodd’s family said in a statement that they had “quietly lived through the turmoil, the uncertainty and the heartbreak surrounding the circumstances of Charlotte’s death”.

“We have each carried an indescribable pain of losing our daughter, sister, granddaughter, niece and friend, whilst also watching her two young girls try to come to terms with losing their mummy,” they said.

“It has taken so long to reach a Crown Court sentence hearing,” the statement continued.

“Due to the lies and deception by one person from the very beginning, thereby perverting the course of justice, we still do not know the full truth of what really happened to Charlotte.

“There are no witnesses. There are some questions that remain unanswered, and we will have to live with those questions for the rest of our lives.

“Justice has now been served, yet we do not believe this reflects the enormity of what has been lost and the devastation that Charlotte’s death has caused.

“Charlotte has not been able to live her best life because one person has senselessly taken that life way, stolen her future.

“For us, no custodial sentence or punishment will ever be enough.”

DCI Hutcheon added: “It hasn’t been determined how Charlotte came to leave the van.

“The defendant overshot the junction causing him to perform an emergency stop.

“He then reversed and parked his van on Arnside Avenue and went to Charlotte.

“He then concocted his story to cover up that he was responsible for her death.

“His lies were caught out by the roads policing officer and the detailed forensic analysis of his movements led to him having no option but to plead guilty.”

Canadian figures have met President Donald Trump’s command to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" with ridicule rather than anger.

On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded by unveiling a giant billboard along the Canadian shore bearing the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always".

Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford posed for photos beside the structure near Grimsby, Ontario. Measuring 24 by 12 feet (7.3 by 3.6 metres), the display rests on 6-foot (1.8-metre) legs, reaching roughly 18 feet (5.5 metres) high — about two storeys tall. The text is duplicated in French.

The action follows an executive order directing US federal agencies to adopt the name "Lake America." It comes after months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st US state, and personal attacks on its leaders, triggering a mixture of defiance and humour.

Ford noted that Trump sought the change because Ontario and Canada were "standing up for ourselves", declaring the original name would outlast the president.

open image in gallery A family walks by a sign reading "Lake Ontario, Now and Always" ( Reuters )

“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.

Canadians mock Trump

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit

“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”

The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing.

“The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said.

But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.”

open image in gallery A map labeling Lake Ontario as "Lake America" is displayed as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks after signing an executive order during an event in the Oval Office of the White House ( Getty )

Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.”

Canada and the US trade barbs over collapsed talks

The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month.

Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.”

Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.

Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America.

Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state.

Ontario name has Indigenous origins

The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history.

“I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name.

Richarlison is one three Tottenham players who have asked to leave the club, manager Roberto de Zerbi has revealed.

Richarlison was left out of the Spurs squad for Saturday evening’s 2-0 defeat by Newcastle United, having started last weekend’s 3-0 loss at Brentford.

And De Zerbi said after the game that the Brazilian had requested to leave the club, naming him with defender Kevin Danso and midfielder Pape Matar Sarr as a trio of wantaway players.

“Richarlison, he said too many times that he wanted to leave,” said De Zerbi. “Danso came to me two days ago and said he wanted to leave. Sarr the same, but he also suffered a small injury, but he is almost ready to train.

“I love these players and these are great guys. I have very good relationships. But if they want to leave they have to bring the economic solution to the club and they can go, and we’ll find other players.”

Spurs have spent around £300m on transfers this summer in a bid to dramatically turn around their fortunes on the pitch following a 17th-placed finish last season.

The club are still searching for more additions before Tuesday’s deadline, although they are set to miss out on key target Cody Gakpo, the Liverpool and Netherlands winger, who is widely reported to be on the verge of an £85m transfer to Manchester City.

Richarlison is among those who have asked to leave (John Walton/PA) ( PA Wire )

De Zerbi added: “If I was positive last season when we were in the Championship, because when I came (in March) we were in the Championship, what do you think my thoughts now could be?

“I’m sorry for the fans, for the environment because after two defeats, maybe somebody can think it’s the same story, the same as the last two seasons. I have no doubt it’s not like this. I can’t change my opinion after two defeats. I have a big, big confidence in the qualities of my players.

“I’m sorry for the club, because they are building a great squad but maybe now we are not ready yet, for many, many reasons.

“Today, I think, until the first goal, we played better than Newcastle. It’s the biggest problem, it’s the biggest challenge and it’s the biggest target to find the right mentality. Unfortunately, you can’t buy the mentality in the transfer market or putting many players inside.

“Football is like a magic thing, you know? You can change many players in a window, in one window of transfer market and you can find the balance immediately or you need more time.

“I think we (will) achieve this target and this goal. I would like to achieve this target quickly and as soon as possible because it is crucial to play football, but the plan and the project of the club and what we are doing to build and rebuild a new team with great players is a great plan and a great project.”

Spurs’s next game is a trip to Nottingham Forest on Saturday 5 September.

News.title: £380m = zero points: Big-spending Spurs humbled by Newcastle
News.content:
“After the first goal we lost confidence,” said De Zerbi. “The reaction was not good enough, not what I want to see on the pitch. The solution is not to put the head down, but to react.”

To be clear, Spurs were not quite as bad as they had been against Brentford on the opening day. They did create chances here, taking 17 shots and forcing a few terrific saves from Lukas Hornicek, Newcastle’s impressive goalkeeper. But in the key moments they suffered from the same absence of clarity and execution as they did last season. Troublingly, this seemed to affect the new signings as much as it did the longer-serving players.

Of the five new arrivals who featured for Spurs, Tonali was the least effective. The Italian had been vigorously booed by the away fans before kick-off and the travelling Geordies waited with palpable excitement for his first mistake. Much to their delight, it arrived after only three minutes: an underhit pass, in his own half, which directly led to Micky van de Ven picking up a yellow card. Tonali was outshone by new Newcastle midfielder Nico Gonzalez, who excelled only a few days after completing his move from Manchester City.

News.title: Lawrence seizes his opportunity on rain-ruined day at Lord’s
News.content:
On a bleak day for batting, Dan Lawrence seized an opportunity that he must have feared had passed him by.

Lawrence was one of the victims of Bazball excess, shoved up to open in place of Zak Crawley two years ago in a punt that backfired and could have ended his Test career.

It took the sudden retirement of Ben Stokes and an injury to first-choice replacement Sam Curran to open up a position at No 6, Lawrence’s natural home, and it has come at just the right time.

At 29 he is a much more rounded cricketer than the one who debuted in Sri Lanka under Joe Root in 2021 and he showed it here with a hard-fought half-century on a gloomy, dank Saturday when only 25 overs were possible between the frequent drizzly showers, forcing MCC into a 50 per cent ticket refund.

It was a second fifty in three innings since his recall and he will not have faced many tougher conditions than this, with the ball seaming around on a spiteful pitch. With Mohammad Abbas teasing the ball off the surface and the athletic Mohammad Rizwan snaffling everything up to the stumps, this was a real challenge of mind and technique.

Lawrence will never win awards for aesthetic beauty but he chose the right balls to put away in a 66-ball unbeaten 50 that stretched England’s lead to 357 at 177 for seven in their second innings. Lawrence settled any wobbles about Pakistan pulling off a miracle recovery.

News.title: Springboks level Greatest Rivalry series with blood-and-thunder victory over All Blacks
News.content:
South Africa aim to bounce back from losing the first game of the Greatest Rivalry Tour as they take on New Zealand in game two from Cape Town. The All Blacks claimed an impressive 33-16 win in game on in Johannesburg last weekend, outscoring South Africa five tries to one. That victory takes New Zealand above South Africa in the world rankings into top spot.

The Springboks know that a defeat today will mean they cannot win the series. They have not lost two consecutive Tests since November 2022. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has been given the nod to start at fly-half but Handre Pollard has pulled out of the matchday squad due to a calf injury.

“There were a handful of positives and negatives last week, but the main thing that let us down was that we created so many chances, but mistakes at crucial times cost us,” South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus said.

“We will put in a lot of work this week to ensure that we are sharp in that regard this weekend because if we had used even some of those chances, the result could have been completely different. That said, we know New Zealand will be charged up after winning last week, and they will want to build on that. But the key for us will be to focus on our game and ensure that we are as effective as possible all around.”

News.title: Iraola fumes at bungling fourth official for costing Liverpool a penalty
News.content:
He did know, though, why Liverpool had needed to drag themselves off the deck again for the second week in a row. Iraola has shown in his opening weeks on Merseyside that he is not someone who seeks excuses.

“A lack of intensity hurt us,” Iraola said with obvious disdain and it was only down to a show of character in the second period that a slovenly first half did not enable Forest to win at Anfield for the third consecutive year, for all that the travelling fans thought it was “happening again!”

Forest, bruised after two defeats in four days to Leeds, looked like an Oliver Glasner side. They were aggressive and well organised, the only failing was that physically they could not see the job through, but the Austrian insisted that will change in due course.

Once Glasner is settled in and he gets his transfer business done – “definitely one, possibly two and probably three,” was his mischievous reply to how the window will unfold – Forest will be a formidable proposition, especially if the first 45 minutes are a barometer.

They had been knocking on the door before Dan Ndoye eventually broke the deadlock, sweeping a left-footed drive past Alisson after Igor Jesus had won a header from a long clearance. It was a simple goal, marginally onside, but it was absolutely deserved.

News.title: Cherki magic helping Maresca to step out of Guardiola shadow
News.content:
Rumours of Manchester City’s supposed demise without Pep Guardiola appear to be much exaggerated.

They swept past Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park with a style of play under new manager Enzo Maresca that was just as swashbuckling as under his predecessor, with Rayan Cherki playing the role of chief architect. The Frenchman’s two goals included a captivating mazy dribble, which will long be remembered by those who had the fortune to see it.

City created enough space for themselves through clever movement. With Cherki zigging one way and Phil Foden zagging the other, they created even more by dribbling past a mesmerised Palace back three that became a back five at times and still could not cope.

Erling Haaland also scored twice. Even with the creative and unpredictable talents of those behind in a four-man attacking City midfield, Haaland remains irreplaceable with his ability to convert chances.

However, this night belonged to Cherki. Guardiola chided him publicly after he set up a City goal with a “rabona” cross last season. The thrust of Guardiola’s comments were that Cherki was not Lionel Messi. Of course not, but he possesses a genius all of his own, which Maresca would surely be foolish to rein in.

The jaw-dropping splendour of Cherki’s first goal drew a collective intake of breath at Selhurst Park.

Collecting a Foden pass, he attacked the Palace area on a diagonal path, slaloming between Jaydee Canvot, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chris Richards, before having the spatial awareness and technique to flick his left foot at the ball to send it rolling on a perpendicular trajectory past Dean Henderson.

News.title: England light years ahead of lamentable Pakistan
News.content:
Who needs Ben Stokes? Actually, it is hard to think of any side that would need him against this Pakistan team.

After just five days of cricket, and despite their own limitations with the bat, England are on the cusp of a series victory at Lord’s with a 261-run lead and power to add thanks to the prowess of a seam attack that has emerged quickly from the shadow of its former captain.

It will take longer to feel the full effects of Stokes’s absence. When England need a spinner in the side, they will miss the seam-bowling all-rounder to balance the XI. There will be times when they are up against it on a flat deck on a boiling day and be desperate for Stokes’s sheer will to win. It is still hard to think he will not play some part in the Ashes next summer.

For the final two years of his career it was Stokes’s bowling that was top class, his batting having become ordinary. But with bowlers of the quality of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson gelling, England are more than making up for Stokes’s retirement. This bowling attack against Pakistan’s batting was a complete mismatch.

Joe Root has stepped into Stokes’s shoes confidently, laying down the law off the field and tactically he has been spot on, although Pakistan have hardly stretched him. The only stir they have made since arriving was the stink they kicked up over Sky Sports’ interview with Imran Khan’s sons.

Conclusions are impossible to draw with any confidence against such poor opponents. Sri Lanka and West Indies two years ago put up a stronger fight in the first two Tests of their series. Tamim Iqbal scored two hundreds as Bangladesh at least landed some blows in 2010. Pakistan have managed one fifty in three innings and were bowled out for 171 and 135 at Headingley and a lamentable 110 here.

They were a batsman down at Lord’s because of a calf injury to opener Imam-ul-Haq, but only reached three figures because England dropped top scorer Azan Awais on eight; he went on to score 46.

England’s batting is hardly firing, but with a 180 first-innings lead, they could afford to be 13 for two without panic spreading. Losing Root for 24 kept Pakistan interested, but Emilio Gay toughed it out in the gloom to reach stumps unbeaten on 30; England 81 for three, light years ahead in the game.

Robinson’s astonishing figures of 13-6-11-4 set him on the way for a probable third man-of-the-match award in a row and continued his unexpected resurgence. Rarely did his pace go above 78mph, he just landed the ball time and again on a length and let movement off the seam do the rest.

News.title: I’ve lived in Norfolk for more than 30 years. Here’s how to explore England’s windswept east
News.content:
Norfolk’s vast sandy beaches are its chief draw for visitors: even on the busiest summer day there is always space for games, kite-flying or a family picnic in the dunes. Boating, crabbing, digging for cockles and wading in creeks provides hours of entertainment for all.

But there’s much more to Norfolk’s coast than its beaches. It’s also a landscape of dense pine forest and large expanses of salt marsh, which flush purple with sea-lavender in August. Birdlife is astonishingly rich, and wildflowers include yellow-horned poppies and lilac-flowering sea pea.

Inland, the undulating countryside and sleepy flint-built villages are perfect for gentle cycling, walking or touring by car. Grand stately homes make enjoyable days out, and almost every village has a sublimely beautiful medieval church at its centre.

Lively Georgian towns such as Burnham Market and Holt offer quirky shopping – and, wherever you are, you’re never far from an atmospheric pamment-floored pub serving local ales, or an excellent delicatessen selling the region’s specialities. Look out for pungent cheeses, smoked fish and salt-marsh flavoured honey.

The latest transfer news from the Premier League and further afield, including updates on Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and many more

Welcome to Mirror Football's transfer blog for Saturday, August 29.

Bradley Barcola's seemingly imminent transfer from Paris Saint-Germain to Liverpool has continued to dominate the headlines, as one of the most exciting sagas of the summer is set to come to an end. It is claimed that an agreement has been reached between the two clubs, and that the Reds will pay a total of £123million for the 23-year-old winger.

That's broken down into a guaranteed £106m, as well as £17m in add-ons. A move to Anfield is expected to be formalised in the coming days. Barcola isn't the only talent that could bolster Andoni Iraola's first-team in the coming days, however.

The Reds are also reportedly setting their sights on Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr, with Nicolo Schira claiming that an agreement in principle over a contract running to 2031 has been met between Liverpool and the player. A new bid is expected to come, after Palace rebuffed an initial offer of around £51m.

In the English capital, meanwhile, Arsenal are still chasing Julian Alvarez's signature, with his future with Atletico Madrid up in the air. The 26-year-old centre-forward has missed training thrice this week, albeit, citing illness as the reason for his absence, as the Gunners prepare to table a £130m bid to secure his signature.

Manchester United's search for a new left-back also runs on, having seemingly ditched their pursuit of Lews Hall as a result of Newcastle United refusing to sell the 21-year-old. While Alejandro Balde was considered an ideal candidate, the 22-year-old has now told Hansi Flick that he wants to fight for his place at Barcelona.

Stay tuned as we bring you all of the latest news in our transfer blog below...

Sports.title: Newcastle get last laugh vs rotten Spurs as Sandro Tonali flops vs former club - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
Newcastle get last laugh vs rotten Spurs as Sandro Tonali flops vs former club - 5 talking points

SPURS 0-2 NEWCASTLE: Matthias Jaissle has his first victory as Newcastle boss with the Magpies having put on a second-half show at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium

View 3 Images Yoane Wissa celebrates his first goal of the season (Image: Getty Images)

A rejuvenated Yoane Wissa helped Newcastle to a 2-0 win against Tottenham on Saturday afternoon.

‌



Spurs, aiming to recover from their opening-day defeat by Brentford, struggled once again against their North East opponents. And they found themselves 1-0 down just after the hour mark as Anthony Elanga scored with a lethal finish.

‌



Wissa then doubled Newcastle's lead with an acrobatic effort from a corner, leaving Spurs staring at back-to-back defeats at the start of the campaign and without a single goal.

‌



Newcastle in the meantime have had a positive start to life under new boss Matthias Jaissle.

Here are all of the talking points from the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Elanga again

After scoring in Newcastle's opening game of the season against Liverpool, Anthony Elanga was at it again in North London. The winger had twice threatened before he actually scored, having gone close early on, while he was also unfortunate not to scored having gone past Spurs goalkeeper Antonín Kinský.

But just after the hour mark, he did get his goal. Nico Gonzalez's brilliant crossfield ball was nodded down by Admir Dedic.

Elanga picked up the ball, span and then placed it with pinpoint precision into the bottom corner via the post. Having only scored three times last season, Elanga looks a good bet to beat that record this season.

‌



View 3 Images Anthony Elanga has two goals from as many games this season (Image: Getty Images)

Wicked Wissa

While Elanga faced severe criticism for his displays last season, the same could certainly be said of Yoane Wissa. The forward struggled in his debut campaign at St James' Park following a move from Brentford.

But he looks a player reborn this term. He was brilliant against Liverpool and now has his first goal of the season after hooking home acrobatically after Spurs failed to clear a corner.

‌



It might be early days but if Newcastle can get both Wissa and Elanga firing throughout the season, they could be in for a very promising year indeed.

Porro a problem

Not necessarily for Spurs, but Pedro Porro is a problem for opposition teams. The Spanish defender had a brilliant World Cup and looks set to be a major star for the North London side again.

He had two brilliant opportunities to open the scoring in the first-half, having had an effort blocked by Lewis Hall, while he also lifted a couple of efforts over the crossbar.

‌



Despite two defeats, Porro has been a bright spot for Tottenham.

Tonali's tough reception

It wasn't quite a baying St James' Park but Tottenham midfielder Sandro Tonali still received a less-than-welcoming response by supporters of his former club Newcastle. The £92.5m midfielder saw his every touch booed by those assembled in the away corner of the ground.

He was taken off in the 75th minute to loud cheers from Newcastle fans. While his reception will have left a bitter taste, the result might even more so.

‌



View 3 Images Tonali was making his first appearance against former club Newcastle (Image: Getty Images)

Spurs' poor home record continues

Roberto De Zerbi had yet to lose on home soil since being appointed as Tottenham boss. But he's not quite managed to escape their dreadful record at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

The North London side were woeful on their own patch last season, winning just three Premier League games in all. If this display is anything to go by, it could potentially be another season of pain for the home supporters - and that's simply not good enough given all of the money they have spent this summer.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola fumes at officials and Alisson SMASHES board after Liverpool controversy
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola fumes at officials and Alisson SMASHES board after Liverpool controversy

Liverpool were angry with fourth official Tim Robinson because he didn't have the substitution boards ready in time for a triple change and Nottingham Forest subsequently scored

View 4 Images Andoni Iraola criticised the officials post-match (Image: TNT Sports)

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has questioned the professionalism of the fourth official after a controversial incident in the 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forest.

‌



Victor Munoz's late strike earned a point for Liverpool in Saturday's early kick-off at Anfield after a chaotic game. Iraola was honest about his side's poor performance in the first half, but also raged at the officials, who he felt may have inadvertently benefited Forest.

‌



The Liverpool boss had been trying to make a triple substitution in the build-up to Forest's second goal, which came via Morgan Gibbs-White from the penalty spot after Alisson fouled Neco Williams in the box. But fourth official Tim Robinson didn't have the substitution boards ready in time, meaning Forest were able to take a quick throw-in and catch Liverpool off guard.

‌



Alisson dived in at Williams' feet, fouling the Forest wingback and Gibbs-White scored the spot-kick to make it 2-1. Iraola was seen shouting at Robinson while he attempted to get the numbers on the boards and the Spaniard hasn't cooled down in his post-match interview.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

"I will analyse the penalty, yes, but a professional fourth official cannot take three minutes for the subs," Iraola told TNT Sports.

‌



"We gave the subs two or three minutes before. I was angry because in the previous stop we couldn’t make it. And before the throw-in I said 'let’s do it now', but I don’t know how to explain it but it has taken ages to prepare two boards."

Alisson was furious with the penalty decision and was booked for his protestations to referee Sam Barrott. The veteran goalkeeper was still seething at full-time, too, and was seen kicking one of the substitution boards, smashing a hole in it.

View 4 Images Tim Robinson didn't have the boards ready to make the triple change (Image: TNT Sports)

‌



Former Premier League referee Graham Scott wrote on X: "The subs boards are not fit for purpose. Each number has to be entered manually, and they only count up one at a time. Entering number 38 on its own could take several seconds and there are six numbers to plug in here.

"Also, the sponsors’ advertising makes them heavy and unwieldy, which is why the 4th has them on the ground. In UEFA comps the clubs have to enter the numbers themselves, which means they can get the subs done quicker. The PL only did this during Covid.

"The 4th official would have had to check and double check the names and numbers of all six players involved in the substitutions against the official team sheet in case the club has made an error, which happens frequently enough to make such checks necessary."

‌



4 View 4 Images The damaged substitutes board after Alisson's kick 4 View 4 Images Alisson was furious with the penalty call (Image: Jan Kruger/Getty Images)

The draw was Liverpool's second in succession to start the 2026/27 campaign following the 2-2 draw against Newcastle last weekend. Dan Ndoye put Forest ahead after Liverpool failed to deal with a long ball.

‌



Alexander Isak equalised with a tap-in from Cody Gakpo's cross before the penalty put the away side ahead once more. Munoz then earned Liverpool a point in the 82nd minute with a powerful shot off the underside of the crossbar.

"It’s not the result we want. I think two very different halves," Iraola said. "I think we were poor in the first half, even being poor, we were unlucky in terms of their goal.

"We were very poor in the first half. We were much better in the second half. The intensity was different - if you are going to lose, you have to lose like in the second half. A lot more intense, more threatening, happy with the second half, but it was late in the game."

Sports.content:
Steven Gerrard delivers huge verdict on Liverpool's £123m transfer deal for Bradley Barcola

Liverpool are set to sign Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola for a reported £123m fee, and Steven Gerrard has given his verdict on the arrival of the 23-year-old at Anfield

View Image Steven Gerrard has spoken on Bradley Barcola (Image: PA)

Steven Gerrard has explained that Bradley Barcola can "take Liverpool to the next level," as the club look to complete a £123million transfer for the Paris Saint-Germain man. The Reds have pursued the winger for the bulk of the summer window.

A move that was considered nigh-on impossible a matter of months ago, Barcola falling behind Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue in the pecking order with PSG, coupled with the arrivals of Maghnes Akliouche and Mika Godts in the French capital, quickly changed matters.

Taking into account the 23-year-old's ability and importance to Luis Enrique's first-team, a £145m price tag was slapped on Barcola. However, Liverpool have now managed to shave that price down to £106m plus £17m in add-ons.

‌

"Growth. He can evolve into an even better player which is very exciting. But it's the type of level of player that's gonna help take Liverpool to the next level.. So I think it's a fantastic deal."

Man Utd striker on Atletico Madrid radar as Julian Alvarez transfer plan made

Atletico Madrid are determined to keep hold of Julian Alvarez but in the event he does leave the Spanish club could turn to Manchester United for a replacement

View 2 Images Joshua Zirkzee has been linked with a move away from Manchester United (Image: Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)

Atletico Madrid are keeping tabs on Joshua Zirkzee as they make plans should Julian Alvarez leave the Spanish capital late in the transfer window.

‌



Alvarez's future has been front and centre for much of the summer with the Argentine expressing a desire to leave as he skipped training this week. Barcelona are his preferred destination but Atletico are refusing to sell to their La Liga rivals.

‌



The only obvious exit route is Arsenal, who retain an interest but the £100m plus price tag could prove an issue. If any move does materialise it will be in the final days of the window and Atletico could look to Manchester United's out of favour Dutchman as a replacement.

‌



The Daily Mail reports that Atletico are tracking his situation with Zirkzee poised to move on in the coming days. Juventus have been heavily linked throughout the window but Fiorentina now look to be leading the race ahead of a possible loan move.

Zirkzee's best football came when he was i Italy with Bologna, which prompted United to sign him two summers ago. However he's struggled for goals and the club have since poured money into their frontline, adding the likes of Benjamin Sesko and Bryan Mbeumo, which has pushed Zirkzee down the pecking order.

‌



Marcus Rashford has also returned to Old Trafford following 18 months away from the club. He came off the bench in the opening day defeat at Hull and would appear to be above Zirkzee in Michael Carrick's mind.

Since moving to Manchester for £36.5million the Dutchman has scored just nine times in two seasons - coming up with two goals last term.

View 2 Images Julian Alvarez wants out of Atletico Madrid (Image: Angel Martinez, Getty Images)

‌



Atletico have relied on Alvarez to be their main man in attack, but would still possess quality even if he does leave. Diego Simeone has the likes of Norwegian Alexander Sorloth and former Atalanta man Ademola Lookman among his options.

The club's CEO Gil Marin has doubled down on the fact Alvarez will now head to the Nou Camp. He told Spanish media: "I’ve been in the football world for more than 30 years. My word is one of the few things I have. As long as I am CEO, Julian Alvarez will not be transferred to FC Barcelona. That is absolutely certain."

Sports.title: Fery's dreams of maiden ATP Tour title ended in Winston-Salem Open final
Sports.content:
Arthur Fery's hopes of landing his maiden ATP Tour title at Winston-Salem Open was ended in emphatic fashion by Peruvian Ignacio Buse on Saturday.

From 3-3 in the first set, Fery lost six straight games before eventually going down 6-3 6-2 to Buse.

The promising 22-year-old clinched his second trophy of the season having lifted his maiden tour-level trophy at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg.

Fery was aiming to add to his already memorable season having reached the semi-finals at Wimbledon.

With his spot in the Winston-Salem final, 24-year-old Fery has moved up to a new career high of No 33 in the live rankings, overtaking Cameron Norrie as the British No 1 in doing so.

Eight weeks ago, Fery was outside the top 100.

More to follow...

Sports.title: De Zerbi highlights biggest problem at Spurs as Carra slams 'worst start'
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi believes changing the mentality at Tottenham is his biggest challenge after Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher said their start to the season "couldn't have gone any worse" following defeat to Newcastle.

Tottenham have lost their first two Premier League games without scoring a goal and sit at the bottom of the league despite spending £320m in the transfer market this summer.

De Zerbi's side had been better than Newcastle until Anthony Elanga struck the opener midway through the second half, with Spurs unable to respond and conceding another when Yoane Wissa hooked in from close range.

Asked whether mentality was the biggest issue he faces, De Zerbi said: "You are right, yes. It's the biggest problem, it's the biggest challenge, the biggest target is to find the right mentality.

"Unfortunately you can't buy the mentality in the transfer market. Football is like magic: you can change many players in one window of the transfer market, and you can find the balance immediately, or you need more time. I would like to achieve this target quickly, as soon as possible, because it's crucial to play football.

"But the plan, the project of the club, what we are doing to rebuild a new team with new players, is a great plan, is a great project, and I have no doubt about the result of this project."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League match between Tottenham and Newcastle

De Zerbi reinforced his belief that this season would be different to Spurs' previous two, which have seen them finish 17th in the past two seasons.

He said: "I'm disappointed with the result, and I'm sorry for the fans, for the environment, because after two defeats, maybe somebody can think it's the same story, the same as the last two seasons. I have no doubt it's not like this. I can't change my opinion for two defeats.

"I have big, big confidence in the qualities of my players. At the end, when we become a team, when we improve the connection between the players, when we improve the quality of the play, when we improve the defensive space, this group, with me or with another coach, nothing changes, because they are two good players.

"I'm sorry for the club, because they are building a great squad, but maybe now we are not ready yet, for many, many reasons."

'Tottenham will go into market again'

Sky Sports' Carragher said on co-commentary at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium that he reckons Spurs will sign another player after their poor start.

"Tottenham's start to the season couldn't have gone any worse," he said. "But it's going to take time at Tottenham. A lot of new players have come in; they've paid top dollar, but they're quality players, certainly in the midfield area, like [Mateus] Fernandes and [Sandro] Tonali.

"We saw signs today in terms of [Jan Paul] Van Hecke on the ball, but it won't be finished. I think there will be more to come.

"It's natural that people will panic a little and Tottenham will go into the market again, there's no doubt about it.

"Not just because they've lost twice, but it makes you more decisive. If you've won both games and a couple of games and some of the players looked alright, you'd look at a couple of deals and think 'maybe we're OK, maybe we give those players until Christmas'.

"That certainly won't be the case on the back of two really bad defeats."

'Spurs project will take time'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Redknapp blamed Tottenham captain Micky van de Ven for 'jogging back' when Anthony Elanga was closing in on Newcastle's opening goal

Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp called for patience on Saturday Night Football.

"There's a lot of new players at Spurs and it's going to take time," he said. "The manager has got a jigsaw puzzle and he's got to figure out how to fit the players in, what system to use, who the best three players are in midfield.

"There are going to be teething problems. I also look at the senior players and players like [Micky] Van de Ven didn't do enough to lead today and certainly with the goals.

"Players who have been there for a long time can do better."

Sports.title: Lavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of soul and spine | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
Time for Tottenham to start panicking? This is, of course, a subtle trick question. Tottenham is one of those clubs that never actually stops panicking. They panic when they concede and they panic when they score. They panic when they have the ball and they panic when someone else does. They have a coach in Roberto De Zerbi whose face evokes a state of permanent alarm, the expression of a man perpetually having a toilet door opened on him. One year they even managed to panic their way to the Europa League. For the ever-rattled Spurs fan, this club is less a treasured devotion and more a lifelong haunting, broken up by occasional panic substitutions.

You could intuit that sense of encrusted resignation pretty much from the moment Anthony Elanga’s improvised shot kissed the post and trickled over the line to give Newcastle the lead. Since beating Aston Villa 4-1 in late 2024, Tottenham have gone behind 44 times in all competitions and come back to win precisely zero of them. There is something innate and endemic here, a chronic case of Long Tottenham for which – despite the new coach, the new leadership structure and more than a third of a billion pounds in transfer fees – there remains no proven cure. Yoane Wissa’s clincher was of zero surprise to anyone.

And so welcome back to the temple of pain, the Theatre of Everyone Else’s Dreams, a stadium that fittingly still has no naming rights because pretty much every visiting side gets to own the place. Over the past 12 months, Aston Villa have won the same number of domestic fixtures at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (two) as Tottenham. Unai Emery’s men may well get the chance to retake their lead here in three weeks’ time. In the meantime it was Newcastle, with one clean sheet in their last 18 matches, who feasted on Tottenham’s neuroses, stayed tight and stayed patient, waited for the train that always arrives.

Perhaps as Matthias Jaissle’s team climbed all over the duels and the second balls there was also a certain reassuring symbolism here: a lesson in the enduring value of culture over commerce. Newcastle have lost half a team but kept their soul; Tottenham have bought half a team and are still searching for theirs. There were inevitable boos for Sandro Tonali, who was actually fine: one of those rare Tottenham players who actually treasures the ball and wants to do interesting things with it. Alongside him Mateus Fernandes was restless, classy, excellent. Omar Marmoush on his debut looked fit and sharp. But of course the individuals were never the problem here.

View image in fullscreen Sandro Tonali tussles with Anthony Elanga. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

The problem was the little things: the lost headers, the fractional pauses on the ball that kill momentum, the rushed shots, the extra touches, the tackles not quite committed to, the barely perceptible signs of a deep-rooted softness. Take Elanga’s goal, which sprang from an unpressed Nico González long ball, a poorly challenged Amar Dedic header, a cool turn and finish. Three very simple things in a row, at least two of which should probably have been prevented. No screaming howler or smoking gun here. Just a run of lost battles, a sum of marginal flaws, a team that for all its moments of promise and competence has not yet been welded together into a coherent whole.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How De Zerbi fixes this is anyone’s guess. It feels increasingly clear that for all the new blood there is still a kind of generational trauma here, perhaps dating back to the injury crisis of 2024-25, when a threadbare squad was pushed beyond the boundaries of wellness and sanity. For the veterans of that campaign, your Archie Grays and Micky van de Vens, your Destiny Udogies and Rodrigo Bentancurs, you occasionally glimpse that accumulated tension in the 50-50 tackles and big physical clashes, the sense of players still not quite trusting their bodies. And oppositions really do pick up on this stuff. Right now there is a clear blueprint for beating Tottenham: compete, do the simple things well, and eventually bully them into playing your game.

How much worse does this get before it gets better? Are Spurs fans ultimately in for another season of discontent and disgruntlement, of taking an unhealthy interest in the latest score from the Coventry Building Society Arena? The instinct here is still to be patient and wait for the required chemistry to develop. But what if two defeats become four, or six? What if it’s November and the top scorer is still somehow Richarlison with two? How does a club so medicinally addicted to panic possibly avoid it?

Quietly, there is now some ridiculous creative talent at this club. The signings of Marmoush and Sávio, the new-look midfield, the return of Mohammed Kudus and Dominic Solanke, the prospect of James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski and Xavi Simons to come. A World Cup finalist in Marcos Senesi sitting unused on the bench. It feels inconceivable that Tottenham could be in relegation trouble again. But as with so many clubs before them, Tottenham are discovering that buying new footballers is the easy part. Growing a spine will take considerably longer.

Sports.title: Iraola’s Liverpool start slowly again but Muñoz strike denies Nottingham Forest
Sports.content:
A malfunctioning electronic board will not have been on anyone’s bingo list of Liverpool complaints for the first Anfield game of Andoni Iraola’s tenure, but others sounded all too familiar. A slow start, a lack of intensity and defensive shortcomings were again evident as Liverpool salvaged a point against Nottingham Forest, while showing stronger foundations are required along with the excitement of £123m Bradley Barcola.

In front of some of the billionaires behind Liverpool, Iraola’s opening act on home soil offered more food for thought than the feast they may have been expecting. Forest were good value for the second 2-2 draw of the new Liverpool head coach’s reign and created enough clear openings to justify their frustration at the final outcome. A superb finish from Liverpool’s summer signing Víctor Muñoz cancelled out Morgan Gibbs-White’s penalty, after Alexander Isak had done the same to Dan Ndoye’s opener.

“I’ve got two emotions,” said Oliver Glasner. “I’m very proud of the performance and how many chances we created, but I’m disappointed with the result. It could and should have been a win, but after 60, 65 minutes our defending was not as clinical.”

Iraola’s irritations veered from his team’s first-half display to the bizarre situation of being unable to make a triple substitution because the assistant’s electronic board would not work. Liam Delap, Forest’s record signing who made a good impression, took a quick throw that led to the visitors’ second goal while Ryan Gravenberch, Rio Ngumoha and Kostas Tsimikas waited to come on.

Watching on from the directors’ box were Liverpool’s prospective new vice-chair Amit Bhatia and his father-in-law, the Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal. Bhatia and Mittal, who has given financial backing to 1892 Holdings acquiring a 38% stake in Liverpool, were the invited guests of John W Henry. Jeff Bezos and Eduardo Saverin, other members of the consortium, were not in attendance. The club’s principal owner was present to witness the start of a brave new era. Turns out it looked very much like the old one, even down to Dominik Szoboszlai ending the game at right-back.

After a rousing tribute before kick-off to Kevin Keegan Liverpool were soon exposed by the pace and movement of the Forest attack. Long balls released Ndoye behind the defence twice in the opening six minutes and, while the attacking midfielder lost his footing on both occasions, Liverpool failed to deal with the source of their problems.

View image in fullscreen Víctor Muñoz marks his first league start with Liverpool’s equaliser. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

Forest carried the only consistent threat in the first half with Igor Jesus, thwarted by Jérémy Jacquet’s fine intervention, Ndoye and Igor Jesus again having chances before the breakthrough. Having cleared a Forest corner, Liverpool were undone by Matz Sels’s long clearance back over their defence to Igor Jesus.

The striker, just onside, held up the goalkeeper’s delivery despite the close attentions of Jacquet and Alexis Mac Allister to find Gibbs-White, who rolled a simple pass to the unmarked Ndoye. The Switzerland international steered a precise finish low beyond Alisson’s left hand.

Anfield erupted shortly afterwards when Florian Wirtz swept a smart finish on the turn inside Sels’s right post. A much-needed goal for Liverpool and their £116m playmaker, however, was disallowed by the video assistant referee for offside against Jeremie Frimpong in the buildup.

Patience in Frimpong is in short supply at Anfield judging by the exasperation that greeted his poor crossing and defensive toils. Iraola would replace both of his full-backs before the afternoon was over.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Liverpool were indebted to Alisson for denying Forest a second goal on the stroke of half-time. Ola Aina flew past Muñoz before picking out Igor Jesus near the penalty spot. Alisson produced a superb, crucial save to turn the striker’s first-time shot on to his crossbar.

View image in fullscreen Morgan Gibbs-White restores Nottingham Forest’s lead from the penalty spot. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

The Brazilian’s intervention assumed greater significance when Liverpool levelled on the hour. Cody Gakpo, a transfer target for Manchester City and Tottenham, gave a timely reminder of his quality when receiving Wirtz’s pass and spinning away from two defenders, Neco Williams and Murillo, in one movement. He then supplied a perfect pass across the face of the goal for Isak to tap home.

Delap’s quick-thinking caught Liverpool cold – Jacquet and Frimpong in particular – as his throw-in released Williams into the area with the defenders asleep. The former Liverpool full-back flicked a shot high and wide of the goal before being felled by the keeper, who was booked for protesting the harsh penalty decision. Gibbs-White swept an emphatic penalty kick to the keeper’s right as Alisson dived left.

Liverpool, improved by the substitutions, fought back for a second time when Wirtz pierced the defence with an excellent pass behind Murillo to Muñoz. The £34.5m summer signing from Osasuna marked his home debut with a brilliant finish off the underside of the crossbar to rescue a point for Iraola’s work in progress.

Sports.title: No country for old men: Premier League grind is why managers are getting younger
Sports.content:
One of the problems with getting older is that you’re never quite sure whether it’s you or them. Is the world really changing, or is it just you, struggling to adapt? There’s a milestone in life, probably as you’re contemplating university or a first job, when you realise you’re watching a footballer who is younger than you. Then, 15-20 years later, you realise you’re watching a manager who is younger than you. And 15-20 years after that, especially if you’re watching the modern Premier League, you realise that almost every manager is younger than you.

At which you do two things: give thanks for David Moyes; and check to see whether it’s actually happening, or whether this is just the football equivalent of the policemen-getting-younger cliche.

It turns out it is true. Managers used to be ashen-faced men with nicotine-grey hair dressed in the sports jackets of grim experience. They spoke with a rasping melancholy of the depths of human fallibility and of fates that were not to be trusted. Now they’re trim, sprightly figures in T-shirts, convinced that analytics can explain the world.

There are fewer Premier League managers now aged 50 or over than at any point in the past 20 years: only four, and two of those have only just made it over the threshold. Moyes is 63 (three months younger than José Mourinho, which, like Aberdeen being further west than Bristol, is a fact both true and too counterintuitive to be worth believing). Then there is Unai Emery at 54, Oliver Glasner at 52 and Régis Le Bris at 50. Most Premier League managers are in their 40s, with the youngest two Matthias Jaissle, 38, and Fabian Hürzeler, 33.

This is not coincidence; rather it seems the result of two interconnected trends. Even at the turn of the century, when Mourinho was starting out, it was unusual for a manager not to have played the game to at least a reasonable level, which meant they were starting their managerial careers in their mid-thirties. That’s still the route many take – Andoni Iraola, Michael Carrick, Gary O’Neil or Álvaro Arbeloa, for instance.

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola’s first appointment as head coach was at AEK Larnaca in 2018, aged 35. Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP

But there’s also a recognition, to use Arrigo Sacchi’s phrase, that a jockey does not need first to have been a horse. Coaching is regarded as a job in its own right, requiring a very different skillset to playing. Hürzeler came through the youth systems at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich but, aged 22, in part because of an ankle injury, decided to focus on coaching.

Jaissle was a member of the Hoffenheim side that soared through the divisions to win promotion to the Bundesliga before knee and achilles tendon injuries ended his playing career at 26. The early switch into coaching seems particularly common in Germany: Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann have similar stories.

That greater receptiveness to career coaches explains the wave of younger managers. But there are also fewer older coaches.

In part it may be coincidence: an experienced generation – Sam Allardyce, Tony Pulis and Alan Pardew – grew old together. That the process occurred just as many of their tactical characteristics – low blocks, direct play, a focus on set pieces – re-entered the mainstream may not simply be irony. The old must be cast out before it is reinvented as new; the modish cannot be represented by a 60-something football man.

But it’s also because modern management is exhausting. At Ipswich, Kieran McKenna would have his coaches present their plans to him for the day at 6am, altering anything he felt wasn’t quite right. That plan would be sent to the staff at the training ground to set up all the various pitches and drills. McKenna would then go to check everything was laid out properly. It was all extraordinarily detailed; everything was marked out, down to where players should stand when they weren’t directly involved and where water bottles would be placed.

During sessions, McKenna would walk between each unit, stepping in to offer advice and make amendments. After sessions, coaches would watch them back and report to McKenna on what could be improved before planning the next day’s drills to be presented at 6am the following morning.

View image in fullscreen Kieran McKenna’s relentless coaching at Ipswich was exhausting so it was no surprise he needed a break following their third promotion in five years. Photograph: Cat Goryn/Action Images/Reuters

During 11 v 11 practice games, McKenna would be the only one who coached. Over his five years at Ipswich, no drill was ever repeated in exactly the same form; repetition and possible staleness were to be avoided at all costs. Little wonder that after a third promotion in five seasons at the club, he felt exhausted, in need of a break rather than taking on an uneven fight in an ungrateful Premier League that could only sap his reserves further.

Brian Clough would take holidays during the season. He would turn up only infrequently at training. His input was sharp, erratic, impressionistic. Four decades on, a top-level manager is running a team of coaches and analysts that probably outnumbers the players with whom he has direct contact.

He cannot simply ignore the board until he needs money for a signing but has to manage up to whatever structure of sporting directors exists above him. He often will have little autonomy, although the success of Mikel Arteta, who has a more traditional role and seems to micromanage everything at Arsenal, may change that. And he is liable to be sacked after a month of poor form. The pressure is enormous, the margin for error minute.

That perhaps explains why so many top managers are now drifting into international football. Management, it’s commonly said, is a drug, but perhaps that fix is more palatable when it is delivered in five doses spread over a season, plus a major tournament every other year, rather than in the relentless drudgery of the club game. Carlo Ancelotti took his break from the club game at 66, Jürgen Klopp at 56, Tuchel at 50. None have demonstrated any great desire to return to the remorselessness of the league.

The Premier League may be the greatest stage in management. It may be where the best salaries are paid. It may be where every manager wishes to test himself. But it is an exhausting and capricious world that requires extraordinary reserves of energy, physical and mental. It is no theatre for old men.

Sports.title: James Tarkowski pounces at the death as Everton deny Bournemouth win
Sports.content:
Through wind and rain, the end of summer and a new era at the Vitality. In the Europa League, Milan will visit Dorset and trips to San Sebastián, Galicia, Norway and Czechia await Bournemouth. The stadium is under renovation, towering exoskeletons waiting to be filled, new security cordons to negotiate, the team under the new management of Marco Rose.

An unbeaten home record that stretches back to 3 January sustains, though so does Bournemouth’s tendency to concede late goals. James Tarkowski’s equaliser came in injury time. Other songs remain the same. Set pieces retain huge importance in the Premier League. From an outswinging corner from Hayden Hackney, Marcus Tavernier and Ryan Christie got in a terrible tangle. Tarkowski, unmarked, stabbed home an unlikely equaliser.

“It’s not even a set-piece goal, it was just slapstick,” said Rose. If Bournemouth’s stance is that Alex Scott remains whatever the offers, his first-half goal and overall performance will only add to the cachet. In a game played at regulation Premier League 1.5x speed, while others skidded on a sodden surface, the Channel Islander made time and space bend to his will. “A top performance,” said Rose of Scott.

Everton’s situation is volatile, racked with uncertainty, insurrection bubbling. Before kick-off, the away contingent sang for the 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong, linked with a £40m move to Nottingham Forest. Should he be sold “you’re going to have a riot on your hands”, fans warned.

As if joining the protest movement, David Moyes started a player Evertonians hope does not follow the decades-long drain of young players sold. Wayne Rooney, John Stones, Francis Jeffers, the list is long. Selling Armstrong to a peer in Forest will cut yet deeper. “It would be a club decision,” said Moyes, disassociating himself from any sale, though not ruling it out. “I don’t really want to talk about it,” he said, before talking about it.

Finances and regulations dictate that every Everton player has a price, is a bargaining chip. The scorer of last season’s winning goal at Bournemouth, Jack Grealish, may return from Manchester City as part of a swap deal with Iliman Ndiaye. Such are the equations supporters must accept.

Still, Everton began confidently enough. Eight shots registered in the first 30 minutes, beginning with an attempt from Jarrad Branthwaite, another jewel, though one whose fitness record dampens interest.

When Bournemouth found their momentum, Rayan came to the fore, Vitaliy Mykolenko struggling with the Brazilian’s incursions. Scott increased in influence, socks rolled down, gliding across the turf. He was calmness personified in controlling Evanilson’s pass, dropping his shoulder and drilling his shot beyond Jordan Pickford.

View image in fullscreen The impressive Alex Scott scores just before the break to give Bournemouth the lead. Photograph: Matt Impey/Shutterstock

Moyes’s fusty reputation belies his indulgence of talent if players marry aesthetics with hard yards. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall is delightful to watch, as can be Tyrique George, while Ndiaye and Armstrong also fit the School of Science ethos. Yet soccernomics, an expensive legal dispute with Burnley and squad cost ratios are likely to diminish Everton.

The manner of Scott’s goal, the defence far too open to Evanilson’s escape, offered reasons why Moyes, whatever the window brings, might soon cork the fizz. Were he able to add players, Barry clanking wide a chance laid on by Dewsbury-Hall suggested a striker would be high on his want list, despite Barry’s four goals this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The first half suggested Rose’s immediate influence on Bournemouth is increased directness, Evanilson chasing plenty of long balls. From the beginning of the second half, with Scott directing traffic and Adrien Truffert galloping from full-back, their interchanges frayed Everton’s resolve.

Three points should have been long secured by the time Christie and Tavernier collided. Pickford was kept very busy, he and Hackney combining to somehow deflect goal-bound efforts from Rayan and Evanilson.

“We could have scored a second goal two, three or four times and now we have to deal with a point,” said Rose. “I have to get used to the Premier League. It’s quite different. It’s always an open game.”

Moyes’s agitation was made apparent as his team ground the gears, only to feel the benefit of Bournemouth’s mishap. By then, Scott had departed to an ovation. It fell short of being a victory lap.

Sports.title: Amin Nabizada sparkles for Watford as draw puts pressure on West Ham’s Nuno
Sports.content:
When a club is an established part of English football’s upper echelons, plays its home games inside a 68,000-seater stadium, and promptly breaks the Championship transfer record following relegation from the top flight, there are expectations that naturally follow. By all accounts, West Ham were supposed to breeze through what is only meant to be a brief dalliance with a second-tier existence. To be winless three league matches into the season was inconceivable.

If the travelling contingent’s boos after this draw at Watford were fleeting, their subsequent burst of “you’re getting sacked in the morning” directed at their team’s manager left no ambiguity. No matter how embryonic this campaign is, the repeated impotency is already unacceptable, and now Nuno Espírito Santo is in the firing line.

A 46-game Championship season is long and there remains abundant time to turn things around. But when you suggest that spending £22m on Arne Engels is with a view to him playing in the Premier League – as Nuno did earlier this summer – you leave yourself little wriggle room when things do not follow the expectedly smooth course.

“We are a big club, we are favourites to go up,” said Nuno. “We have three games, we have two points. Who is happy? But me? I believe. I trust my boys. I work very hard with them. We are building a team. Things will change. I am positive.

“The fans are the most important part of our club and I respect them so much. I understand everything. I just ask again to keep believing, keep trusting us, keep going and we will try to reverse it. The win must come, hopefully on Tuesday [against fellow relegated side Wolves]. We need it.”

That this draw – which followed another against Burnley and defeat to Charlton – came against a Watford team openly treading water only emphasised West Ham’s struggles.

A side that only finished 16th last season has barely strengthened in the intervening months, with the lack of depth leaving new manager Alessio Dionisi no choice but to alter training sessions to cope with having so few first-team players at his disposal. A bench that included two goalkeepers sent a silent message to those tasked with providing Watford reinforcements in the closing days of the transfer window.

Yet after what was anticipated to be a horror start to the campaign – with fixtures against promotion favourites Southampton, Wrexham and West Ham – Dionisi’s side are unbeaten. The Italian admitted he did not know of Amin Nabizada before arriving in Hertfordshire, but few Championship followers are now unaware of the 19-year-old academy product’s unbridled talent now.

View image in fullscreen Nuno Espírito Santo is confident West Ham will quickly find their feet in the Championship. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA

The English-born Afghanistan international had never started a senior game prior to this season, but has been ever present in Dionisi’s side so far this campaign, frequently providing Watford’s most potent attacking threat. His second goal in three appearances put the hosts ahead when a neat stepover created sufficient space on the left side of the penalty area, and he delicately curled the ball over Mads Hermansen and into the top corner.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

For all that West Ham’s vigour rose as the match wore on, they ended it with just a solitary shot on target. A hefty dose of fortune was required for their equaliser, which arrived eight minutes after Nabizada’s opener. Watford’s culprit was Kévin Keben, who attempted to shepherd the ball out of play on his own goalline, only for Valentín Castellanos to nick it off him and prod across goal where it deflected off the unfortunate Mattie Pollock and into the Watford net.

As Jarrod Bowen increasingly exerted his influence on proceedings, so Watford dropped deeper and West Ham enjoyed the type of territorial dominance expected of a side with vast Premier League experience and an England international in their ranks. But it counted for little, with Watford coming closest to a winner when Iker Bravo’s shot deflected over following a rapid counterattack.

“We will gel, we will click and we are positive that, with the quality we have, we are going to do it,” insisted Nuno. If West Ham’s travelling fans are to be believed, time might be in short supply.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: on-song Durán lifts Celtic spirits in win over Falkirk
Sports.content:
Camilo Durán, in his preferred position of centre-forward, scored both goals for Celtic in their 2-1 win over Falkirk.

The Colombian hit two striker’s goals in the opening 29 minutes and also set up several teammates for chances. Falkirk improved after the break and their ambition was rewarded by Colby Donovan’s own goal in the 72nd minute.

The win continued Celtic’s perfect start to the domestic season, but it was preceded by a display of frustration over the club’s inability to secure Champions League qualification after a four-goal aggregate lead was squandered in Thursday’s 5-1 defeat by LASK.

The Celtic ultras mocked the club board’s declaration that they aim to be “world class” in everything they do with banners listing the teams who have beaten Celtic in the Champions League qualifiers in the past 14 years, below one that read “‘world class’ embarrassment”.

View image in fullscreen Fans hold up banners with the names of teams that have eliminated Celtic from Europe. Photograph: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock

However, fans got behind the team throughout the afternoon and one chant of “sack the board” emanating from the standing section did not take off around the rest of Celtic Park.

Hearts held firm at the end of a gruelling week to close out an unconvincing 2-1 home win over St Johnstone and climb to second in the table. The Jambos – buoyed by their midweek Conference League playoff triumph away to Rapid Vienna – were good value for their two-goal lead after James Wilson’s early strike was followed by a second that went down as an own goal from the Saints debutant Enes Alic.

But the hosts faded after the break and they were left clinging on in the closing stages after Ruari Paton pulled one back for the visitors early in the second half.

Dundee United produced a fine performance in the absence of their manager, Jim Goodwin, as they thrashed Kilmarnock 4-0 at Rugby Park. Goodwin was admitted to hospital on Thursday and the club said on Saturday morning the 44-year-old “continues to deal with an ongoing medical matter”.

His players, under the guidance of assistant Lee Sharp, did him proud as three first-half goals helped ease them to a first Premiership victory of the campaign. United, who had not scored in their previous three games in all competitions, were three up by 41 minutes thanks to Emmanuel Agyei’s opener, Zac Sapsford’s penalty and a Will Ferry beauty.

Jesse Randall added a late fourth as Killie conceded for the 13th time in three top-flight matches to remain bottom of the table without a point.

On Sunday, Rangers visit Aberdeen in a noon kick-off, three days after their elimination from the Conference League on penalties by Jablonec. Hibernian, who went out of the same competition against Gent, are at Dundee, while Motherwell, well beaten by Freiburg, travel to St Mirren.
