This is a developing story and we will bring further details as they become available.

World.title: Homeless Stann Creek man fined $105 for crack pipe
World.content:
Homeless Stann Creek man fined $105 for crack pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 39-year-old man who told the court he is homeless was fined $105 after pleading guilty to possession of a pipe used for smoking drugs.

Rugero Mazariego, originally from the Stann Creek Valley area, appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday morning.

Police said Mazariego was found earlier that day with a white metal pipe measuring about three inches in length and fitted with wire mesh. The object was described as being used or adapted for smoking drugs.

Mazariego pleaded guilty to the charge and told the court he would try to change his ways.

“I will try to do better if given the opportunity to do so,” he told the court.

As a first-time offender for the charge, Mazariego was fined $100 plus $5 in court costs. He has until September 30, 2026, to pay the fine or he will serve one month in prison.

World.title: Garrick Hemmans remanded after allegedly opening fire on Rio Bravo Crescent
World.content:
Garrick Hemmans remanded after allegedly opening fire on Rio Bravo Crescent

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-five-year-old Belize City resident Garrick Hemmans has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged with aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a shooting incident on Rio Bravo Crescent.

Hemmans, a labourer of the Fabers Road area, appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in Court #6 on Friday, where he pleaded not guilty to a single charge of aggravated assault with a firearm.

Police allege that on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, Hemmans intentionally and unlawfully assaulted a 32-year-old technician with a firearm.

According to police, the complainant reported that at around 7:28 p.m. he was standing in front of a yard on Rio Bravo Crescent when a maroon Nissan Murano approached from the direction of Tapir Street. He told investigators that the driver slowed the vehicle and that Hemmans, who was allegedly seated in the front passenger seat, pulled out a firearm and fired several shots in his direction.

The complainant reportedly ran behind a cement fence and escaped without injury. The vehicle then drove off in the direction of Fabers Road Extension.

Police processed the scene and reportedly recovered two 9mm Aguila-brand expended shells and a fragment. Investigators later located the Nissan Murano parked on Jimmy Dyer Street, where another 9mm Aguila-brand expended shell was reportedly found on the front passenger seat. The vehicle was impounded.

Hemmans was detained later that night and subsequently charged.

During Friday’s arraignment, Hemmans asked permission to address the court and began saying, “Two weeks ago, this young man…” before Senior Magistrate Dennison stopped him and cautioned that, because he was unrepresented, he should avoid making statements about the alleged incident that could potentially incriminate him.

Due to the firearm-related nature of the charge, bail was denied under the Crimes Control and Criminal Justice Act.

Hemmans was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 29, 2026.

World.title: Cooper’s Pen pledge
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) in dialogue with Cooper’s Pen resident Debbie Lewis (second right) during a tour of the community on Friday. Looking on are (from left) minister of state in the Office of the Prime Minister Senator Abka Fitz-Henley; Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett; and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern Tova Hamilton. Photo: Horace Hines

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has given a commitment to “personally oversee” the relocation of residents of Cooper’s Pen whose houses were demolished during a dispute over privately owned land, saying he may have to invoke emergency powers to get the process started by December.

Residents will be provided with a relocation grant to replace belongings damaged during the eviction, but they will have to pay for the land and utilities once they are resettled. Two sites within Trelawny are being contemplated for the subdivision which will house them.

Holness — who on Friday toured the community alongside Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett, Trelawny Northern Member of Parliament Tova Hamilton, and state minister in the Office of the Prime Minister Abka Fitz-Henley — said his intention is to move eligible residents into a properly planned community instead of shifting them from one informal settlement to another.

“My wish is that by December we could start the process of the relocation,” Holness told residents.

He cautioned, however, that the December timeline was not a firm commitment, given the number of factors involved, including the need for contractors and infrastructure works, as well as possible delays caused by weather.

“It means that I may have to use emergency powers to address some of the situation,” he said.

The prime minister also pointed out that of the two sites being contemplated, the one closer to Cooper’s Pen may not be large enough.

“I don’t believe we can accommodate all the legitimate claims that are here,” Holness said, explaining that by legitimate he meant individuals who had been acknowledged as squatters on the land before the court action and orders.

The lots will be surveyed and pegged, there will be roads, water, and electricity, and land titling will also be part of the plan.

But Holness was emphatic that the land would not be free.

Options available to residents, based on their circumstances, include long-term leases, outright purchase, and social housing arrangements for those assessed as unable to afford the cost.

Some residents who contribute to the National Housing Trust (NHT), he noted, could access their contributions to assist with acquiring the property.

For those found to have little or no means, the prime minster said there could be fully or heavily subsidised lots, with some contribution from residents through “sweat equity”.

“Government’s role is to make it affordable,” Holness said, adding that the objective was to put residents on a legitimate path to property ownership rather than perpetuate what he described as a “freeness” mentality.

He also explained the rationale behind the relocation grant.

“The Government couldn’t take up public taxpayers’ money and pay for damage caused by a private action,” he said, adding that the distinction was important to avoid setting a legal precedent that would lock the Government into being held responsible for similar circumstances in the future.

Holness framed the Cooper’s Pen saga as a pivotal moment in the country’s long-running battle with a culture of squatting.

“I see Cooper’s Pen as the watershed. This is the incident that must change Jamaica’s spatial settlement for the better,” he argued.

The prime minister said a social survey is already being conducted to determine who should benefit from the relocation programme. The Ministry of Housing has interviewed about 70 per cent of the occupants, he said, while the survey team is being augmented by the Social Development Commission along with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

The combined exercise, he said, will provide a clearer picture of the households, families, and vulnerable people in the community and help determine who qualifies for assistance.

Holness also warned that people who had not been living in the community before the demolition should not attempt to move in to take advantage of the Government’s response.

“I want to make it clear that anybody [who is] trying to scam the system, it won’t work!” he said.

“Bear in mind that we don’t have limitless resources, so the more people we have to accommodate, is the less you get,” he told residents.

He also reiterated that his Government does not condone or encourage squatting, adding that he has tasked Minister with Responsibility for Land Titling and Settlements Robert Montague to review the Government’s policies for dealing with squatter settlements and return with a broader proposal on regularisation and relocation.

Holness used the occasion to criticise previous administrations which, he argued, encouraged people to occupy land informally with the expectation that their status would eventually be regularised.

“The answer can’t be to acquire property illegally. The answer must be to create a process through which all Jamaicans — regardless of your colour, your class, your place of birth, your religion, your status in society — you have a fair opportunity to acquire property,” he said, adding that he was determined not to repeat those missteps.

Still, the prime minister struck a sympathetic tone with the displaced residents, saying the Government recognises the difficult circumstances in which they now find themselves.

“I don’t want any of you to feel as if the State has abandoned you. I don’t want you to feel shame, and I don’t want you to see the Government as your enemy,” he said.

“The fact is that you are also a victim of history and a victim of bad government policy… My objective is to make all of you here property owners,” he added.

World.title: ‘A master of the craft’
World.content:
Former Calabar Head Boy Dervan Malcolm, on one of the many outside broadcasts he did for Power 106.

THE Jamaican media fraternity lost one of its most distinctive voices on Thursday with the passing of veteran broadcaster Dervan Malcolm after a long illness.

Members of the media, political, business, and Diaspora communities were effusive in their tributes to Malcolm who entered the media landscape in 1993 at the now-defunct

Power 106 while still serving as head boy of Calabar High School.

Leading the tributes was Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, who remembered Malcolm for his “calm, distinct and trusted voice”.

“Through his work at Power 106 and especially his programme, Both Sides of the Story, he created space for meaningful conversations on the issues that matter to Jamaicans at home and in the diaspora.

“Dervan was a consummate communicator who used his platform to inform, educate, and empower. His commitment to public discourse, road safety, child protection, entrepreneurship, and the Jamaican Diaspora reflected a deep desire to make a positive difference,” said Holness as he expressed condolence to Malcolm’s family, friends, colleagues and the wider media fraternity.

“Jamaica has lost a respected broadcaster and a distinctive voice whose contribution will not be forgotten,” added Holness.

In the meantime, Opposition spokeswoman on information Nekeisha Burchell described Malcolm as “a super talent and a master of the broadcast craft”.

“Dervan Malcolm was blessed with a powerful, silky voice, but his gift went far beyond the quality of his voice. He was poised, controlled, and totally unruffled behind the microphone, with a signature style that was unmistakably his own.

“He was among that early generation of broadcasters who helped to shape Power 106 and define it as an informative, accessible, middle-of-the-road station where Jamaicans could engage seriously with the issues of the day while still being entertained,” said Burchell.

“Under the leadership of Newton James, Dervan and others helped to establish the character of the station. Even in his earliest programmes, his talent was evident. There was something wonderfully Jamaican about the call-in programmes he hosted. Each exchange felt familiar and authentic, while remaining respectful and entertaining. Dervan could connect with people from every walk of life without ever losing his composure or command of the programme,” added Burchell.

She said Malcolm’s extraordinary range distinguished him even among accomplished broadcasters.

“He was an adept voice impersonator who could portray characters with remarkable ease and precision, and his command of Spanish was another dimension of his talent. He would weave Spanish effortlessly into his broadcasts, never boastfully or simply for effect. You could leave his programme having learnt something new, sometimes even in another language. That was Dervan: Informed without being overbearing, confident without being boastful, authoritative without being disrespectful. His versatility reflected the breadth of the man and his mastery of communication,” said Burchell.

For his part, veteran journalist and head of Nationwide News Network Cliff Hughes said, with Malcolm’s death Jamaica has lost one of its most talented exponents of the art of broadcasting

“Blessed with a rare ability to communicate flawlessly, Dervan distinguished himself as a hard-working professional, a dedicated pro who evolved as an advocate of the diaspora community,” said Hughes.

The Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) also paid tribute to Malcom, noting that he “was a respected and influential voice in Jamaican broadcasting whose career spanned more than three decades”.

“He dedicated 31 years of service to the Independent Radio Company, building a reputation as a consummate professional, a trusted journalist, and a passionate advocate for public education and national development,” the PAJ said.

The PAJ pointed out that Malcolm’s journey into broadcasting was rooted in his success in the performing arts, including his participation in the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission’s Festival of the Performing Arts.

“Dervan represented the very best of Jamaican broadcasting and journalism. He understood that journalism is not simply about reporting what is happening; it is about helping people understand the issues that shape their lives,” PAJ President Dashan Hendricks said.

“His work with the diaspora is particularly noteworthy. We will remember Dervan for his professionalism, warmth and commitment to public service, all of which earned him the respect of colleagues and audiences alike,” Hendricks added.

The PAJ said that throughout Malcom’s “distinguished career”, he served in several key roles, including news presenter and editor, sportscaster, talk show producer and executive producer of programmes.

“In 2007, he launched and hosted Both Sides of the Story on Power 106 FM, a programme that became synonymous with informed and balanced public discourse. Through that platform, Dervan sought to educate, empower, and enlighten listeners while championing entrepreneurship and civic engagement,” the PAJ said.

It added that Malcom’s impact extended well beyond the studio as he was a strong advocate for road afety, child protection, and issues affecting Jamaicans living overseas.

“His dedication to the Jamaican Diaspora earned him numerous accolades, including the Union of Jamaican Alumni Associations’ Diaspora Ambassador in Media Award and the Team Jamaica Bickle Award for his service, journalism and commitment to Diaspora-related issues. His work was also recognised by the City of Los Angeles and the Jamaica Awareness Association of California,” the PAJ said, adding: “His voice may be silent, but his contribution to Jamaican journalism and public service will not be forgotten.”

World.title: Holness to tighten eviction rules
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness is welcomed by head of the Trelawny Police Division Superintendent Velonique Campbell during his visit to Cooper’s Pen, Trelawny, on Friday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness says he will move to tighten rules governing security-force involvement in evictions after displaced Cooper’s Pen residents complained about the conduct of police and soldiers during the early-morning demolition of their homes on privately owned land.

Holness said he will take the matter to the National Security Council to establish clear rules for how security forces should operate when supporting evictions.

“What is clear is that the operation, as it was executed, needs policy guidance,” Holness told residents during a tour of the community on Friday.

“That is where I come in as your prime minister, to make sure that subsequent operations are done according to the law, and with respect for your dignity and your rights,” he added.

Holness was responding to complaints from residents that members of the security forces had detained men from the community before the August 11, 2026 demolition which was carried out on a court order.

The action sparked questions about whether the Government knew the operation was going to take place.

On Friday, Holness reiterated that he had no prior knowledge of the demolition as he was neither informed nor consulted about when it would be carried out.

“Nobody wrote to me or advised me of it,” he said.

He also rejected suggestions that the operation was directed by his Administration, stressing that there is a separation between the Government and the police when it comes to police operations.

“No prime minister or minister of national security can direct police operations, and I want that to be clear,” Holness said.

He explained that while the Government is responsible for setting policy, it does not interfere with operational decisions by the police.

Holness said the police have a duty to maintain peace and may act preventively where there is a risk of loss of life or destruction of property.

“So yes, the police are in the right to support the eviction, to give support to the eviction process,” he said.

But the prime minister suggested that the authority of the security forces to support an eviction must be distinguished from the manner in which the operation is carried out.

It is that aspect of the process, he said, that will form part of the policy discussion with the security forces at the National Security Council.

Holness also accused some critics of using the Cooper’s Pen controversy for political gain, saying he is often blamed when problems arise.

“I represent the source of solutions, and equally, if solutions don’t come, and you need somebody to blame, it’s ultimately me,” he said.

“But I think it is being used in a political way to gain political advantage, and when it reaches that, then I have to stand up and say ‘No, it is not true’,” he added.

World.title: Vincent Chen eulogised as a man of quiet strength
World.content:
Vincent George Chen (Kasey Williams)

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — The patriarch and co-founder of SuperPlus Food Stores, Vincent George Chen, was on Thursday eulogised as a man of few words with a strong measure of work and worth evident in his legacy through his children.

Chen, the father of SuperPlus Chairman Wayne Chen and husband of the late Hyacinth Gloria Chen, died on August 17 at age 96.

Together the couple raised nine children — NCB Chairman Michael Lee-Chin, Wayne, Charles, Jody, Lisa, Bobby, Collin, Jeremy, and Richard.

“Dad was the product of two people — Edward, the frustrated scholar who came across an ocean from a small village [Ten Sim Wui in China] to start a life in a strange place, and Iris, who came from a small village [Kilmarnock in St Elizabeth], the descendant of rebellious and freed former African slaves. [They] came to Port Antonio,” Wayne Chen told congregants during the thanksgiving service held at Saint Paul of the Cross Cathedral in Mandeville.

He explained that there was strong economic activity in Port Antonio, which pulled many people there to settle.

“Port Antonio was the most prosperous town in Jamaica in the 1910s and the 1920s; it was the birthplace of the global fruit trade. The banana industry was king. People were making fortunes…” he said.

According to Chen, his father was sent to Kingston to learn the Chinese language, but left after two years.

“He felt bullied. He felt targeted and discriminated against. He said there was one particular housekeeper that, if anything went wrong… [said] he must be at the centre of it,” said Wayne Chen.

The elder Chen then went to Titchfield High for two years where he completed school.

“He… never sat the final exams. By the time it came around to pay exam fees [his father] didn’t have any money so fees were never paid, and there ended dad’s formal education,” said Wayne Chen.

From a young age Chen worked in grocery stores at Snowhill, St Margaret’s Bay, and Port Antonio.

While working in Port Antonio he met Hyacinth Gloria and got married. Life then quickly transitioned in what would become the growth and moving of their family and the building of many businesses.

“They started their own dry goods store (named Chen’s) on West Street in Port Antonio. My dad also worked as a projectionist in the Delmar Theatre. He became a salesman at the Singer sewing machine company and travelled all over [Portland],” said Wayne Chen.

In 1967 the family moved to Priory, St Ann, when Chen was promoted as regional manager at the company.

“In 1968 he was again transferred, this time to Mandeville, to be regional manager for the southern region. Mandeville became our home,” said Wayne Chen.

In 1969 Chen left the company and joined his wife at her toy and baby store, Humpty Dumpty, at Manchester Shopping Centre.

“In 1973, amidst the shortages and lack of import licences, they sold the toy and baby business and bought a supermarket in Christiana. In 1978 they sold it and were planning to immigrate to the United States. They stayed home for a year,” said Wayne Chen.

The couple then bought another supermarket in Mandeville, called L & M, at Park Crescent in the town centre.

“I won’t get into the long history of the grocery business,” Wayne Chen said in moving on to speak personally about his father, whom he described as a gentleman who was gracious, quiet, patient, iconic and a man of few words.

“Mom was the more voluble, outgoing partner. More people knew mom. She was the one everybody saw and heard first and most often,” he said, adding that his dad was the ying to his mom’s yang.

“They formed a strong and successful partnership that raised a large family and built a business,” said Wayne Chen.

“He worked very hard at it for decades in the business. Six days a week, very long hours — oftentimes working a second job after the shop had closed to provide for this large and growing family — but he always still found time for the Sunday drives,” said Wayne Chen.

The elder Chen was described as being very artistic.

“Mom used to say if dad had completed his education properly he would have been an engineer, but in hindsight… he may well have been an artist because he had a very natural talent for drawing, and his handwriting was unique and brilliant right up to the end,” said Wayne Chen.

Thursday’s thanksgiving service was attended by hundreds of people, among them business, health, education and civic leaders.

World.title: Leon Bailey among donors for St Andrew NC back-to-school treats
World.content:
Member of Parliament for St Andrew North Central Delano Seiveright engaging with children at the back-to-school treat in Donmair/Common in the constituency.

JAMAICAN international footballer Leon Bailey is among a number of individuals and private sector interests supporting a series of more than a dozen back-to-school treats across St Andrew North Central, through a coordinated effort led by Member of Parliament Delano Seiveright.

More than 1,500 children are expected to benefit from the treats which have already been held on Mannings Hill Road, Donmair/Common, Cassava Piece and Long Lane, with more scheduled across the constituency through the end of August and into early September.

Other treats are scheduled for Cameron Lane, Park Lane, 85 Red Hills Road, Boonan Gully, Lady Huggins, Mason Bush, 100 Lane, Shortwood Avenue, and Miller Heights/Ward Lane.

Bailey supported the Cassava Piece back-to-school treat, undertaken in partnership with the Cassava Piece Youth Upliftment Group and community volunteers.

According to Seiveright, he has been working with several new community groups while reaching out to business interests to mobilise school supplies, refreshments and other assistance for children.

Seiveright told the Jamaica Observer that the treats are deliberately being spread across communities rather than concentrated in a single major event, allowing local groups to take the lead in shaping activities for their children. The treats combine school supplies and educational support with food, refreshments, entertainment and family activities, while providing an opportunity for residents, volunteers, businesses and other stakeholders to work together.

In Donmair/Common, where children and families gathered at Common Sense Square on Saturday, community leader Shenae Fisher said the initiative was warmly received.

“The children and parents were genuinely excited. Back-to-school can be challenging for families, so this provided practical support while bringing the community together around our children. It lets them know that their community is behind them,” Fisher said.

The Donmair/Common activity was undertaken in partnership with the Donmair/Common Upliftment Youth Club, working alongside residents and supporters.

In Cassava Piece, community representative Aisha Stone said the involvement of community groups and outside supporters helped make the activity especially meaningful.

“The children were excited and the parents appreciated the support. It showed our young people that people believe in them and want to see them succeed. Every bit of assistance also helps families prepare for school,” Stone said.

Seiveright said the programme demonstrates what can be achieved by connecting community and youth organisations with businesses and individuals willing to assist.

“The community groups know their communities best. My role is to help bring people and resources together so we can reach as many children as possible,” Seiveright said.

He noted that the activities are also part of a broader effort to strengthen community organisations and encourage greater participation by young people in positive community initiatives.

Seiveright said sustained partnerships among residents, the private sector, law enforcement and other stakeholders are particularly important in communities where greater social intervention and opportunities for young people are needed.

He also acknowledged the private-sector companies, businesses, individuals, and Superintendent Randy Sweeney and the team from the St Andrew North Police Division, who have responded to requests for assistance, particularly those with connections to St Andrew North Central and its communities.

“A lot of people and organisations have quietly stepped forward to help. I am grateful to every supporter, including Leon Bailey, our private sector partners, Superintendent Sweeney and his team, and especially the community and youth groups and volunteers doing the work on the ground,” Seiveright said.

He added that while back-to-school expenses can place pressure on households, the programme is also intended to send children a broader message about education, discipline, ambition and community support.

World.title: GATHERING STEAM
World.content:
Saim Ayub of Jamaica Kingsmen hits a boundary during the men’s Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League match versus Saint Kitts and Nevis Patriots at Warner Park in Basseterre, Saint Kitts and Nevis, on August 27, 2026. (Photo: CPL T20)Photo: CPL T20

CAPTAIN Rovman Powell credited Saim Ayub and a disciplined bowling plan as Jamaica Kingsmen held their nerve to beat St Kitts and Nevis Patriots by 11 runs in their Caribbean Premier League (CPL) match at Warner Park, Basseterre, on Thursday.

The Pakistani hit 102 runs off 58 balls to rescue the Kingsmen from 4-63 from nine overs to post a total of 182 for 7 from 20 overs, then returned to take one for 20 runs as the Patriots were restricted to 171 for 6 from 20 overs.

The Kingsmen rebuilt through a 72-run, fifth-wicket stand, off 42 balls between Ayub and Powell, to steady the innings. Powell made 21 before falling to Wanindu Hasaranga. Ayub then added 29 with Keemo Paul for the sixth wicket, and 15 with Odean Smith for the seventh as Jamaica pushed to their total. Ayub hit six fours and eight sixes in his knock. Paul finished it with 25 not out off 13.

Only Hasaranga kept it tight for the Patriots with 2-18. Naseem Shah and Obed McCoy took two wickets each but went expensive.

“One of our overseas players stood up and won a game for us,” Powell said in a televised interview.

“You know, it’s good to see Saim get 100. Previously he has been a good performer in the CPL so it’s good to see that he came with us and is continuing that form,” he added.

With the ball, Powell said the plan was simple.

“I think that’s the benefit of watching them bowl on the wicket. We know it’s a good wicket, we know there’s a lot of runs on the wicket, but having said that, we also feel as a bowling group [that] if you have a plan, you can execute.

“We came with a clear plan at the halfway mark… we know that if we can bowl 24 yorkers, whenever we’re under pressure as a team we can do that — and then Hunain [Shah] led us beautifully in the bowling,” Powell explained.

Shah led the way for the Kingsmen with 2-23 from four overs, removing Mikyle Louis (9) and Patriots Captain Jason Holder (34). Jediah Blades also took 2-50 while Ayub broke the back of the chase by having Andre Fletcher caught and bowled for 55.

Paul got Johnson Charles (14) early to finish 1-31, and Dasun Shanaka was left on 35 not out as the Patriots fell short.

Powell, however, slammed the schedule, with the Kingsmen due to depart St Kitts on Friday to face Trinbago Knight Riders in Port of Spain on Saturday.

“Yeah, we fly out [Friday] and then and then we play the very next day,” he said.

“You know, it’s a tough schedule, and sometimes it’s a schedule that we as players say, ‘That don’t make no sense.’ You know, teams are in Trinidad already and they are not playing the next game, but we have to fly and play… players can get injured, those kind of things,” Powell stated.

World.title: WATCH: PM says he has no power to keep Cooper’s Pen residents on land
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrew Holness speaking to residents in Cooper's Pen, Trelawny on Friday, August 28, 2026. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica – Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness told residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny, whose houses were demolished earlier this month, that he has no power to keep them on the land.

He made the revelation to the residents during a tour of the community Friday, accompanied by Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern, Tova Hamilton.

Before beginning the tour of the demolished area, the prime minister spoke with residents and told them he would meet with them again after the tour.

He said he would announce possible solutions following the tour.

On August 11, some 20 houses were demolished in the community, leaving roughly 20 families homeless and affecting approximately 40 families overall.

Since the demolition, residents have staged two separate demonstrations calling for the prime minister’s intervention and assistance.

– Horace Hines

World.title: Courage under fire
World.content:
Firefighters battle the inferno at Super Parts Limited on Hagley Park Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Employees of Superior Parts Limited and a taxi driver battled to save millions of dollars worth of motorcycles and cars on Thursday as a raging fire tore through the company on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew, while firefighters were hampered by a lack of water amid the severe drought that has triggered water restrictions in sections of the island.

Although firefighters from seven stations in Kingston and St Catherine responded, the majority of the stock was destroyed in the midday inferno that sent thick black smoke into the air and created traffic snarls on Hagley Park Road and adjoining thoroughfares.

In the midst of the chaos and destruction, 71-year-old Leroy Terlon used a forklift to remove numerous wooden boxes from the premises and placed them on the road.

“I had to put out the energy and the effort to get certain things saved. I have been here for 20 years and I helped to build the company to where it is now, with labour and loyalty. This event shouldn’t have happened,” Terlon told the Jamaica Observer as he sipped a cold beer at a nearby gas station following his heroics.

He said he was cooling off after his exposure to the intense heat.

“This hurts me. This company is like mine. If I talk about it, tears will come to my eyes. I have been there for so long. It hurts me. I don’t have liquid cash in the business, but I have years of service,” he added as he received congratulatory messages from friends for his bravery.

Other employees also rushed to move stock from the building, while taxi operator Kemal Dunn used his car to tow motor vehicles from a car mart adjoining the burning property.

“I just saw it and said I had to help. I knew it would spread because Superior has a lot of boxes,” he told the Observer.

“I was just driving past. My uncle owns a car dealership up the road. This car dealership just started. For a trying man, I decided to just assist him as best as I could,” Dunn explained.

“Only one car got damaged out of more than 30 that were there. I helped them rescue a good 20 of them. I used my car to pull out some. We used a wire to jump-start others because they were parked for a good while and they had no power to start. I am glad I helped them to minimise the loss.

“I was just watching the electric wire. The fire, you just have to know how to stay a good distance because you are going to feel the heat. The wires were sparking and gashing.”

“I love to help a person and he can pass it on to a next person. I am not going to take my phone and video when I can help,” he added, taking an apparent jab at the many onlookers who stood recording the fire with their cellphones.

Dunn said he banged on the windows of neighbouring houses to ensure that no humans were inside.

“All of these things are material things that can be replaced. A lot of people won’t have a job tomorrow, but they still have life,” Dunn reasoned.

As the fire raged, people in a number of adjoining residential and commercial premises moved out as many supplies and furniture before the flames spread.

One Superior Parts employee, who wished to remain anonymous, speculated that welding sparked the blaze.

“There was welding going on around the back. The fire started around that side. Nobody is allowed to smoke on property, so we believe it started with the welding. We don’t see any other way the fire could have started,” the worker said.

Amid the devastation wrought by the fire, police were kept on their toes by onlookers who wanted to get close-up shots to post on social media. Cops were heard repeatedly telling them to remove from the area for their safety.

Other onlookers were heard venting that the motorbikes were being destroyed and the police did not allow them to go in and grab one for themselves.

Throughout the ordeal, power lines caught fire, sending sparks flying and forcing people to take cover. At the same time, numerous loud explosions were heard coming from the premises.

Three firefighters were reportedly injured during their attempt to put the blaze out.

The Observer was told that the Jamaica Fire Brigade had received a call alerting it to the fire at 12:08 pm. Units from Trench Town initially responded, but according to a firefighter who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, the magnitude of the fire was so great that units had to be requested from other stations.

“There were units from York Park, Half-Way-Tree, Rollington Town, Port Royal, Stony Hill, Portmore, and Spanish Town,” the firefighter said, while pointing to the difficulty they experienced accessing water at the scene.

“The water challenges were expected because of the drought conditions. A lot of the hydrants have no water or low water pressure and it was a massive fire,” he added.

Up to 6:00 pm, the fire had not been fully extinguished.

World.title: Russia plans new ground attack on Kyiv, Ukraine warns
World.content:
Ukrainian flag fluttering as smoke rises from a warehouse following an air attack in the Kyiv. | Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP via Getty Images

Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office reveals new intelligence about Kremlin plans for an offensive against the capital.

Ukraine has intelligence that Russia is planning new ground offensives against Kyiv and Chernihiv — while Moscow ramps up drone strikes on Ukrainian cities.

Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told reporters that Russian military chiefs have been tasked by the Kremlin’s political leaders with planning and preparing for attacks on the two cities, according to intelligence received and verified by Ukraine.

Palisa said there is not yet evidence that Russian troops are gathering to carry out the attacks, and that Ukraine’s priority is to “prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to launch any offensive actions at all.”

World.title: Trump-shaped ecstasy pills can be fatal, Dutch drug institute warns
World.content:
The tablets are shaped like the U.S. commander-in-chief’s head, researchers say.

An ecstasy pill shaped like the head of U.S. President Donald Trump is potentially lethal and should not be taken “under any circumstances,” a Dutch drug institute has warned.

The pills come in different colors, are shaped like the commander-in-chief’s head and are stamped with the words “Trump” and “NL,” according to a red alert issued by the Trimbos Institute, a drug and addiction research center based in Utrecht, on Friday.

It's currently not possible to know how many of the pills are in circulation, but "multiple" drug-testing locations have received them, Anniek Groothuis, a spokesperson for the institute, told POLITICO. Testers have previously encountered pills shaped like Superman logos or featuring car brands, Groothuis said.

World.title: Germany plans to blame Russia for Leipzig attack as tensions with Putin escalate
World.content:
One of the officials familiar with the matter said that in response to the Leipzig drone incident, it was no longer enough to expel individual Russian diplomats or close the Russian House in Berlin. Tougher measures were needed, such as intensified sanctions or even more extensive arms deliveries to Ukraine. The three officials declined to provide further details on which precise measures Merz plans to announce.

It is unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold individual Russian actors or the Russian government responsible for the attempted drone attack. Berlin is already preparing for a sharp counter reaction, as the officials said Germany must prepare for punitive measures from Moscow.

The planned move lands amid high tension with Russia, amid a spate of incidents on European soil that top officials have described as "hybrid warfare." On Tuesday, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow where he warned the Russian government against escalating tensions with NATO.

But the timing of Merz's expected announcement is also domestically sensitive. On Sunday next week, elections will take place in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, followed by elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin two weeks later. In Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — known for its pro-Russia stance — is leading in the polls.

Merz had already announced Tuesday that there would be severe consequences for the Leipzig incident, though without naming any specific party.

“The drone attack in Leipzig, among other things, shows that we are also facing very real threats,” he said. “The federal government is making the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this.”

World.title: Russia kills dozens as drone hits ammo warehouse near homes in Ukraine
World.content:
The warehouse appears to have been storing ammunition; Zelenskyy referred to a detonation after the drone strikes, and to a police investigation into why ordnance was stored close to residential properties, which is prohibited. Criminal proceedings on charges of negligence have also begun. “Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions,” he said.

Russia is bombarding Kyiv with “virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones,” Zelenskyy added. In a separate video address Friday evening, he admitted Ukraine needs to “significantly accelerate” production of interceptors capable of taking down the Iranian-designed, jet-powered Shahed drones.

In response to Russia’s increased attacks, Ukraine plans to launch 1,000 long-range drones into Russia every day, up from a current average of 300. There “must be more” strikes, Zelenskyy said Friday night.

Kyiv’s use of long-range drones — striking deep into Russia, disrupting its economy, logistics and bringing the reality of the war to ordinary Russians previously shielded from it — has in recent months improved Ukraine’s position in the conflict. One Ukrainian commander has described them as “our most important card in this war.”

While noting Kyiv's priority is to strengthen defenses against jet-powered drones, sending more long-range drones into Russia will make it “feel even more responsible for its choice to continue this war,” Zelenskyy said Friday night.

In the same address, he also pointed to signs that Russia’s economy is ailing, including the fact that it is now importing gasoline, an unusual step for one of the world's largest oil exporters.

Zelenskyy also said American representatives briefed Ukraine on the recent unexpected visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who warned Russian officials not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies. Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for the "necessary tone of the conversation with Russia."

This article has been updated.

Strand, Sonne und ein erbitterter Kampf um das politische Überleben. In Rostock-Warnemünde begleitet Gordon Repinski Manuela Schwesig auf einem Spaziergang durch den Wahlkampfendspurt in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Die SPD-Ministerpräsidentin will ihr Land unbedingt gegen den erstarkenden AfD-Herausforderer verteidigen.

Um die Menschen an der Ostsee zu überzeugen, schlägt Schwesig ihren ganz eigenen Weg ein und geht auf maximale Distanz zur Bundespolitik. Sie attackiert den wirtschaftlichen Kurs von CDU-Kanzler Friedrich Merz schonungslos und fordert einen staatlichen Preisdeckel für Sprit. Die arbeitende Mitte dürfe in diesen Zeiten nicht länger die Hauptlast tragen, ist ihr Mantra.

Neben scharfen Angriffen in der Rentendebatte zeigt sich Schwesig beim Spaziergang aber auch von der persönlichen Seite. Sehr offen reflektiert sie ihre überstandene Krebserkrankung und wie dieser Schicksalsschlag ihren politischen Fokus verändert hat.

World.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief Fedorov takes advisory role with Italy
World.content:
Fedorov, who called for wartime elections after being pushed out of government in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s latest reshuffle, also stressed that he is not decamping to Rome. “My main focus remains unchanged,” he wrote, adding he will continue working in Ukraine on projects to strengthen the country’s defense and attract international resources.

Crosetto first offered the position in July, saying he called Fedorov the day after his dismissal and asked: “When would you like to come to Rome to work with me as an adviser?” He praised Fedorov as an innovator who had “completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield.”

The former minister was dismissed in mid-July after roughly six months at the helm of Ukraine's defense department amid tensions with the country’s military leadership and policy disputes. His removal triggered rare wartime protests.

He has since sharpened his criticism of President Zelenskyy, calling for elections earlier this month despite Russia’s ongoing invasion and warning that Ukrainians “cannot endlessly live” without understanding how major decisions are made.

Zelenskyy has rejected the idea, warning that wartime elections could “destroy” the country.

World.title: Climate and AI to loom large in von der Leyen’s State of the Union
World.content:
During Friday's discussion with the cabinet chiefs, Seibert linked the expected focus on climate to the damage caused by floods and wildfires over the summer, according to the two officials, who were briefed on the gathering. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks.

The climate focus comes as von der Leyen’s Commission tries to defend its 2040 emissions-cutting target while responding to mounting pressure from industry and national capitals to limit the economic cost of the green transition.

The discussion also touched on how to present AI’s impact on jobs. Von der Leyen’s team has asked the Commission’s relevant policy units, in particular DG Connect, to provide fresh statistics for the speech on the number of jobs likely to be lost and created as AI adoption spreads, according to one of the officials.

Seibert also raised migration as a likely topic in the address, referring to the crisis in the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta, according to one of the officials. The Commission is expected to revamp the mandate and operations of EU border agency Frontex, a third official said.

The Commission president's speech is expected to include references to social policy around the 10th anniversary of the European Pillar of Social Rights next year, alongside Ukraine and enlargement, according to one of the officials. But the topics have yet to be finalized.

The meeting was the second major opportunity for commissioners to get their priorities name-checked, with their cabinets having already submitted two- to three-page pitches to Seibert. The Commission's policy units, known as the directorates-general, also submitted documents outlining the topics they want von der Leyen to cover.

World.title: What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
World.content:
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.

Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.

But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.

But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.

“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”

As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.

World.title: Bardella, Faure, Lecornu, Hollande, Philippe: Political season begins in France
World.content:
Before France knows who its next president will be, it must first adopt a budget for the year 2027.

 

That is the main task facing the French Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, he told French daily Le Parisien in an interview.

With less than eight months to go before the first round of the presidential election and no majority in the National Assembly, Lecornu said he hopes to avoid a political stalemate by promising a budget"with measures that, for the most part, can be reversed by the new majority that emerges from the ballot box."

Lecornu is not planning to raise taxes, but is instead preparing an agricultural "rescue plan" and a reform of sick leave.

As for 2027, he repeats:"I don't know in what language I have to say it, I am not a candidate in the presidential election. I am not getting involved in the presidential campaign."

The Prime Minister was in Sens this Saturday for the summer school of the Laboratoire de la République, the movement set up by former education minister Jean-Michel Blanquer.

Olivier Faure calls for 'ecological socialism'

For his part, the First Secretary of the Socialist Party (PS), Olivier Faure, warned: "If the document that comes out of these debates is the one put forward by Messrs. Attal and Philippe with the support of the far right, then I am telling you we will vote to censure it!"

In his speech at the PS summer meetings, he also urged the left to "build a barrier"against the alliance between"the far right" and "big money". "The hour of ecological socialism has struck", he added, while continuing to keep everyone guessing about his intentions ahead of the left-wing primary.

Jordan Bardella believes the RN can 'win this election'

Visiting the Châlons-en-Champagne fair in the Marne, the president of the Rassemblement national (RN), Jordan Bardella, insisted that his party had "worked hard this summer on a programme to get the country back on its feet" and on the "presidential campaign".

For a time tipped as the far-right party's candidate, Jordan Bardella ultimately had to fall in behind Marine Le Pen.

A debate between Édouard Philippe and François Hollande

Another presidential contender, Édouard Philippe (Horizons), took part on Saturday in a debate with former Socialist president François Hollande, whose ambitions for 2027 appear to be growing.

At the Laboratoire de la République summer school, the two men agreed on what they see as the need to beware of the RN and La France insoumise (LFI)."In a country that is so divided, where discord has taken hold, where there is a form of radicalism, of populism, where people are set against one another, we must unite (…) against all those who divide,"François Hollande said.

Édouard Philippe, who hopes to bring together the right and the centre, also urged caution with regard to the two parties,"not because they are illegitimate in the public debate, but because they divide."

While they both sound the alarm over the state of the French economy, the former head of state and the ex-prime minister are not prescribing the same remedies: François Hollande is calling for an _"_increase in taxation", whereas Édouard Philippe advocates "keeping a lid on"social spending.

World.title: Solidarity Armada sails to Ceuta with 50 boats in support amid migration crisis
World.content:
A flotilla of around 50 vessels from the Costa del Sol and other Spanish ports set sail on Saturday for Ceuta to show their support for the city after the migratory crisis that has been unfolding since the end of July, according to local media.

 

The initiative, dubbed the Fleet of Solidarity with Ceuta, brings together around 120 participants under the slogan "We are all Ceuta, Spain responds as one". The organisers have arranged up to 60 free berths in the city's harbour for the participating boats.

The vessels have not departed as a single convoy, with each skipper leaving from their home port to cross the Strait of Gibraltar independently bound for Ceuta, where the participants have various activities planned over the weekend.

The call went out after the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta on 30 and 31 July, when tens of thousands of people crossed irregularly from Morocco into the autonomous city, in one of the episodes of greatest migratory pressure seen on the border in recent years.

Once in Ceuta, the participants will take a guided tour of the city and attend a dinner at the Yacht Club. On Sunday the vessels are expected to undertake a trip through the waters surrounding the autonomous city.

Later, the boats from mainland Spain and those based in Ceuta will gather in the southern bay to send a message of unity "between Spaniards on both sides of the Strait", according to the programme for the initiative.

A weekend with no demonstrations expected

Ceuta faces a weekend with no new demonstrations planned, after several days of protests over the presence of thousands of migrants who entered the city on 30 July.

The latest rally on Friday brought together hundreds of residents on Trampolín beach, where they demanded the return of the migrants to Morocco and the clearance of the camp set up next to the Temporary Stay Centre for Immigrants (CETI), which remains overcrowded. The protests have been organised mainly through groups on social media.

For now, there are no new calls for protests this weekend, although local sources warn that they could take place at any time. On 2 September a demonstration is scheduled, organised jointly by the Provincial Federation of Neighbours' Associations (FPAV) and the association Foro Ceuta Siglo XXI.

World.title: Iceland's EU referendum sees high preliminary voter turnout in expected close race
World.content:
Iceland's capital Reykjavík recorded a higher voter turnout in the high-stakes EU referendum by noon than at the same time during the country's parliamentary elections in 2024, preliminary figures showed on Saturday.

 

In the hours after voters began casting their ballots in the referendum that will determine whether to reopen EU accession talks, 13.7% had voted by noon in the Reykjavík North constituency, compared to just over 10% in the 2024 election.

In Reykjavík South, just over 14% had voted by noon, compared to just over 11% for the parliamentary election.

More than 20% of voters cast early ballots in advance of election day, Iceland’s national broadcaster RÚV said.

A close race is expected, with a final poll on Friday indicating 50.4% of voters plan to vote yes and 49.6% no.

Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir casts her ballot at Álftamýrarskóli polling station in Reykjavik, Iceland, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. AP Photo/Marco Di Marco

Backers of EU membership say it’s best for Iceland to get closer to its European neighbours to combat issues that don't respect borders, such as climate change. They also say the euro would bring more stability than Iceland's volatile króna currency.

Opponents say the current setup is just right and that Iceland already enjoys all the benefits of European integration without the sovereignty compromises that inevitably come with full membership. They cite trade deals, such as one with China, that are more favourable.

"I think that we should be a part of a bigger unity. I think it's worth looking into it," Unnur Jokulsdottir, a 71-year-old retiree, said after casting her ballot in Reykjavík's City Hall.

In contrast, Olafur Thorsson, a 53-year-old fish trader, said he was sceptical.

"I used to like the European Union back when it was a good thing. But today it's become a sort of big economic prison," he said.

The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.

Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.

A voter places a ballot into a ballot box at Reykjavik City Hall in Reykjavik, Iceland, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. AP Photo/Marco Di Marco

A yes vote would trigger renewed negotiations with the European Commission covering 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.

The issue of fisheries — a pillar of Iceland's economy and over which Reykjavík wants to retain exclusive control — would have to be hammered out with Brussels, which this time around appears more willing to compromise.

On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.

Trump's unpredictability and his threats to take over neighbouring Greenland — which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions — have added to Icelanders' concerns.

Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.

The result of the vote will be followed closely by the EU, which has not welcomed a wealthy, net contributor to its budget since 1995.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s government steps down as newly elected Kurultai holds first session
World.content:
Kazakhstan has entered a new political season with a reshaped political system after the country’s newly established unicameral parliament, with its lawmakers gathered for its first session on Friday in Astana.

 

It comes Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in last Sunday’s parliamentary election, that was triggered by a new constitution adopted earlier this year.

The session attended by all 145 members opened with an address by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who formally declared the first session of the first convocation of the Kurultai open and described it as the beginning of an important new stage in the country’s development.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the first session of the Kurultai in Astana. Copyright: Aqorda Press Service

“From this day, the process of renewing the country’s political system begins. … The Kurultai will fundamentally modernise the system of government and give a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.

By improving the quality of national legislation, the Kurultai will provide a strong foundation for the country’s legal system,” Tokayev said.

A new political system

Under the Constitution, the government is required to step down before a newly elected Kurultai. Kazakhstan’s government therefore relinquished its powers as the new parliament convened.

However, the country will not be left without a functioning government during the transition period. President Tokayev signed a decree instructing the cabinet to continue performing its duties until a new government is formed.

Under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which came into force on 1 July 2026, the previous bicameral parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis and the Senate, was replaced by a unicameral parliament called the Kurultai.

The term “kurultai” dates back centuries and historically referred to an assembly or council among the peoples of the Great Steppe.

The new Constitution was adopted in a nationwide referendum held on 15 March 2026.

“By coming together, our people accomplished a great deal in a very short period of time. Thanks to the nationwide referendum, the country successfully implemented a sweeping constitutional reform,” Tokayev said.

The Kurultai consists of 145 lawmakers elected for five-year terms and representing five political parties. The Adilet party, which absorbed Amanat, the successor to the long-dominant Nur Otan party, holds a commanding majority with 110 seats.

It is followed by the Auyl party with 10 seats, Respublica with nine, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (OSDP) with eight and Ak Zhol with eight.

New speaker of the Kurultai

During the session, President Tokayev nominated Aibek Dadebai for the position of chairman of the Kurultai. Dadebai has headed the Adilet party since 7 May 2026 and has held several senior government and diplomatic posts, including serving as head of the Presidential Administration from February 2024 to May 2026.

Aibek Dadebai, Chairman of the Adilet party. Copyright: Aqorda Press Service

Tokayev said Dadebai had extensive experience in public administration and described him as an educated, patriotic and responsible citizen. “I consider him worthy of this position and ask the members of the Kurultai to support his candidacy,” Tokayev said.

Later in the day, lawmakers backed the nomination and elected Dadebai chairman of the Kurultai in a secret ballot.

Lawmakers also elected three deputy speakers: former senator Nurlan Beknazarov, former Mazhilis deputy speaker Dania Espaeva and Children’s Rights Commissioner Dinara Zakiyeva.

The Kurultai will have eight standing committees, seven of which will be chaired by representatives of the ruling Adilet party, while the remaining committee will be headed by a member of the Auyl party.

What happens next?

Kazakhstan’s new political structure will continue to take shape in the coming weeks. Once the Kurultai is fully organised, President Tokayev will put forward candidates for vice-president and prime minister, before appointing the new government following consultations with lawmakers. A deputy chairman of the Security Council will also be appointed to a newly created post.

Tokayev said he would deliver his annual address to the nation once the new parliament and government are fully formed.

The institutional changes will continue into September, with the Kazakhstan People’s Council expected to be established in the second half of the month. The new constitutional body will represent the country’s ethnic, regional, social and political diversity and will have the right to initiate legislation.

According to Tokayev, the process will renew “almost all key institutions of power” within a relatively short period.

World.title: Hundreds of foreign nationals among the missing following deadly Nepal floods
World.content:
Hundreds of foreign nationals are among the nearly 3,000 people missing following devastating floods that hit the border area between Nepal and Tibet earlier this week.

 

A tsunami-like wall of water and debris ripped through the Himalayan region on Wednesday, killing at least 682 people and sparking a huge rescue effort.

On Friday, Chinese officials said 260 foreigners remained missing following the deadly flash floods, while Nepal's disaster agency said 517 foreign nationals were missing. Nepal's tourism board put the number of tourists still "out of communication" at 622 - 471 of which were foreign tourists.

The tourism board's figures included 98 people from India, 61 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 33 British, 29 Latvians, 25 Canadians, nine South Koreans, and nine Singaporeans.

Nine Russians and eight Germans were also still unaccounted for, as well as six from South Africa, five from Japan, five from New Zealand, and four from France, according to the figures.

Nepalese army soldiers load relief supplies onto a helicopter for survivors stranded in areas cut off by flash flooding in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The other countries with people on the tourism board's missing list were Belgium, Hungary, the Netherlands, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Italy, Belarus, Finland, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Serbia, Switzerland, Sweden, and Vietnam.

The US State Department said on Thursday that 90 US citizens also remained unaccounted for, while the Australian government announced on Saturday that the number of its missing nationals had risen to 41.

The Nepal Tourism Board reported that two of the three missing Spaniards had been located, although the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not commented on the matter.

China has not provided a breakdown of the nationalities of the foreign nationals it reported as missing.

Europe pledges support

The European Union has pledged its support for aid efforts in the wake of the floods, activating its Copernicus Earth observation satellite system to help monitor the aftermath.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc would also allocate €2 million in humanitarian aid for Nepal "to deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest."

World.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
World.content:
Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the attackers.

Turkey’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia’s government said on Saturday.

"During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship."

The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries.

The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey."

According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national.

Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast

The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year.

At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

Maritime police patrol to ward off piracy off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024] Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu/picture alliance

These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somaliain the 2000s. It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.

The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.

In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank
World.content:
Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, pelting them with rocks and trapping residents in their homes.

The incident was the first major attack by Israeli settlers since they began a siege in the villages of Qusra and neighboring Jalud earlier this month.

On Saturday, settlers descended on Qusra and began pelting Palestinians with rocks. When dozens of residents sought to barricade themselves in a home, settlers followed them in, according to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

"The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside the house," said an IDF statement.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is the IDF protecting in such situations?

Although the IDF said settler vehicles had been impounded and authorities were gathering evidence, Palestinian media said the IDF protected the settlers during the melee.

A number of Palestinians said they were injured after being pepper sprayed by settlers, and reported that other Israeli settlers had tried to burn nearby fields owned by Palestinians.

One Palestinian said the IDF had fired tear gas into the home that he was in and held several people inside while at the same time letting Israeli settlers go free.

Other Palestinians said IDF officers had handcuffed, blindfolded and beaten residents trapped inside before letting them go.

Local Palestinians told international news teams that they had been trapped in their homes for hours waiting for help from the IDF.

The IDF did not comment on the use of tear gas nor accusations of handcuffs and beatings.

Saturday attacks elicit rare criticism from Netanyahu

Saturday's attacks took place just yards away from three other Qusra homes that radical Jewish settlers targeted in a siege that began three weeks ago.

Despite a massive Israeli military presence that local Palestinians say has kept them imprisoned in their houses, residents report near-daily settler encroachments.

Rights groups say settler aggression is part of an — illegal — effort to seize land from residents in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians hope to one day found their own independent state. The Israeli government has rejected accusations of illegality. Various Israeli political figures have justified the settlements for security reasons or argued there are biblical grounds for the creation of the settlements.

The IDF has said it will continue "to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area."

Although settlers have been emboldened by the stance of Israel's far-right government — which has encouraged settlement building despite broad international opposition — the Saturday attack managed to elicit rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On Saturday, Netanyahu released a statement on X saying, "I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world."

Increasing Israeli settler violence has even garnered criticism from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who recently denounced radical settlers in the West Bank as "Israeli terrorists," adding that those behind the siege of Qusra could face US sanctions.

Palestinian American watches as West Bank house under siege To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
World.content:
Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.

At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.

Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.

The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.

Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.

Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis

Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.

Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.

Rescue personnel work at the site of a bus accident on a major highway near Harare [FILE: January 18, 2015] Image: Xinhua/imago images



Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.

This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.
