World.title: Opinion: Mdinaradze resignation ‘prelude to Kobakhidze’s downfall’
World.content:
Opinion on Mdinaradze’s resignation

According to political analyst Gia Khukhashvili, Georgian Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze’sdeparture from politics is not simply the end of one politician’s career, but part of a process whose ultimate target is Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Khukhashvili likened Kobakhidze’s current position to that of “a child left home alone”.

Earlier, Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze said he was stepping down from his post and leaving politics altogether. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to spend more time with his family.

Gia Khukhashvili: “This is a logical continuation of the processes already under way. Mdinaradze himself is of little interest. The main question here concerns Kobakhidze. Whose prime minister is he now?! The only subordinate he had was Mdinaradze. There is no one else in the government under his authority.

Kobakhidze is now like a child left home alone: he can do foolish things, but no one will let him do anything meaningful. Accordingly, Mdinaradze’s resignation is a prelude to Kobakhidze’s ultimate downfall, a kind of preview, and nothing more. Mdinaradze himself was of no real significance; the true target of his resignation is Kobakhidze.

Kobakhidze had already been lined up to be pushed out for quite some time. I use that term because this is characteristic of [ruling party founder] Bidzina Ivanishvili. Kobakhidze has now been left ‘home alone’, because the government is purely technocratic. No one in the government answers to him or has listened to him for a long time. It is a technocratic government with no political component left.

I am not predicting that this will happen tomorrow or the day after, because Bidzina Ivanishvili naturally needs to saddle Kobakhidze with the blame for the problems that have accumulated recently and send him on his way carrying that baggage. Ivanishvili has to gain something from his departure, after all. When he decides to do that is another matter. But there can be no doubt that Kobakhidze has been left ‘home alone’: one only has to look at the composition of the government to see that

As for Mamuka Mdinaradze, after leaving the State Security Service, he effectively held only nominal positions and was left in limbo. In reality, his entire career ‘odyssey’ was part of the process of isolating Kobakhidze. We have now reached a point where Kobakhidze has no real control over anything, and Mdinaradze was the only person left in the government he could talk to.

So Kobakhidze is a child left home alone who still has matches in his hands, but I doubt anyone will let him start a fire. Mdinaradze’s resignation means nothing in itself; it is merely a prelude to Kobakhidze being pushed out.”

World.title: Abkhaz experts discuss fuel crisis, Georgian debate on Georgian-Abkhaz conflict resolution. VIDEO
World.content:
The fuel crisis in Abkhazia

Editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda Inal Khashig and political analyst Astamur Tania discuss recent developments:

The fuel crisis in Abkhazia and unexpected petrol supplies from Tbilisi;

Georgian opposition politician Nika Gvaramia ’s statements that Abkhazia may want to rejoin Georgia once Georgia becomes part of the EU;

’s statements that Abkhazia may want to rejoin Georgia once Georgia becomes part of the EU; A campaign launched in Turkiye calling for measures to end Abkhazia’s isolation.

Main arguments:

Fuel crisis in Abkhazia and commercial contacts with Tbilisi: The experts see this as a positive step towards de-escalation and building a climate of trust. They call for pragmatism and openness to unconventional economic solutions amid broader instability.

The experts see this as a positive step towards de-escalation and building a climate of trust. They call for pragmatism and openness to unconventional economic solutions amid broader instability. Nika Gvaramia’s statements on ways to resolve the conflict and Georgian domestic politics: The experts say violence was committed by both sides during the war. In their view, Georgian society still has a taboo around discussing abuses committed by its own armed forces during the Abkhaz war, although acknowledging them is necessary to understand the causes of the tragedy.

The experts say violence was committed by both sides during the war. In their view, Georgian society still has a taboo around discussing abuses committed by its own armed forces during the Abkhaz war, although acknowledging them is necessary to understand the causes of the tragedy. Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation launched in Turkiye: The experts believe ending Abkhazia’s isolation is in the region’s long-term interests and does not contradict Georgia’s interests, despite Tbilisi’s continued efforts to create obstacles.

Full text of the discussion

Inal Khashig: Hello! On the air is “Chegemskaya Pravda.”

The past week was very event-filled. Strictly speaking, that is what we will be discussing. Many events occurred there, both in foreign and domestic policy. And today, our regular political expert, Astamur Tania, is visiting us. Astamur, good day!

Astamur Tania: Good day!

Inal Khashig: Yes, the problem with gasoline, with fuel, which has gripped Abkhazia and not only Abkhazia – Russia is reeling from a gasoline shortage as well. And today I refueled at 110 rubles per liter.

Astamur Tania: You can be congratulated.

Inal Khashig: Yes, two or three weeks ago this would have seemed, probably, like something unnatural.

Astamur Tania: Maybe you’ll save the gasoline and sell it in a week for 150.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but that’s how it turned out. I refueled and I’m happy. It turns out one doesn’t need much for happiness. And in this context, of course, there is a lot of all kinds of talk regarding this shortage. A certain portion of the shortage was compensated through deliveries from Georgia.

This is no humanitarian aid; it is pure business, but nevertheless, a heap of all kinds of talk. By the way, I took a look with my own eyes at who said what officially. The Abkhaz government acknowledged the shortage and said that it would not obstruct it. In Georgia, the authorities said that the Georgian government has nothing to do with it; it is pure business. Nevertheless, in Georgia itself…

Astamur Tania: They also said that they would not obstruct it.

Inal Khashig: They won’t obstruct it, yes.

A portion of our society is chronically opposed to any contacts with Georgia in this regard. On the other hand, as for me… Well, you know, not all contacts are the same. When your entire economy is at a standstill due to a lack of gasoline at the height of the resort season, and you have the opportunity to buy, to acquire this gasoline in Georgia, then it seems to me that here one needs to set what is more important—certain conventionalities, or the fact that a lack of gasoline primarily hits the security of the country. It seems to me that this is the most important thing.

On the other hand, in Georgia itself, there is also a scandal. That is, there are also people unhappy there with the fact that gasoline is being sold to Abkhazia. And there it is being presented under the sauce that this gasoline goes directly to Russian military bases. That is, such nonsense as well, but which many willingly believe. Nevertheless, such is the situation. And based on what is happening with oil refineries in Russia, the end of this crisis is not visible in the near term at all.

How do you generally view this entire situation with this fuel, with all these deliveries from Georgia, and so on?

Astamur Tania: Over many years, you and I have spoken with enviable regularity about the need to search for and expand contacts in areas representing mutual interest. In particular, we spoke about the development of border trade, about the legalization of trade relations. So it would be strange if I were now to say that I am against these deliveries.

If we speak about the political component of our relations, despite this, we have quite fruitful relations in the field of energy. And why hide it, there are very many Georgian agricultural products on our market. It can be said that an expansion of the product range has occurred.

Despite the fact that both Abkhaz and Georgian representatives of their respective authorities state that they are not obstructing it and that it is linked to humanitarian and other issues, even here it was openly acknowledged that this gasoline comes from Georgia. They even came up with the term “gasoline from alternative sources.” It makes it seem as though we border Russia to the west and alternative sources to the east. A political science term for local application could already be coined: “Abkhaz-Alternative negotiations took place…”

Joking aside, I think this is ultimately a positive step. When you and I discussed this, we were aiming precisely at the point that a de-escalation of our relations is necessary. There is a lot of propaganda and hate speech involved in all of this, yet steps like these help build a climate of trust—that much cannot be denied.

It is another matter entirely whether this will remain a one-off occurrence or project into something broader, leading to significant decisions in other areas. Time will tell.

Naturally, we see that the reaction on the Abkhaz side is also mixed. However, our main political figures refrained from using this situation to issue statements condemning the Abkhazian leadership. We know that voices within opposition circles have also repeatedly stressed the need for a negotiation process with Georgia. In that sense, a certain consensus exists. The situation in Georgia, of course, is quite different, as internal political tensions there are much sharper.

Inal Khashig: They’re jailing people there.

Astamur Tania: Yes. In general, if we look back—even if we trace things back to the origins of the armed conflict—I believe domestic political circumstances were among the main drivers that triggered it.

The illegitimate State Council regime in power at the time held onto authority almost purely through force. In suppressing the supporters of the ousted president, Gamsakhurdia, they conducted bloody raids into Western Georgia. Their position was extremely precarious, so they shifted the center of escalation to Abkhazia to address their internal political objectives.

They ultimately lost control over Abkhazia, but it must be acknowledged that Shevardnadze’s regime managed to retain power back then. That was the price.

Today, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict continues to be used primarily for domestic political ends.

We saw how former president Saakashvili, currently imprisoned, suddenly re-energized. It appears this entire wave was initiated by him. He provoked it, drawing on his substantial base of supporters, effectively giving the green light to inflame the crisis surrounding gasoline deliveries to Abkhazia.

I view this entire affair as a maneuver in an internal political struggle.

How much restraint and patience the current authorities will display remains to be seen. As for the opposition spectrum, it is naturally heterogeneous.

Even if we imagine a scenario where a power shift takes place in Georgia, it would be naive to expect liberals to take charge. Judging by the prevailing tone in the media space, there is a serious threat that populist-chauvinists could come to power—figures with whom it would be far more difficult for us, and indeed for Georgian society, to deal. That risk is by no means zero.

The real concern is that we risk once again becoming a tool for aggressive domestic political propaganda, and we must keep that in mind.

There is another aspect that directly concerns us: we must diversify all risks related to fuel supplies and secure multiple sources. If the Georgian side were to become the sole supplier of fuel, that position would quickly turn into a lever of economic coercion.

Our approach must remain highly flexible and rely on diverse sources—from Georgia, from Russia, and from other avenues we have yet to explore.

Inal Khashig: As before. There was Romania, Bulgaria.

Astamur Tania: Yes. All these possibilities need to be explored.

In general, we need to get used to the idea that, unfortunately, the stable period—stable in an economic sense, in terms of deliveries, financial inflows, and so on—is, in my opinion, behind us. Our authorities and political circles must be prepared for extraordinary steps and new, unexpected challenges.

We simply need to understand that we are living in such a time, and it is not getting any better.

In this sense, it seems to me that these emerging contacts with the Georgian side still need to be brought into the realm of political detente as well. I believe there is someone to talk to in Georgia.

The tragedy is simply that Georgian legislation on occupied territories prohibits Georgia itself from conducting negotiations with Abkhazia. As a result, our relations are reduced to exchanging mutual claims in the public sphere.

Even regarding this decision on gasoline—localized as it is—if such a situation had occurred during the existence of the Coordination Council prior to 2008, I don’t think it would have caused such upheavals. The two sides would have sat down, agreed, signed a protocol, and affixed the signatures of international representatives, as the UN and others did. It would have been a bilateral agreement, and no questions would have arisen from either side.

Therefore, I say once again: we need to think about how to revive a full-fledged negotiation format where two sides exist. Otherwise, we will encounter these issues continuously and will have to solve them manually.

Inal Khashig: The topic of Georgia has been quite prominent in recent days. I don’t know whether it is connected to another anniversary of the start of the war, the events of August 8, or something else, but nevertheless, while this discussion around the conflict isn’t the primary headline in Georgia, it remains on everyone’s lips.

Former State Minister of Georgia Gia Baramidze gave an interview to a Georgian YouTube channel. In it, he stated that during the war he participated on the Georgian side of the commission for the exchange of prisoners, refugees, and the search for missing persons—working alongside Paata Zakareishvili. Beslan Kobakhia represented our side. To clarify his role back then: he stated that during the war, the Georgians could not execute prisoner exchanges with the Abkhazians because they had no leverage or prisoner pool left, as they were actually executing Abkhazian captives.

Naturally, a scandal erupted in Georgia, leading to a very telling reaction from the Georgian authorities: they opened a criminal case against Baramidze under the charge of high treason—not under slander, mind you, but high treason.

Astamur Tania: Because he was an official who possessed relevant information. And he presented this information, which was classified, in an open format. All of this is being hidden.

Inal Khashig: But on the other hand, this means that they do acknowledge it after all. I see another opportunity here. The war and what happened during it—how it started, how it developed, how it ended, and so on—constantly becomes a tool tailored to the political climate within Georgian society, serving both domestic political agendas and external audiences.

If you remember, it originally started as a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict. Now, however, they deny that it is a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, choosing instead to view it strictly as a conflict with Russia, with the Abkhaz framed as mere bystanders.

This admission might actually serve as a starting point for them to confront the root causes of the war internally and finally acknowledge what they ultimately did.

If we look at the facts, I can name a dozen Abkhaz right now who were taken prisoner and executed. For example, in August, at the very beginning of the war, Oleg Ashba was captured and shot. The same happened to the Akirtava brothers, Sasha Mirzoyan, Amichba, and many others who were taken prisoner and ostentatiously executed right at the funerals of Georgian soldiers. These facts are well-attested. On our side, thank God, all of this is fully documented: there is the White Book, and the Prosecutor General’s Office formally recorded these cases at the time.

If people in Georgian society truly want to understand what happened and how, it costs nothing to present these documents. The names, surnames, dates of capture, and execution details are all fully recorded. I think this could serve as a genuine starting point in searching for a resolution to the conflict. Obviously, the overall issue is vast, but concrete steps are necessary. If they want to understand why the war started and how it unfolded, this is where they ought to begin—especially now that there is a public admission from a former high-ranking Georgian official who directly handled missing persons and prisoner exchanges. Let them investigate it; I believe it is vital.

There is another interview currently sparking active debate in Georgian society—an interview with Nika Gvaramia, the former Prosecutor General and an opposition leader who recently served time and is now free. By the way, he is originally from Sukhumi. He pointed out that Georgian society spends far too much time clinging to memories, dwelling on what Abkhazia used to be, grieving its loss, and so on. He argues that they need to abandon this mindset and focus instead on the future—discussing what lies ahead rather than constantly digging through the past.

I think this is a very important message. How he visualizes it in practice and how it will unfold remains another question. Nonetheless, he asserts that the Abkhaz must be shown progress toward the European Union, demonstrating that they would feel secure and comfortable within it.

I believe any real initial steps must begin with trust, right? If trust is the goal, then we inevitably return to that ill-fated Law on Occupied Territories that restricts us in every way. That law would likely need to be repealed if you want to achieve results on the other side…

Astamur Tania: Well, at the same time, he sharply criticized the idea of fuel deliveries to the territory of Abkhazia.

Inal Khashig: There is no cohesive approach.

Astamur Tania: In my view, all of this belongs mostly to domestic political discourse. Abkhazia is simply being used there to heighten emotional intensity. That applies to Gvaramia’s statement, and I would emphasize once more that no one should draw far-reaching conclusions based on a single remark. We need to watch how public sentiment evolves.

As for Baramidze’s statements, there is nothing new for us here. Parties in any armed conflict live within a standard narrative—at least one generated for public consumption and propaganda—where only noble knights like Ivanhoe or Wilfred of Ivanhoe fought on your side, while the other side was made up of savages. In reality, to chart a path toward understanding this problem—despite all the complexities of our pre-war political relations with the Georgians (which, by the way, were barely evident at the everyday level, but certainly present politically due to differing national projects)—the primary responsibility always rests with the side that made the moral choice to resort to violence.

If a side made that moral choice, one must expect that military abuses of the kind Baramidze described would stem primarily from them. They did not dispatch regular units into Abkhazia without a track record; these were people whose hands were already stained with blood. They had just brutally suppressed the Zviadists in Samegrelo, gaining extensive experience in illegal detentions, arrests, and crackdowns. They were well-practiced in these methods, and naturally, such behavior came seamlessly to them.

For the residents of Abkhazia, it was an absolute shock—not only for the Abkhaz, but for local Georgians as well. They could not believe their own countrymen were capable of such actions, given the notorious criminal background of the leaders driving the entire process and the figures actively carrying it out.

Of course, as a conflict expands and intensifies, violations inevitably occur on all sides. It would be naive to imagine that the Abkhaz are the kind of people to turn the other cheek in such a situation; it is a completely different reality, and that must be understood.

Crimes were committed on both sides, but the fundamental responsibility for initiating the process rests with the party that started it.

As for their methods… why stick our heads in the sand? Those methods are well known, not just from what happened in Abkhazia, but from what took place within Georgia proper.

It is clear that due to current domestic political issues in Georgia, they prefer to sweep this topic under the rug. I see virtually no public discussion about what transpired in Western Georgia on the eve of the Georgian-Abkhazian conflict. A taboo has been placed on that topic for obvious reasons—nobody wants to reopen those raw wounds when society already faces so many problems. Nevertheless, it must be taken into account.

Sooner or later, history always resurfaces in its darker manifestations if we attempt to study it in a sanitized form. We must know this history in its entirety. As for that… I suppose that is everything I wanted to say on the matter. Yes.

We are operating against a very heavy historical backdrop, yet there are occasional glimmers showing that people are attempting to look at the problem from a different angle. This is even happening within government circles.

Take, for example, the statements made by Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze. We certainly do not expect him to tell us how wonderful we are or that they intend to recognize Abkhazia’s independence, but he did mention the restoration of confidence-building measures. That is a very important step. Occasionally, articles appear offering a relatively objective look at the history of our relations since ancient times. Furthermore, some Georgian writers are even addressing the notorious pseudo-scientific theory of Ingorokva, which has poisoned the minds of multiple generations. Granted, such pieces are rare amid the vast sea of opposing literature, but they do appear.

In that sense, there are small glimmers of hope that genuine realization will come.

We also need to draw conclusions regarding our own policies—for instance, concerning the Gali district. That is something we will inevitably need to address.

However, given the current lack of trust, any step forward is easily misinterpreted as granting unfair advantages to the other side. For that reason, I do not believe in grand, immediate solutions, nor do I think it is productive to debate overarching political questions right now. Instead, targeted measures—focusing on transport, communication, humanitarian concerns, and the movement of people and goods across the border—are precisely what would help establish the foundational conditions needed for genuine dialogue.

Inal Khashig: Let’s move on to another topic: the de-isolation of Abkhazia. In Turkey, a campaign to de-isolate Abkhazia is gaining momentum. On the one hand, it includes the recognition of Abkhaz passports as valid travel documents; on the other, it seeks to restore direct communication—specifically maritime links—between Turkey and Abkhazia that existed immediately after the war. For a time, those connections operated, people could travel, and passenger boats ran. Although that was later cut off, a campaign to revive it is unfolding now.

At first, this was an initiative driven by private individuals within the Abkhazian and Adyghe civil sector. It then expanded to the point where eight political parties represented in the Turkish parliament formed a united front, declaring that Abkhazia must be de-isolated. Initially, our Confederation of Abkhaz Communities in Turkey (Abkhazfed) reacted with a certain degree of possessiveness, arguing that the movement had no right to take the lead and that Abkhazfed should have authored the idea. It was a completely unnecessary friction. However, after Abkhazian society here voiced strong support and our Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement, a course correction took place. Representatives from both the initiative group and Abkhazfed met and reached a consensus that a consolidated movement for de-isolation is essential.

How do you view this prospect overall? On the one hand, these eight political parties belong to the opposition, spanning a varied spectrum from left to right. How viable is this initiative, and to what extent might it simply be an element of internal Turkish political maneuvering to capture votes—specifically from the Abkhaz and Adyghe diaspora, who by various estimates number up to four million—ahead of upcoming parliamentary and early presidential elections?

In your view, is this driven purely by domestic politics, or is there a real opportunity here to translate this into a broader movement originating from the civil sector and picked up by the opposition? Could Ankara actually take concrete steps such as de-isolating Abkhazia, recognizing Abkhaz passports, and reopening maritime transport?

Astamur Tania: Naturally, I supported this initiative—as did you and many others. It would be foolish not to support it. Indeed, many on our side did.

At the same time, we must recognize that over the last few decades, there has been an obvious degradation in our expert and public outreach across all fronts, including the Turkish direction.

I carefully read what Elchin Adzinba wrote. Fortunately, we have experts of such high caliber who understand the inner workings of Turkish politics. We must take his insights into account in our work, as there are bound to be hidden undercurrents. But in politics, nothing is ever entirely positive or entirely negative; it is a constant struggle. He called for expanding the circle of people with whom we engage because decisions on such a significant issue—whether made behind the scenes or officially voiced—are ultimately crafted in government corridors. This strategy ensures the effort does not look like a mere pawn in Turkey’s internal political competition. He specifically warned about this, and we must keep it in mind.

Returning to the reaction of our own society: it often resembles a sparkler. Something reactive happens, everyone flares up instantly, and then all at once it goes out, gets forgotten, and passes. In six months, no one will even remember it. That is the tragedy.

We still have public organizations and specialized institutions that operate on state funding. Previously, we periodically held conferences, including on legal issues, where our situation was discussed from the perspective of international law—specifically how our rights are restricted regarding freedom of movement, education, and other matters.

In international politics, only that which exists in the information space actually exists. If we say nothing ourselves—well, thank God Turkish Abkhazians stepped up to raise this topic. But the initial momentum ought to stem from here, as they do not face direct isolation problems themselves; they hold passports that allow free movement worldwide. Yet no initiative originated from our side.

As a proposal, we could hold a scientific conference—one with real public resonance. Rather than merely recounting history, it should analyze how this tightening of constraints came about, which norms of international law it violates, and what consequences it brings. Even if we set aside the Georgian side’s internal political confrontation, the de-isolation of Abkhazia does not contradict their interests either.

Obstacles are always created from that side. For instance, after the armed conflict, we conducted negotiations and signed documents on the non-use of force, peacekeeping forces, and refugee return procedures. Then they claimed it did not suit them because the return was too slow. Now they make empty claims about 300,000 refugees, even though that many people never lived in Abkhazia to begin with. Meanwhile, we returned about 50,000 refugees to the Gal district—which apparently was still not enough for their narrative.

Later, we held negotiations on confederate relations and union structures—using various terminologies from 1997 to 1998, up until the May events. Domestic political circumstances intervened again. In the end, who won? Neither the refugees nor Georgian society. The exact same logic applies to this issue.

Honestly, I would consider it rational if the Georgian side did not obstruct Abkhazia’s de-isolation, as it could easily be included in a package of measures to build mutual trust.

As for Ankara, everyone understands that if the Georgian side stated it had no objections, the matter would be resolved much more easily. Otherwise, it is difficult to predict how long it will take or whether it will yield concrete results.

However, the fact that both our society and our diaspora are actively engaged around this vital issue is a result in itself. Regardless of whether our passports are ultimately recognized in Turkey, it demonstrates that society is thinking about its prospects and modeling its future. It shows a living society.

And this is not our only challenge; we have plenty of other problems. Sometimes one recalls how dynamic things were in the 1990s and early 2000s—the proactive responses, the strong stances taken by different individuals and organizations. Now, it feels like a stagnant swamp, with only the occasional outburst. You cannot achieve results in such a state. We must work on all fronts and in all directions. Some efforts will succeed, others won’t—but it can be said with certainty that if you do nothing, nothing will happen.

Life recently forced us to deal with pressing issues like fuel supplies. We will face many more such challenges, and we will have to manage them. If you claim to be an independent state, you have to act like one. Independence is not just a collection of legislative acts and political declarations; it requires active work to fill those structures with real substance. It is a creative process.

If a nation lacks that creative drive, it begins to fade and dull. Unfortunately, we are observing this trend. You and I spoke about the Abkhaz language earlier—it is good that there is activity, though whether it will yield results remains to be seen. But above all, society must show signs of life. Nobody will look out for us if we don’t stand up for ourselves. That is what I wanted to say.

Inal Khashig: In any case, during our turbulent times—and not only in turbulent times, but in any period, whether peaceful or turbulent—there must be clear plans for the future. Moreover, there should be multiple options across all directions, including a Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C, along with continuous modeling of potential scenarios.

I am basing this once again on the recent gasoline crisis, when under Aslan Bzhania, a sudden decision was made to hand the entire fuel market over to a single pair of hands. One ought to have considered the consequences beforehand and anticipated how all of this would play out—not just focusing on how beautiful and well-maintained our gas stations would look, but realizing that the primary problem arises when there is no gasoline at those stations in the first place. That situation highlights a lack of deep analysis and the absence of a pragmatic, truly calculated strategy.

Astamur Tania: Well, you understand that we aren’t experts in all fields of government, right?

Inal Khashig: No, of course not.

Astamur Tania: On gasoline, I’m definitely not an expert, nor on these monopolies. One simply needs to involve the expert community where we do not understand. Give public resonance to the problem. I see many things being done, but they lack competent public coverage.

Inal Khashig: Astamur, say you have money, right? No level-headed businessman will tell you that all your money needs to be placed in one specific bank. He spreads it across different banks.

What I’m getting at is that when we have no oil of our own—oil might be lying around somewhere, but there is neither refining, nor extraction, nothing—and we buy this gasoline… When you buy this gasoline, there must be different sources.

Astamur Tania: Now you and I are going in circles. I agree with you, which is why we spoke about diversification.

Inal Khashig: On that note, we will actually conclude our conversation: with the fact that Astamur agrees.

Astamur Tania: To each his own sore point. As for me, I don’t drive.

Inal Khashig: I drive. It somehow turned out that not only I, but probably the majority of Abkhazian drivers go to sleep in the evening with the thought of where to refuel tomorrow, where to find this gasoline. And in the morning they wake up with the same thought. And I think that for the state, this should be the very last problem in reality—when for its citizens, their main thought consists of how to get gasoline. In short, so that we don’t have such problems, I will wrap up. Astamur, thank you very much.

Astamur Tania: Thank you. All the best.

Inal Khashig: Let there be light. Goodbye.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: ‘No to occupation and de facto annexation’: Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia
World.content:
Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia

A new public association, the Anti-Annexation Platform, has been established in Georgia.

Its founders say the group will be non-partisan and apolitical, with its main goal being to oppose Russia‘s occupation and de facto annexation of Georgian territories through legal and peaceful means.

At the platform’s launch at the Tbilisi Marriott hotel, a declaration entitled “No to occupation and de facto annexation – yes to justice, peace and Georgia’s territorial integrity” was adopted.

According to the declaration, the platform brings together Georgian citizens who regard the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principles of international law, freedom and human dignity as core values.

The founders say that Russia’s occupation in any form, the de facto annexation of the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions, support for separatism and forced demographic changes in the occupied territories constitute violations of international law and fundamental human rights.

The declaration also states that the organisation is ready to cooperate with members of any political party, regardless of their political affiliation.

Among the platform’s main objectives are supporting Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and promoting a legal assessment of Russia’s continuing occupation and de facto annexation.

The group plans to work to protect the rights of internally displaced people and refugees from the occupied territories, prepare legal research and analytical papers, and raise public awareness of developments in the occupied regions.

The platform also intends to cooperate with international partners, think tanks and diplomatic missions. Its activities will include organising conferences, discussions and educational events, as well as helping to protect the rights of people affected by the occupation and de facto annexation.

The platform supports targeted international sanctions against the leaders of the de facto regimes in the occupied regions and individuals involved in the annexation process. The declaration also calls for efforts to initiate international criminal proceedings.

The document stresses that the group’s activities will not be limited to the political agenda.

“We believe that the struggle against occupation and de facto annexation by the Russian Federation is not only a political issue. It is a struggle for justice, human dignity, historical truth and the security of future generations,” the declaration says.

According to its founders, the platform is based on the peaceful and legal resolution of conflicts, respect for international law and the protection of human rights.

“Russia’s de facto or de jure annexation will never become a legal reality, and borders changed by force will never acquire moral or legal legitimacy,” the declaration says.

The declaration was signed by the founders of the Anti-Annexation Platform:

World.title: Azerbaijani athletes win seven medals at fourth stage of Beach Wrestling World Series
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Azerbaijani athletes won seven medals at the fourth stage of the Beach Wrestling World Series.

At the competition held at the Sea Breeze resort complex, Vusal Aliyev (80 kg), Ashraf Ashirov (90 kg), and Jamal Feyziyev (+90 kg) won gold medals.

Sahib Dadashov (80 kg) and Nargiz Samadova (60 kg) claimed silver medals. Javid Niftalizade (80 kg) and Ramiz Hasanov (90 kg) finished the tournament with bronze medals.

The Azerbaijani men's national team topped the team standings with 84 points. Georgia finished second with 62 points, while Ukraine took third place with 45 points. In the women's team standings, Azerbaijan ranked second with 40 points. Ukraine finished first with 100 points, while Spain came third with 24 points.

It should be noted that 55 wrestlers from 14 countries participated in the competition, which was held in Azerbaijan for the first time. The final stage of the World Series will take place on September 26–27 in Katerini, Greece. The world champions will be determined based on the points accumulated across all stages following the final event.

World.title: All media entities operating in Azerbaijan must comply with legal requirements – Media Development Agency
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Some information resources operating in the Republic of Azerbaijan act on behalf of various communities residing in the country, attempting to position themselves as media outlets representing the interests of these national minorities, the Media Development Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan (MEDIA) said.

“In this regard, we emphasize that all media entities operating within the territory of the Republic of Azerbaijan must comply with the requirements of the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan ‘On Media’ and be registered in the Media Registry Information System in accordance with the procedure established by law.

The website ‘Ajmedia.news’, which presents itself as an information portal established at the initiative of the Azerbaijan Jewish Media Center and public figures of Jewish origin, does not comply with media ethics requirements in its published materials and is not registered in the Media Registry Information System.

Furthermore, in connection with violations of the requirements of the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan ‘On Media’, the court has issued a relevant ruling concerning this resource, and its activities have been deemed unlawful.

We once again emphasize that all media entities, including those acting on behalf of any community or social group and engaged in media activities, must strictly comply with legal requirements and provide the public with accurate, objective, and transparent information about their legal and professional status, area of activity, and nature of representation,” the statement said.

World.title: Calls for better solutions as Kalgoorlie marks 10 years since protest
World.content:
Ten years on from a riot that erupted in the centre of Western Australia's gold capital, some local leaders say not enough has been done to engage the region's youth.

WARNING: This article contains information about an Indigenous person who is deceased.

It was August 30, 2016, when 200 people descended on Kalgoorlie's main street in anger.

The day before, 14-year-old Elijah Doughty had been killed when he was run over by a man attempting to recover a stolen motorbike.

The community was expressing frustrations at what they described as racism that had reached "boiling point".

A protest broke out in front of the local court house, where a 55-year-old man made his first appearance on charges related to the teenager's death.

Police in riot gear confront protesters on Hannan Street, Kalgoorlie, on August 30, 2016. (ABC: John Wibberley)

The man, whose identity is suppressed, was later found not guilty of manslaughter, but was convicted of a lesser charge of dangerous driving occasioning death, and sentenced to three years in jail.

As the court proceedings ended, Indigenous leaders and the community turned their attention to what needed to change in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

Big promises

The spotlight was on Kalgoorlie-Boulder, 600 kilometres east of Perth, which resulted in state and federal politicians flying into the city for a summit to address racial tensions and social issues in the community

Protesters confronted officers as tensions escalated in August 2016. (ABC: John Wibberley)

The summit identified eight key areas for improvement, with the lack of targeted family and youth support identified as the number one issue holding back the city.

Youth centres such as a safe house and drop-in centre were identified as priorities, with relatives, experts, youth, and teachers saying the town was in dire need of more dedicated targeted support.

Despite the attention and agreements made, some on the ground say not much has changed 10 years later.

A decade on

Bill Ring is the chair of the Eastern Goldfields First Nations Council and a former youth justice worker who has spent years fighting for better outcomes for Indigenous youth in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

Mr Ring said he had seen improvements, but feared politicians had forgotten about the issues identified as time had passed.

"There's a lot of ideas chucked around by what can be changed with youth … one thing that was brought up was a drop-in centre," he said.

Bill Ring says not enough has been done in the past decade to support young people. (ABC News: Robert Koenig-Luck)

"That could have been one of the things that could have happened, and also support for young people who are sort of going through a rough time … like through community camps and things like that.

"But those didn't eventuate and it just got mothballed."

Eastern Goldfields First Nations Council vice-chair Leanne Eriksen said there was a strong push for many of the outcomes of the forum to be community-led.

She said there was little follow-up to actions promised in the forum.

"[There's a] lack of integrity around follow-through, listening to community voices, and then actually managing and maintaining these programs and services and actions," Ms Eriksen said.

"The Aboriginal community was obviously extremely distressed and angry and hurt and sad and everything in between.

"It was another of those situations where a critical incident happens and then government at all levels obviously [jump] into the space," Ms Eriksen said.

So what changed?

Items that were actioned by the state Liberal government at the time included re-opening Kalgoorlie's Department of Indigenous Affairs office, which had been closed in 2015.

The Federal Government also provided $660,000 towards expanding the Goldfields Land and Sea Council's ranger program as another pathway.

In 2017, the Police and Community Youth Centre (PCYC) received federal government funding to run safeSPACE, a service aimed at early intervention and engagement.

The candlelit vigil was held at the place where Elijah died, after the conclusion of court proceedings. (ABC News: Charlotte Hamlyn)

Mr Ring said the PCYC programs were a step in the right direction, but the community wanted a dedicated centre for all youth.

He also believes some young people may be put off by the presence of police, and that a better result would come from a dedicated cross-cultural centre.

Authorities at Fitzroy Crossing credited a youth night space with reducing youth crime in the remote town. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Aboriginal-led night space services in other parts of the state provide refuge, food, and activities for young people.

"You've got places up in the Kimberley, in Wyndham, they used to run their own sort of youth hub and they have programs and they set the program themselves and that works," Mr Ring said.

"So why can't it work in the Goldfields?"

Then-mayor John Bowler said at the time it was too expensive for the city to run a full-time youth centre. (ABC Goldfields-Esperance: Nathan Morris )

The City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder has not ruled out the idea of a drop-in centre, with its youth action plan stating it was "exploring" the feasibility of an indoor drop-in space.

Manager of community development Lauren Chapman-Holle said the city was running ongoing activities to engage with young people.

"It's less-intensive than a full-scale drop-in centre, but it's trying to find the right model that works for the community," she said.

WA Premier Roger Cook didn't have an answer as to why Kalgoorlie-Boulder does not have a drop-in centre, but said it was important to ensure social services were made available to young people.

An alternative model

Leonora, 200km north of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, has a population of 567 and has introduced programs to engage young people with similar issues.

Leonora is a remote town about 800km east of Perth. (ABC Goldfields: Giulia Bertoglio)

Rene Reddingius is the coach of the Blazers Basketball team, which aims to provide young people with a sense of purpose.

"Our program is using basketball as a conduit to engage kids and build life skills and a sense of purpose," he said.

"By implementing the program and, you know, developing strong relationships and safe places for children, children will choose to come to a space or engage.

" Creating a new normal [and] having a counterbalance for a lot of negative choices that are out there is very, very important and that's really what Blazers does. "

Blazers' coach Rene Reddingius, affectionately known as "Pop", engages youth through sport in Leonora. (ABC Goldfields: Giulia Bertoglio)

Community leader Colleen Berry, who operates a women's community hub in the town, believes Kalgoorlie needs a similar program.

"It would be lovely to have a big youth centre in Kalgoorlie. We have one here that keeps our younger ones occupied," Ms Berry said.

Colleen Berry has helped set up youth support in Leonora, and says Kalgoorlie desperately needs something similar. (ABC Goldfields: Robert Koenig-Luck)

"[Without support] they'll continue down the road they're going until … they turn 18 [and then] they will be going to the big boys' prison, and we don't want that.

"We don't want that because it's not good."

World.title: A 'pigeon overlord', celebrity visits and iconic spheres: Rundle Mall turns 50
World.content:
Fifty years ago, then-SA premier Don Dunstan decided to remove cars from a section of Rundle Street to create the country's first major pedestrian-only shopping mall.

It was a controversial move at the time to pedestrianise the area.

"In one corner you've got the cars, in the other corner you've got the pedestrians, then you've got the small traders over there, and the big traders who want it," said local historian Keith Conlon.

"There was a lot of friction about whether this ought to happen, which seems strange now.

" It was almost like we had the [boxing] ring set in the middle of Gawler Place and Rundle Mall to be. "

Rundle Mall was opened on September 1, 1976 to a crowd of about 10,000 people, complete with a champagne-filled fountain.

Vehicles, pictured in 1928, on Rundle Street, which would become Rundle Mall. (Supplied: History Trust SA)

Dunstan promised a space that would be for more than just shopping.

"It wasn't just going to be a shopping place, but where people could come and stroll, meet one another, enjoy an open-air activity, and at the same time, of course, go and purchase what they wanted to," he told the crowd.

About 10,000 gathered for the opening of Adelaide's Rundle Mall. (Supplied: Rundle Mall)

Fifty years later, Rundle Mall's executive manager Andrew White said he was excited to celebrate that approach on its anniversary.

"It's not just about coming and doing shopping, it's also where culture and social life occurs in South Australia," he said.

Andrew White says Rundle Mall is about more than shopping. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

A 'pigeon overlord' and other iconic art

One of the most well-known elements of Rundle Mall is the public art, with Mr White describing it as "an outdoor art gallery" — including the iconic Mall's Balls, installed in 1977.

"It really now is part of what you automatically think of," Mr Conlon said.

The Mall's Balls are an iconic Adelaide landmark. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

But some of the art has been met with friction over time.

The original designer of the Mall's Balls — officially named Spheres — was "dismayed" by the decision to move them in 2013.

And the four pigs which call Rundle Mall home — Horatio, Oliver, Truffles and August — were met with some questions when they were installed in the 1990s, according to Mr Conlon.

The Rundle Mall pigs. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"Of course now, they're Instagram favourites around the world," he said.

Most recently a giant pigeon was installed in 2020, a piece the artist said was in tribute to the "proud flaneurs, promenading through our leisure and retail precincts".

The Pigeon is a newer addition to Rundle Mall. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We had the Mall's Balls come in, we've got the pigeon overlord, which is quite iconic now," Mr White said.

"All these things that start off where people are a little bit unsure, they become part of the fabric of this place."

Famous faces at the Mall

Rundle Mall has also seen its share of famous faces.

In 1977, not long after it was opened, Queen Elizabeth II visited.

Queen Elizabeth II was among the most notable visitors to Rundle Mall. (Supplied: University of Melbourne Archives)

A few years later, about 25,000 people descended on the Mall to listen to British pop star sensation Boy George.

Boy George performed in Rundle Mall in 1984 to a crowd of thousands. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

"We've had some of the great Australian artists here [too], but as well as that, it's where you celebrate things," Mr Conlon said.

"You celebrate multicultural festivals, you celebrate when your netball team wins, when the Thunderbirds win the whole mall turns pink.

Hundreds of Thunderbirds fans flocked to Rundle Mall to celebrate the recent premiership win by Adelaide. (ABC News)

"It's a place where you come, not just to shop, but to meet and do things."

Although much has changed since the 1970s, Mr Conlon said he believed Rundle Mall had kept in step with what was a cutting edge idea 50 years ago.

"It's always moving and changing but I think the continuing thread for the mall is that it's a community hub, a people hub," he said.

"The really continuing flavour of the mall for me is the people and what they come to see. So this has always been much more than a shopping mall."
