World.title: Older Australians weigh cost of changes to health insurance rebates
World.content:
For most of her life, Sue Donnelly has paid for private health insurance.

But now, with price increases on the way, she and her husband are considering ending their cover.

"We're 78 and 81; we really need to have it," Ms Donnelly said from her home in regional Victoria.

" But, at present, I'm paying $349 a month and it's going to go up further. "

The federal government this year proposed legislation to reduce the private health insurance rebate that currently applies to over-65s.

The change would mean rebates would be "age-neutral" and determined by income alone, leaving impacted premiums with an increase of between 4 and 8 per cent.

Ms Donnelly said she didn't have a lot of incoming funds and was worried about how the change would impact them.

"It's money I have to really make sure I put to one side every month," she said.

" Surely, they don't need more from us. I think that's not fair. "

Public system under pressure

Estimates from Private Healthcare Australia show 62,000 older Australians would likely cease their private health insurance as a result of the proposed changes, with another 200,000 potentially downgrading theirs.

The Shadow Regional Health Minister and Member for Mallee, Anne Webster, said she was worried about how the public health system would cope if a large cohort of older Australians suddenly shifted away from private health insurance.

"When private services disappear, patients do not. They are pushed into the public system," she said.

Anne Webster wants to see the legislation walked back, following backlash from the states, insurance companies and senior advocates. (ABC Mildura Swan Hill)

" Regional hospitals are already struggling with workforce shortages, long waiting lists and limited specialist access. "

Dr Webster said the Mildura Base Public Hospital, located in her electorate of Mallee, already has "enormous wait times" and concerns around staffing, which she said could worsen under the change.

Health ministers from South Australia, New South Wales, Queensland and Tasmania have also spoken in opposition, citing concerns for older Australians and hospitals in their own states.

Funds already losing members

Mildura Health Fund is a not-for-profit member-owned fund, with more than 40,000 members, 41 per cent of whom are over 65.

Chief Executive Officer Gerard Op de Coul has been lobbying against the proposed legislation. He said rising costs had already led to customers ending their cover, even before the proposed reduced rebate comes in.

National Seniors Australia has a cost calculator on its website to help people estimate how much their bill will increase by if the bill becomes law.

The organisation estimated, from the rebate cut alone, annual payments could grow by more than $1,000 for a couple with "gold level" cover.

Gerard Op de Coul says the increase in memberships at Mildura Health Fund is not as strong as usual. (Supplied: Mildura Health Fund)

However, Mr Op de Coul said premiums could increase by as much as 12 per cent for older Australian come April, due to a mix of both the proposed rebate reduction and rising costs in the medical industry.

"This is going to affect a huge amount of people locally … there will be people dropping out," he said.

"Our [over-65] membership base is above average, so we would expect that we would be hit harder than in other areas."

Minister says no 'material impact'

The rebate change was first put forward in in the 2026-27 budget and is tipped to save the government $3 billion over four years.

Mark Butler says there will be no impact on public hospitals as a result of the change. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Speaking on ABC Radio Perth, Health Minister Mark Butler hit back against claims the public health system would get busier.

"Some of the modelling put about by the private health insurance industry itself thinks that it will, but our modelling says no, there won't be a material impact on private health insurance membership," he said.

A government spokesperson revealed the commonwealth expected the overall number of people with private health insurance would increase, including for people aged over 65.

Mr Butler said "every single dollar" saved through the change would be invested in new aged care services "that, frankly, we just have to start putting in place if older Australians are going to get the care and dignity that they deserve".

Conflicting data

University of Melbourne Professor Yuting Zhang is the co-author of a recent report analysing how tax penalties and subsidies impact private health insurance.

Professor Zhang says older Australians need to evaluate benefits versus cost. (Supplied)

She said it was unlikely older Australians would end their private health insurance, as the benefits outweigh the costs.

"[The impact on public hospitals] is going to be quite small because not a lot of people are going to drop [their private health insurance] because of this bill," Professor Zhang said.

"[Older Australians] still get lots of benefit by holding their private cover and they are most likely not going to switch into the public system."

The report estimates about 42,000 people would drop their cover across Australia.

The National Seniors Australia director of policy and research, Brendon Radford, said the organisation was "disappointed" by the bill and said the government was "downplaying" the issue.

Dr Radford says private health insurance is one of the top concerns in terms of affordability for older people. (Supplied: National Seniors Australia)

He said the data used in the government's models was "not as good as it should be".

"It only accounts for people dropping their policy," he said.

" There are [also] the significant number of people who will actually downgrade their policy, which is just as much of a concern, because when they downgrade their policy, the private health insurers need to find money elsewhere, so they'll raise prices. "

A Senate Community Affairs Legislation Committee's inquiry into the bill will be presented on October 7.

The government will need the support of the Greens or crossbench to pass the legislation.

World.title: Can tiny bubbles restore health to the Torrens lake?
World.content:
Locals and business owners are calling for the Adelaide City Council to trial an emerging technology that could help end regular closures of the Torrens Lake due to bacteria.

The current closure — due to enterococci bacteria — is the third time this year where parts of the River Torrens has been made inaccessible to users, including rowing clubs and boat operators.

High levels of E. coli bacteria infiltrated the lake earlier this year as thousands of dead fish were seen on its banks.

The Torrens Lake has been regularly closed on public health grounds in 2026. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Singer-songwriter and local resident John Schumann is leading a charge to clean up the river with 'nanobubble' technology, which has been previously tested in New South Wales.

He has made a submission calling on the council to test the technology in the lake.

"It's supposed to be the centrepiece of Adelaide, and it doesn't have to be like this, and that's my frustration," Mr Schumann said.

"I live nearby and I use the path around the lake and through the parklands.

" I am aware, painfully aware, that this lake is a disgrace. "

John Schumann has made deputations to Adelaide City Council to trial nanobubble technology. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

What is 'nanobubble' technology?

Nanobubble technology generates microscopic bubbles using gases like oxygen and ozone, then mixes them throughout water bodies to help break down chemical contaminants and also reduce microbial growth.

Dr Arash Zamyadi is a senior lecturer of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Monash University and researches nanobubble technology in Australia.

"We use a really, really low amount of energy to diffuse the solution, which is the nanobubble," said Dr Zamyadi.

"That has the capacity to break down the contaminants, both the microbes, the pathogens, and the chemicals like the toxins."

It was recently used in a year-long trial by Wagga Wagga City Council in NSW to remediate Lake Albert.

The technology was put forward by Council Charles Sturt to tackle the algae in West Lakes last year but was opposed by SA Water and the state's Environmental Protection Authority, due to a lack of scientific evidence and uncertainty of its impact on wildlife.

Dr Zamyadi understands authorities' hesitation.

"It's a very new, innovative technology, which definitely needs more feasibility studies and understanding its performance," said Dr Zamyadi.

"I totally understand that there is concern from the regulators, from the authorities, from the managers, from the engineers, and I believe that's the role of the science [to perform] independent evaluation and assessment.

"When you look at the case of Lake Albert in Wagga Wagga, there was no report of loss of any other form of aquatic life, it really targets the algal blooms and the associated contaminants."

Trial to be discussed by council

Closures of the Torrens Lake restrict access to rowing clubs and boat operators like Tony Shuman, who operates cruising riverboats.

He supports the push to trial nanobubble technology in the river.

"Let's try something rather than nothing," Mr Shuman said.

Tony Shuman would like to see action taken to improve the health of the River Torrens. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

In a statement, the Adelaide City Council said it was "in discussions with other councils and government agencies about ways to improve the management of the River Torrens system and catchment area".

"The proposed nanobubble technology trial is a separate matter which will be discussed by elected members in coming weeks," the statement said.

Deputy Lord Mayor Carmel Noon is supportive of the trial and said it was council's responsibility to look after the Torrens Lake.

"I'm very adamant that we have a major role here to be able to mitigate this," she said.

Deputy Mayor Carmel Noon is supportive of the trial. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

"So I'm wanting a trial. It would be amazing that we could actually stop the closures of this part of the river that affects so many businesses and livelihoods."

If the trial proceeds, nanobubble technology would be installed between the Torrens Weir and Albert Bridge at Frome Road.

Cr Noon said she hopes to expand it further along the river and across multiple council areas if a trial were successful.

World.title: Learner's licence needed to keep pedalling under new Queensland laws
World.content:
Sophie Tobin-Webb has been forced to get her learner's licence to continue riding her e-bike, as Queensland becomes one of the only places in the world with such a mandate.

From August 31, riders will need to be at least 16 and hold a driver's licence to ride an e-bike or e-scooter solo in Queensland as the new stage of the state's laws cracking down on e-devices rolls out.

Children aged between 12 and 17, without a learner's licence, will be able to ride under parental supervision after the government watered down its initial proposal of a blanket ban on under 16s.

Since July, police have had the power to seize and destroy illegal devices, randomly breath test riders and to fine parents when children under 16 are found to be riding illegally.

A man was charged with riding a personal mobility device while over the general alcohol limit in the early hours of July 1. (Supplied: Queensland Police)

Devices faster than 25km/h have been banned and riders have been limited to riding at 12km/h on footpaths, while fines for a range of offences have increased.

Over three years, Ms Tobin-Webb has clocked up 5,000 kilometres on her e-bike across Brisbane, with its pedal assistance giving her "a little bit of oomph".

"I use it basically every day to get to work, drop the kids off at kindy, for groceries and general outings," she said.

Sophie Tobin-Webb rides her e-bike across Brisbane, including to work and with her children. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

"For me, I have never needed a licence. I have relied on public transport, my bike or walking.

"I realised I had to get my L's if I wanted to keep riding my bike.

"I thought about going back to my analogue, so my non-e-bike, but getting two kids around on that in Brisbane's humidity is pretty challenging."

While Ms Tobin-Webb had to fork out $80 and complete an online test for her learner's licence, she understands it will not be as simple for others.

Sophie Tobin-Webb says she initially felt conflicted about having to get her learner's licence to keep riding her e-bike. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

'Reluctance' among health professionals

Those who are unable to drive due to a medical condition or disability will be eligible to apply for an exemption, with a three-month grace period until November 29 to allow riders to comply.

The legislation introduced to parliament was amended to include the exemption after community backlash to the initial proposal.

Queensland Advocacy Incorporated chief executive Matilda Alexander said while the move was welcome, she was concerned people with disability "already have to grapple with the administrative burden of accessing multiple schemes and exemptions just to live an ordinary life".

To be granted an exemption, a rider is required to complete a form, which needs to be signed off by a registered health practitioner who can verify they appear capable of safely operating their e-mobility device.

A doctor may put conditions on a person's e-mobility use, for example requiring they be supervised or only ride during the day.

Erica Gannon says the Australian Medical Association has been consistently advocating for a ban on under-16s riding. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Australian Medical Association Queensland (AMAQ) President Associate Professor Erica Gannon said the peak body had never called for, nor supported, the licensing requirement, with protecting the safety of children its primary concern.

A 13-year-old boy died in hospital on Saturday after sustaining critical injuries in an e-scooter crash in the Bundaberg region on Wednesday.

The crash prompted the AMAQ to reiterate its calls for a blanket ban on under 16s from riding e-scooters.

Dr Gannon said without it, "we will continue to see these tragic crashes, more preventable child injuries and potential loss of life".

"Children under 16 years simply do not have the skills needed to ride these devices safely, especially around vehicles, other riders and pedestrians," she said.

Study reveals scope of child e-scooter injuries Between 2021 and 2024, e-scooter injury-related admissions at Queensland Children's Hospital more than doubled, the study found.

A Department of Transport and Main Roads spokesperson said the new age and licensing requirements would "improve safety by ensuring riders have basic road rule knowledge and the maturity needed to use these devices safely in public places".

Dr Gannon said more engagement was needed with community groups and medical specialists to ensure accurate decisions can be made when assessing whether a person who cannot hold a driver's licence should be granted an exemption.

"GPs, specialists and neurologists have all expressed significant concern and a reluctance to want to sign off on an exemption form without the proper stakeholder involvement and more clarity around those guidelines," she said.

'Very difficult for tourists'

Under the new laws, equivalent interstate and international driver's licences will also be accepted to ride e-devices.

However, Bicycle Queensland chief executive Matthew Burke holds concerns for those who travel without their licence.

Matthew Burke says Queensland's new laws will make it difficult for tourists to ride in Queensland. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"It's going to be difficult, very difficult for tourists. They don't tend to come with an international driver's licence; they tend to come just with a passport," he said.

" We've made Queensland the hardest place in the world to ride a safe, legal e- bike. "

Operators of e-mobility device rentals, including Lime and Neuron, will have until March next year to take reasonable steps to ensure riders meet age and licensing requirements.

This may include written or in-app declarations, sighting a rider's licence at the time of hire and rider declarations in the mobile app.

These rules also apply to short-term holiday rentals and longer-term subscription models.

The Queensland government introduced laws in response to community concern over the dangerous use of e-bikes, especially among children. (Supplied)

Lime's Asia-Pacific leader Will Peters said the operator is continuing to call for an exemption for shared schemes.

"The shared schemes were caught in a little bit of a political football here because we did see completely abhorrent behaviour from some people riding e-bikes," he said.

"They weren't riding share bikes, and I think those bikes should be crushed, they should be cracked down on, and we really want to give people the opportunity to actually access e-bikes and e-scooters."

Lime has e-scooters and e-bikes in Brisbane and on the Gold Coast. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Mr Peters said Lime is working with the Department of Transport to ensure there is a "seamless transition".

"We do think they [the government] went a little too far here, but we are certainly in constant communication to ensure those measures are mitigated on our side and we will continue to watch this space," he said.

The number of people hiring an e-bike and e-scooter is expected to keep growing over summer, according to Mr Peters, with Lime looking towards how Brisbane will respond when the world visits.

"When we have got events such as the Olympics and we have got tourism booming … we need to make sure that any measures or legislation and regulation that is put on to any public transport service is not a blunt instrument," he said.

"We made our views very clear that the shared schemes, they do carry a load-bearing arm of that transport network and they're further going to do that, especially coming up to the Olympics."

World.title: Runway incursions on the rise across Australian airports, says expert
World.content:
With air safety under the microscope after a spate of runway conflicts in Sydney, new research says incidents have significantly risen at Australian airports in the last 22 years.

Since late July, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) has opened six investigations into runway incursions and taxiing occurrences at Sydney Airport, with the two most recent cases announced on Wednesday.

The ATSB said on August 16, air traffic control ‌told a Virgin 737 to give way to a Qantas 737 leaving the runway but the instruction was not relayed correctly and the mistake went unnoticed by air control.

On August 25, incomplete traffic information was passed to a Jetstar Airbus A320, which resulted in a Bombardier Dash 8 taxiing behind the aircraft.

On August 25, incomplete traffic information was passed to a Jetstar Airbus A320. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The ATSB said only one incident, in which a Jetstar crew member was injured on August 9, had been categorised as a "near collision".

It said a second incident has been classed as a "serious incident", while the remaining four had only met the threshold for "incidents".

The incidents piqued the interest of Graham Wild, an aviation discipline coordinator at the University of New South Wales (UNSW), who identified a broader pattern of incidents increasing across Australian airports.

With a specific focus on runway incursions and taxiing collisions or near collisions, Dr Wild analysed data from the ATSB from 2003 to 2025.

In his analysis, Dr Wild measured the count and rate of occurrences per million flight hours, to assess whether runway incursions and taxiing incidents were rising faster than the amount of flying.

He found for domestic aviation, taxiing collisions or near-collision occurrences increased on average by about one additional occurrence every three years.

For commercial air transport, which includes regional, charter and freight aircraft, Dr Wild found the number of runway incursions increased on average by about three additional occurrences every two years.

Dr Wild said overall there was a trend of safety improving but the ultimate goal in the aviation sector was to achieve a zero figure.

"[If] we had modern surveillance [like] what we do with drones … in terms of knowing where aircraft are and having a more connected system, technology would solve a lot of those problems," he said.

'Consistent with average reporting levels'

A spokesperson for Airservices Australia said that "reporting and examining operational incidents is an important part of the aviation safety system".

The spokesperson said since January 2021 it reported on average about 34 occurrences per month at Sydney Airport.

Air safety is under the microscope at Sydney Airport. (ABC News: John Gunn)

In comparison, there were on average 21 monthly occurrences reported at Brisbane Airport, and 12 at Melbourne Airport.

"The number of reports made by Airservices to the ATSB regarding occurrences in Sydney during August is consistent with average reporting levels," the spokesperson added.

" Airservices reviews reportable occurrences in accordance with established safety processes and will cooperate fully with the ATSB investigations. "

A spokesperson for Sydney Airport said safety was its "highest priority" but said it would be "inappropriate to speculate" while ATSB investigations were underway.

Earlier this month, ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said as part of its "wide-ranging" investigations, understaffing issues within the airport's air traffic control fleet would be scrutinised.

Civil Air president Scott Nugent previously told the ABC that air traffic control resources were stretched and Sydney Airport relied on staff doing excessive overtime, with some potentially working 20 extra hours a week.

Future of air traffic control safety

Uğur Turhan says strategic planning is important for the future air traffic control workforce. (Supplied: Libby Moorhead)

Uğur Turhan, who specialises in air traffic management, airport operations and aviation safety at UNSW, said Australia had a strong and transparent aviation safety culture.

He said the recent series of incidents, which remain under ATSB investigation, had understandably placed air traffic controllers under increased professional pressure and public scrutiny.

Dr Turhan said strategic planning was important for the future air traffic control workforce.

He said digital towers, which will be used for operations at Western Sydney Internation Airport (WSI) when it opens in late October, could lead Australia's technology and safety protocols.

Unlike Sydney Airport's manned-air traffic control tower, WSI's air traffic controllers will be stationed at a data centre 20-kilometres away from where the planes will be flying.

WSI will be controlled at a digitised centre in Eastern Creek. (Supplied)

It marks Australia's first digital air traffic control system off the tarmac.

"With digital tower technology, controllers can have additional information and decision support aids such as aircraft tracking and enhanced visual information, which can support their situational awareness," Dr Turhan said.

Managing director for Aviation Projects Keith Tonkin said progress was already underway to integrate Australia's civilian and defence traffic management systems into one.

He pointed to the OneSky Project, an initiative that would technologically advance air traffic control and safety.

The program was announced in 2014 and has faced significant scheduling and cost challenges, but Mr Tonkin was hopeful for a 2027 rollout.

Keith Tonkin says the aviation sector was integrating its civilian and defence traffic management systems. (ABC News: Crystalyn Brown)

He said by integrating the systems, there would be more efficient use of airspace as better information would be available to allocate aircraft into the airspace.

"It also will mean that air traffic controllers will be able to be more effective and be able to more easily adapt to changes in the airspace system," he said.

"And the idea is that they won't need quite as much training to change roles or to change the different parts of the airspace that they're controlling."

Investigations ongoing

In a statement to the ABC an ATSB spokesperson said in its investigations, it would seek to establish or rule out any underlying safety issues and contributing factors common across the incidents at Sydney Airport.

"In each incident there was a level of safety defence, such as the actions of pilots, controllers and ground crews, that has prevented more serious outcomes from occurring," the spokesperson said. "But our investigations will seek to provide assurances around the safety defences in place, and any steps that can be taken to prevent reoccurrences."

Retired airline pilot says Sydney Airport safety incident 'diminished' Sydney Airport could face "catastrophic" consequences if safety issues are not addressed, a former pilot and aviation safety investigator says.

A spokesperson for the Civil Aviation Safety Authority said it was looking closely into air traffic control at Sydney tower and would "not hesitate to act" if any broader safety concerns emerged.

"While the ATSB examines what happened in each incident, our focus is on whether there are any underlying operational or system issues that could affect safety," the spokesperson said.

"The aviation system is designed around managing errors with multiple safeguards in place, and based on the information currently available, none of the incidents indicate an immediate safety risk requiring urgent regulatory action."

Qantas and Virgin Australia are working closely with the ATSB, but declined to comment further when contacted by the ABC.

World.title: Boy dies in hospital days after e-scooter crash
World.content:
A teenage boy has died in hospital days after sustaining critical injuries in an e-scooter crash.

Emergency services were called to Macrossan Street at Childers, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, at about 6pm on Wednesday after a single-vehicle crash involving an e-scooter.

The 13-year-old sustained serious head injuries and was flown to Queensland Children’s Hospital in a critical condition.

He died in hospital on Saturday.

Speaking on Thursday, Bundaberg Highway Patrol officer in charge Sergeant Gordon Hard said the events leading up to the crash were not clear.

"To the best of my knowledge he was wearing a helmet," he said.

"Paramedics performed CPR before that child was flown to Brisbane."

Police say investigations are ongoing.

It is the second fatal e-scooter incident in the region.

A 39-year-old Hervey Bay man died in a crash involving his e-scooter and an electric skateboard in July.

World.title: Families lost everything when a bushfire hit town. This club helped them heal
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Families lost everything when a bushfire hit town. This club helped them heal Danny Russell August 30, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It is Thursday night at Harcourt Football Netball Club, and it soon becomes evident that fire has changed the way they view success. The under-12 side is having a scratch match against their parents. Laughter breaks out when a dad slips over and almost pings his hammy. A son sells his mother some candy as he dances around her outstretched arms and delivers the ball neatly to a teammate. Harcourt’s under-12 side plays a scratch match against the parents. Justin McManus President Mark Dorian is busily unravelling cords and plugging a cash machine into the bar before clearing tables for the Thursday night meals – pizzas and a hearty scoop of Neapolitan ice-cream for the kids. There is a buzz around the club as five teams enter a weekend of finals, including their senior team against Navarre at Maryborough’s Princes Park on Sunday.



Related Article Victoria bushfires ‘A damn lot of luck’: How three Victorian towns were spared by unstoppable fires But evidence of January’s devastating bushfire is never far away. Blackened trees, their branches regenerating with sprouting leaves, stand at the edge of the recreation reserve’s elevated car park, revealing just how close the flames came to engulfing the clubrooms. A damp clearing, to the west of the ground, is all that is left of the Harcourt Cooperative Cool Store – a vital storage base for up to 90 local businesses that was razed to the ground. More than 50 houses were lost. As Dorian emerges from the clubrooms, he trades witty quips with parents enjoying an afternoon drink.



Through his guidance Harcourt Football Netball Club has become a crucial focal point for the community. With support from AFL Victoria and Netball Victoria, one of the first things they did was offer free registration, free uniforms and free equipment for families. Then they provided free meals on a Thursday night. Members of Harcourt Football and Netball Club in the recovering bush at the edge of their oval. From left: Harper, Bonnie, Cohen, senior coach Sam Gale, captain Tom Walters, Austin, Judd, Joel and Raf. Justin McManus “We just made a big effort to try and bring normality to people’s lives. I mean, especially for the juniors, it was really about having a place to go,” Dorian says. “People are still going through all sorts of things now, whether they lost everything, or it affects their work, or who knows? It affects people in different ways. But what this does is gives people a place to unwind, and get away from it, even if it’s for an hour or so, and just enjoy being around people.”



Mother-of-two Shelby is one of those people. The junior coach is putting the under-11 netballers through their paces ahead of their weekend final and also plays for the club’s C-grade team. She admits she is still finding her feet after the fire burnt her rental home to the ground. More than 50 homes were lost in the fires in Harcourt and the surrounding area. Justin McManus Shelby, who asks for her surname not to be used for privacy reasons, and her son and her daughter lost all of their possessions. They are living temporarily at her father’s farm where she works part-time and studies social work.



“It’s a very long process [recovering], especially when there’s already a shortage of houses in the country,” she says. “When you lose 53 [houses] in one community, it makes it very challenging to house everybody. But yeah, this has been a place that we can come, we can enjoy ourselves, we can feel supported, and just find that purpose still. And sport is so good for mental health.” Harcourt Football Netball Club president Mark Dorian during Thursday night training. Justin McManus Members of the Harcourt senior football side are filtering into the ground. The Lions are looking to bounce back after last week’s three-point loss to Talbot. But for some, winning their semi-final on Sunday will be a bonus. “We’re a success-driven club. Like we’ve been strong for a long period of time, and that’s our motive,” captain and local farmer Tom Walters says. “But on the other hand, sometimes things are bigger than footy, so sometimes you have just got to enjoy the experience and help each other out.



“We all donated a match payment or a portion of a match payment during the year that went to families at the club who were directly affected. It just enabled us to give back a little bit to people that needed it more than us.” Seven months after the inferno devastated the town, club secretary Di Selwood experiences waves of “survivor guilt”. Junior members of Harcourt Football Netball Club enjoy Thursday night pizza. Justin McManus She and her daughter left their Harcourt home early, her husband evacuated when the fire became too intense, and yet their house was miraculously saved by their neighbours, CFA veterans Peter and May Wilson. “I don’t know how, but with buckets and whatever they had available, and they managed to keep the fire to the periphery. We had some burnt trees and fencing, but they saved our house,” Selwood says.



“I’m very grateful, extremely grateful. A bit of survivor guilt. You know, there are people in our street that lost everything.” Selwood says she and many others were kept busy after the fire. Coach Shelby (right) takes junior netball training at Harcourt. The fire ran to the fence. Justin McManus She explains the football-netball club had cancelled their Bunnings fundraising barbecue because of the disaster, but were able to use the meat to help feed the town. “We set up and cooked barbecues and fed people probably for the first couple of weeks, and that was part of, I suppose, how the club kept a connection to the community,” she says.



“Then when the council and government and other services came in and took that load away, then we just started focusing on our club, our members, and how we were going to get them back to community sport and back to their friends and what they needed.” The club has smashed its record for participation this year across five football teams and seven netball sides, as well as 52 Auskickers and more than 20 taking part in NetSetGo. Members enjoy a Thursday night drink at Harcourt Football Netball Club. Justin McManus “We’ve had more players across football and netball than ever before, and in fact I think we’ve got the most in our league,” Dorian says. “The biggest thing was really making sure that families were able to have somewhere to go.”



Shelby, 31, says the club became a place for families to heal. “We don’t have a pub, things like that, for people to come together, so this has been one of those places,” she says. Harcourt’s senior side prepares for Sunday’s semi-final against Navarre. Justin McManus “Even people that don’t even have kids playing here any more, they’ll still come down to training and catch up, have a drink, and have something to eat. “It has ensured that children still have the opportunity to play sport without that financial pressure on parents.”



Dorian, who has two teenage sons playing with the Lions, Jack and Tom, says some people have found new homes, others are rebuilding, some have left town and some don’t know where they’re going next. “For some, the struggles are still just as deep at the moment,” he says. Harcourt’s under-12 side plays a scratch match against the parents. Justin McManus But the football-netball club has been a constant. “For me, success is measured on participation and the vibe of the club and that’s more important to me than anything that we may win, hopefully, in a few weeks’ time,” he says. “It’s about community and people being together.”



Related Article Victoria residential property Victorian regional towns that boomed most in the past year Selwood agrees. The mother of two netball-playing daughters, Madi and Rhian, says six of the club’s families lost everything, but “they have stayed around”. “It’s not about whether we win the cups or you know what happens in the finals,” she says. “Maybe the senior footballers would disagree with me. In fact, I’m probably sure they would. But I think success for us is bigger. “It’s not all about the wins. It’s about the club culture. It’s about the people being able to come to a community space and be valued, be a valued member, be heard, be seen, be supported, and I think that’s where the success for us this year is.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Kiss’s winning ways continue as Wallabies outlast Argentina
World.content:
Breaking SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Kiss’s winning ways continue as Wallabies outlast Argentina Iain Payten August 30, 2026 — 7:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’s unbeaten run continued as Australia posted a third straight win under the new Wallabies coach with a tense 27-21 win over Argentina in San Salvador de Jujuy. The forwards yet again stood up for the Wallabies, scoring three of the side’s four tries in a gritty performance that included a good share of close-quarter combat. Loading The Wallabies led 19-7 early in the game, but Argentina fought back to trail by just one point with 30 minutes remaining. But a 54th-minute try from Tom Hooper pushed the Wallabies back out to a six-point lead, one they held on to in a see-sawing final 25 minutes. Australia’s mistakes down the stretch allowed the Pumas to stay in the contest. But key turnovers won by flanker Fraser McReight in the dying stages saw the Wallabies stave off disaster and claim the tight victory.



It is the first time the Wallabies have won three straight games since Kiss’ predecessor Joe Schmidt began with the Wallabies in 2024. The victory came with several key players sitting in the stands - with captain Harry Wilson rested and Len Ikitau not used. It did come at a price, however, with in-form halfback Ryan Lonergan taken from the field in the second half with a shoulder injury. Tom Hooper of the Wallabies scores a try while being tackled by Ignacio Ruiz. Getty Images The Wallabies led 22-14 at halftime after an opening half where they had the majority of possession and territory. The Pumas defence had plenty of starch early for the Wallabies’ one-out runners but some attacking space - and the first points - was finally found with some slick handling and running on the left edge.



And it was all performed by forwards, when Josh Canham got free as an extra man after quick hands on the left, before dropping a switch of play to lock partner Jeremy Williams, who also ran left and almost made the line. He offloaded to Brandon Paenga-Amosa just short of the line for a sixth-minute try. The Wallabies marched back downfield straight away, after stealing a lineout and then winning a penalty from a contestable kick. A lineout drive was stopped, but Carter Gordon charged onto a ball from a goal line ruck and scored a second five-pointer for Australia. Carter Gordon of the Wallabies is challenged by Ignacio Mendy and Santiago Carreras. Getty Images At 12-0 after 10 minutes, things were going well, but the Pumas responded quickly. A nice inside pass move near a midfield ruck found a gap and fullback Gerónimo Priscinatelli surged over soon after off quick phase ball.



The Wallabies got the benefit of poor Argentina discipline in the next sequence when they were helped back down to the hosts’ line. Multiple lineout drives were repelled before a Fraser McReight pick-and-drive from loose play gave Australia a third try inside the opening 19th minutes. The Pumas were told they were close to a yellow card, but it was the Wallabies who lost a man. Harry Potter was binned in the 24th minute when he stuck a hand out and knocked down a pass in his own 22. Brandon Paenga-Amosa of the Wallabies celebrates after scoring a try. Getty Images The Wallabies were under pressure in the red zone for most of those 10 minutes but survived without conceding points. But as soon as Potter returned, they conceded a try when a quick tap from a scrum on their line was taken by Pumas No.8 Joaquin Moro. He powered through two low tackles and reached out to score in the 37th minute. Australia grabbed last points in the half, however, when Ryan Lonergan knocked over a penalty goal from 30 out after the siren, for an eight-point lead at the break.



Lonergan was taken from the soon after play resumed when he was injured after making a try-saving cover tackle. An error from his replacement Tate McDermott then saw the Pumas score their next try. After a long-range counter-attack try was denied for a forward pass, McDermott had a box-kick clearance charged down, and with enough pressure on the line, Pumas prop Boris Wenger burrowed over. The Wallabies handling was pressured by good Argentina defence, but nice short passing at the line paid off soon after when Hunter Paisami got through, and after some more hard-line running from the Wallabies, Tom Hooper eventually got over. Ben Donaldson missed a simple conversion, keeping Argentina within six points.

World.title: I want to join all the public transport fare evasion, but just can’t deal with the stress
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPublic transport Opinion I want to join all the public transport fare evasion, but just can’t deal with the stress Claire Heaney Writer August 30, 2026 — 6:00am

August 30, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I trundle up the tram steps, look around for a vacant seat. A few sets of eyes avert from phones to me and back to their phones. The tram eventually empties and I grab a seat. Then, as if making a last-ditch qualification bid for the Aussie sprint squad at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, those same people sprint to the door, furtively looking for the next stop. Watching people, including authorised officers, on public transport is the author’s second favourite sport. Matt Davidson/Wayne Taylor It’s then I clock the ticket inspectors, known in the bureaucracy as authorised officers, moving in packs.



The fare evaders are a mixed bunch. Some appear to be students, others sharp in business attire. After two months of free tram travel across April and May, I realise I’ve missed this regular spectacle. My second Melbourne spectator sport, after AFL, is observing people on public transport. Don’t get me wrong. I get no joy from seeing people interrogated and fined. I have a complicated relationship with public transport fares. I never got over the axing of the Zone 1 short trip fare circa 2003, which robbed inner-city dwellers who rode just a few stops of a cheaper trip. I cycled to work for the best part of two decades in protest. The upside was that I got to childcare faster than by the tram, avoiding the late pick-up fee. But these days I’m back using public transport more than ever. Some days I’ve used the tram, train and bus. Apart from V/Line, I’ve rarely had my Myki checked.



When the two-month free tram travel ended on May 31, replaced by half price fares until the end of the year, I pulled the house apart looking for my two Myki cards I put away for safe keeping. Sure, I’ve been tempted not to pay if I’ve been on a packed tram and it’s a struggle to reach a Myki reader. Free is one of the best words in the English language, but I’m a firm believer in Murphy’s Law. Whatever can go wrong for me will go wrong so I expect the worst, try to plan and tap on. Fare evasion Ben Rushton In any case, these days I just can’t run fast enough to get out the door, and I like to relax and not jump at shadows, looking out for inspectors. For some budget-stretched younger people who I’ve spent time with recently in an education setting, fare evasion is a game of chance. Paying fares is an affront. One was miffed when the Myki saved on his phone paid the fare without him meaning to. He’d been riding buses free for 12 months. “Had my phone in my chest pocket and I brushed past a reader and it tapped on. The only time I ever tapped on getting to TAFE,” he said. Another told me that when approached by inspectors she becomes irrational and loud, so they back off.



While inspectors are doing their job, fines are disproportionate for the harm caused. The fine for failing to produce a valid Myki or concession jumped from $296 to $314 on July 1. One of my kids was fined last year. While the registered Myki was tapped-on, they weren’t carrying a concession card, left at home in the university backpack. PTV told me that the authorised officer can see the concession status attached to the Myki card when they use a hand held scanner. It seems disproportionate to hit a young concession user with a fine for hundreds of dollars when they’ve actually tapped on. Notwithstanding they should carry valid concession proof. (I know my daughter taps on every time as the money comes out of my credit card.) Related Article Opinion

Ageing My friends are permitted only two minutes to talk about their ailments Claire Heaney Writer Yet, I’ve seen a well-dressed middle-aged woman tell inspectors she left her Myki in her other handbag and seemingly get off. And don’t get me started on the politically cynical free Youth Myki for under 18s introduced by the state government from January 1. Sold as a cost-of-living exercise, it must be such a relief for the families of kids on some of the lines I use where parents are shelling upwards of $40,000 a year for private schools. In Queensland, they have a budget-friendly 50¢ fare for most public transport, but reports suggest that it hasn’t stopped fare evasion.



International research has shown there are various behaviours behind fare evasion, including so-called radicals who refuse to pay, strategic travellers who evade if they think they will get away with it, ambivalent evaders who sometimes pay and accidentals who forget or face setbacks trying to pay. A Monash University research paper from 2016, based on a survey of 1561 Melbourne commuters, found that repeat evaders were a small but overrepresented group among fare dodgers. “Deliberate evaders were the smallest cluster but the most frequent transit users,” the paper says. They were described as “sensation seekers” and happy to bend the rules to save money. Half of commuters were deemed “never evaders”. Related Article Opinion

Friendship Who suffers FOMO any more? I’m more likely to have ROMO Claire Heaney Writer In recent developments that will be a relief to confused tourists I encounter and those of us who find ourselves digging into pockets and handbags for errant Myki cards, you can now tap on with a credit or debit card. And, as my hardcore bus riding friend will have recently discovered, tap-and-go contactless payments have been enabled across the bus network since July 26. This is going to make it harder for people like him to get out of fare evasion – it’s surely going to be harder to justify not paying or at least convincing a ticket inspector as to why you haven’t paid. In a perfect world public transport would be free. I will begrudgingly tap on but if you aren’t tapping on, do you mind getting up and letting us fare-paying travellers have a seat?



Claire Heaney is a Melbourne writer. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat Bridget McManus August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Danny Estrin, the lead singer of Perth progressive metal band Voyager, was told he had 12 months to live, soon after the band performed at the 2023 Eurovision Song Contest. Three years and several rounds of chemotherapy later, the father of two daughters, aged five and nine, is still here. “I decided, I’m just going to enjoy the time between chemotherapy sessions as much as I can,” says Estrin, who is also still holding down his day job as an immigration lawyer. “It’s probably diametrically opposed to what a normal terminal cancer patient should be doing but I’m enjoying life as much as I can and filling it with good stuff.” Danny Estrin with a Porsche 928 in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Voyager have just returned from touring the Netherlands and the UK, and Estrin is stoked to be back on home soil feeding his “lifelong addiction” – cars. Having combed the car meets and garages of Western Australia for other enthusiasts, he’s making his television hosting debut with a fresh take on the motoring lifestyle genre, SBS2’s Precious Metal: A Love Story. His first automotive love was a Mercedes-Benz S-Class he spotted as a child in Hamburg, Germany, where he lived until his parents moved to Perth when he was 11. “It was the ultimate luxury,” he says. “It was huge. It was a 5.3-metre Colossus driven by executives. It had the car phone and electric everything, which back in the day was just crazy. It’s like, ‘Oh, someone important must be in that car!’”



Related Article Analysis

Australian TV Is Kitchen Cabinet past its use-by-date? Don’t write it off yet More a “man of letters and music than a man of wrenches and spanners”, Estrin leaves the mechanical side to his qualified mate, metal music fan Will Keogh, who appears on the show. Estrin has lost count of how many cars he has acquired, most of which are sitting in the garages of friends “with big hearts”. His very first, the white 1988 Toyota MR2 AW11 sports car that appeared alongside him on the Eurovision stage, is on display at the Motor Museum of Western Australia. “There’s something about the design and the shape of cars, and the fact that cars are objects of freedom and boundlessness. The steering wheels, the way the interior feels, smells, looks. The design, the headlights,” he says. “And the way that every car has a face: this one looks a bit sad; this one’s smiling, it’s a happy car. For me, styling was always much more important than the engine. I really couldn’t care about it. For me it’s about, ‘Oh, look! This has rear headrests! This has 16 ashtrays’ – as was the case in Germany in the ’80s. As part of this show I’ve explored other people’s reasons for their passion.” Danny Estrin and fellow motoring enthusiast Graeme take a vintage ride in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Throughout the series, Estrin, sporting his signature shiny houndstooth suits, meets people from all walks of life. Their wheels are just as diverse, among them a Morris Mini, a Renault Spider, a Porsche 356, a 1927 Chrysler Silver Wings, two Jaguars, and a Tesla Model 3/Chrysler 300 SRT Custom. There are also a Nissan Cube and two Toyota Landcruisers, one belonging to the series’ sole celebrity guest, former Neighbours actor Dan Paris, featured in the first episode.



Related Article Australian TV It’s been 25 years since Tampa. A documentary aims to show the story behind it isn’t ‘black and white’ “They don’t necessarily need to be the most exciting cars,” says Estrin. “It’s the stories that are the main thing. It could be teacups. It could be anything that’s collectible and has a sentimental value. I really wanted to explore what connects these people to these pieces of metal.” Voyager are off to the US next month to play at the ProgPower USA festival in Atlanta, and will then tour Australia in November, with shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney. “I’m still doing chemotherapy but the brakes are on at the moment. Hey! There’s a good car pun!” he says, laughing. “It’s a pretty aggressive form of cancer, unfortunately. It’ll get me sooner or later but, as statistics go, the longer you are alive, the longer you will be alive, hopefully. It’s quite surreal, actually, to think that this show is about to be released after all the turmoil of the last three years.” Precious Metal: A Love Story premieres on Wednesday, September 2, at 8.30pm on SBS2.

World.title: Leah Purcell is renowned for being tough on screen, but it’s what lies beneath that is the secret to her success
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Laughter might not come easily to the characters Leah Purcell plays: taciturn police sergeant Andie Whitford in High Country; fierce but distraught Molly Johnson in The Drover’s Wife; double-crossed undercover cop, now prisoner, Rita Connors in Wentworth. But asked why she thinks audiences have embraced her High Country character, she erupts in raucous and infectious laughter. “Maybe they just like me … everyone fell in love with me!” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Purcell has forged a remarkably varied and successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women battling adversity and hardship. It’s what lies beneath that hard surface that is key to her appeal. Ariadne Sgouros, Leah Purcell and Brendan Cowell in High Country: What Lies Beneath. What Lies Beneath is also the subtitle of the returning season of the mystery thriller High Country, which sees Whitford back in uniform and investigating dark deeds in a small, close-knit town. For those coming in late – no spoilers – High Country evolves around Purcell’s police officer Andie, who is transferred to a picturesque but insular mountain township of Brokenridge to replace retiring cop Sergeant Sam Dyson (Ian McElhinney, the veteran Northern Ireland actor best known as Barristan Selmy in Game of Thrones). It’s a town filled with grievances, suspicion and vendettas and a handful of missing-person cases. Those disappearances dovetail with the discovery of a far-reaching conspiracy involving many of the town’s residents.



Alongside the mystery-thriller element, High Country also dealt with Andie’s new-found connection to her Indigenous ancestry and relationships with partner Helen (Sara Wiseman), teenage daughter Kirra (Pez Warner) and ageing mother (Melissa Jaffer). Related Article Australian TV ‘Oh Jesus’: When Claudia Karvan agreed to go on Australian Story, she didn’t expect this It was filmed in Victoria’s high country, mainly around the township of Jamieson, which is where John Ridley – who created the show with Marcia Gardner – grew up and continues to live. The dramatic mountain landscape is a key element of the show. It also happens to be a region associated with many real-world events, from missing hikers to the cult known as The Family and most recently the notorious fugitive Dezi Freeman. Purcell wears many hats on High Country. In addition to playing the lead, she is an executive producer, which allows her to have input to the script and key production decisions. She is also the cultural consultant, ensuring all protocols are correctly carried out. That haunting voice on the opening soundtrack is hers as well. Leah Purcell with Aaron Pedersen in the first season of High Country, which was a hit in the UK and US. The new season takes up months after the events of the 2024 debut. It kicks off with a double murder on a houseboat, but there are many continuing storylines and characters, most notably Sam Dyson and Andie’s family. Purcell says that many decisions regarding the new, eight-episode series were based on audience feedback. “Everyone fell in love with their relationship,” she says of Andie and Sam.



“We both thoroughly enjoyed working with one another. So we kept [the storyline] open and everyone’s diaries aligned and away we went,” she says. “He’s a great bloke and phenomenal actor and the story lent itself to opening up that relationship. It’s a thriller, so there’s many threads to the story, and it’s a great thread to have him being a part of.” Related Article Streaming Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since Audiences also felt that Andie’s domestic relationships were authentic. “Pez [Warner] reminded me of myself,” says Purcell. “She had no training, comes from Newcastle, is a little go-getter. We all have a great relationship and I think that comes across clearly in the first season.” Andie has now settled into her job and has begun to understand the lay of the land. But she remains very isolated. Work is her life, her family. We only see her wearing her dark blue uniform. “That was all part of trying to show her isolation and what she’s put herself in at home.” The new cast includes Brendan Cowell as a gnarly, surly and possibly shifty detective who has a contemptuous history with Dyson, as well as a troubling personal connection to the victims of the houseboat murder. Purcell has played opposite Cowell on stage, describing him as deep and very smart. She credits Ridley and Gardner for allowing actors to “mould the words to suit their mouths. Brendan is very clever with that shorthand, which suits his character … the abruptness and poeticness around some of his lines.” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Leah Purcell has forged a successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women. Benny Capp



Season two of High Country has a noticeably different palette and setting to the first, which was dictated by the seasons in which the filming took place. “The lakes were down. So you utilise what you’ve got. He [John Ridley] said it’s a great way for any secrets that are hidden in that man-made lake [to be revealed]. When the water goes down, the secrets will rise and that’s what happens.” Where season one was all lush and damp forests, season two is a baked and receding lake (the actual Lake Eildon), a barren mine and the glare of summer. Related Article Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now “We utilised that in the story, the change of landscape,” says Purcell. “The hardness of a mine, the masculinity in this story. It was all a hardened approach to the various landscapes up there. Turn one way and you’ve got lush mountains. Turn and you’ve got a mine shaft. That was all deliberate, just working with the landscape and the time of year we could shoot.” Purcell believes that the success of High Country in the UK and US, where it aired on BBC and Hulu respectively, was due to it breaking the mould of what Australian stories are normally about. Instead of red-hot desert, viewers saw snow, mountains and greenery. But mostly, she says, it was down to the character. “That’s what you want from your leading lady, that the audience falls in love with the character and what she was going through. And it’s a First Nations story, that was something else that makes this different. A woman trying to work out who she is and there happened to be this First Nations connection to Country. “It wasn’t just the landscape; the landscape was talking. A lot of people thought that was a great addition to our cop story.”



Leah Purcell in The Drover’s Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson, which is being turned into a TV series. Brett Boardmen Purcell recently added librettist to her extensive list of credits, having written the opera adaptation of her play, film and novel The Drover’s Wife, which is also being turned into a TV series. The series “is not what people think. It starts with Molly Johnson’s six-times granddaughter in 2020. We’ve flipped it, coming at it from a different perspective. It’s not just the movie in six episodes. We always try to find a different way into those stories.” There’s nothing accidental about Purcell’s confidence and skill as a TV creator. “People have said, ‘Leah you’re so easy to shoot’. Because I understand what they need, what the camera person needs. It’s experience, and time. It’s a talent to be at one with the camera, just me and it. It’s a talent that you learn if you’re aware of it. Some people can be in the industry forever, and it’s not quite their thing, but I’ve had a couple of DOPs come up to me and say you’re so easy to shoot because you understand what the camera is doing.” Related Article Streaming Why the makers of Netflix’s My Brilliant Career tinkered with a classic She recalls one of her first roles on Police Rescue. “It was my training ground. I would sit and watch and understand when the camera was moving or crept in for a close-up. When Steadicam came in, that was magic, that was like dancing. “I love that challenge. Sometimes you can get caught up for a very long time trying to get the take if you don’t understand what they’re trying to achieve with the camera. So I would ask them, what do you need from me? It’s all very clinical, it’s maths when you break it down. It’s our job to make it look natural. I learned very early that the relationship other than [with] your fellow actor is with the camera.”

World.title: A black Swan event raises the question no one asks
World.content:
I have read tens of thousands of words over the past fortnight about the Sydney Swans’ debacle at Melbourne’s Pullman hotel, which has dismantled their season and left the club in crisis. There have been an extraordinary number of permutations and opinions, but one question seems still untouched.

To their credit, the Swans hierarchy has expressed the right priorities – decency, the wellbeing of the women involved, responsibility to the wider club and players. But while police and AFL investigations go on separately, the “Pullman five” have been suspended for the rest of the season by the club because they “breached club standards”. My question is, what precisely are these standards?

The misdoings of five suspended Sydney footballers at the Pullman Hotel raise questions about what exactly “club standards” are. Simon Schluter

At what point did the players breach these standards? When they went out partying all night? When they requested lap dances? Or only when they (allegedly) crossed the line into sexual assault?

The problem is that such moral codes are often highly amorphous and deliberately general. While I don’t doubt that the Swans are genuine in wanting high standards – particularly as the sense of betrayal within the club seems so powerful – such codes also provide a shelter behind which to hide in crises like this.

World.title: From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit
World.content:
CultureTV & radioDisney From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit Michael Idato August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meet the content stream of the future: movies, TV shows and a raft of next-generation spin-offs, coming to a mobile phone near you. While it’s true that bricks-and-mortar cinemas are going nowhere anytime soon, there is one inescapable truth dawning on Hollywood: the future is vertical. YouTube calls them Shorts, Netflix calls them Clips and on Disney+ they are Verts: a bite-sized, swipe-able TikTok-style feed of short-form content, including trailers, typically aimed at upsizing you to the full movie or episode. Loading But following a new deal with TikTok, Disney’s Verts are expanding into fan-created content and, coupled with a suite of spin-offs pitched at younger audiences, including Ariel, The Lion Guard, Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures and Descendants: The Rise of Red, represent the studio’s most significant shift towards younger viewers in decades. Critics might see this as the TikTok-ification of content, in the midst of the YouTube-ification of platforms: shrinking everything to the mobile phone, both in size and scale of ambition. Indeed, under the new deal, fan-created content would be seen on TikTok and inside the Disney+ app. That’s a substantial step past running trailers and preview clips.



But Shorts, Clips and Verts, and their longer form cousin, the “vertical drama”, may not be the cinematic death knell their critics might fear them to be. The key detail: 2026 has also been an extraordinary year for bricks-and-mortar cinemas. Despite fears streaming would destroy movie houses, global ticket sales are up 15 per cent year-on-year, and five films have crossed the $US1 billion mark this year in global box office receipts. Disney chief executive Josh D’Amaro on the main stage at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images They are Michael, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, from Universal Pictures, and Toy Story 5 and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, from Disney’s Marvel Studios and Sony. Two more films – The Devil Wears Prada 2 (Disney) and Project Hail Mary (Amazon MGM and Sony) – are just shy of the $US700 million mark, and Disney has another monster hit due before the end of the year, Avengers: Doomsday, in December.



The Disney+ Verts screen. So what is going on? And why, when cinema is upsizing to IMAX for The Odyssey, is consumable content in the home downsizing? The answer may be generational, as companies like Disney sharpen their aim at new, younger audiences. Earlier this month, as tens of thousands of fans moved through the D23 convention in Anaheim, California, showing off cosplay costumes, buying merchandise and engaging with the studio’s brand “activations”, behind closed doors its executives were outlining the future of the studio’s content strategy. And central to that strategy, says Erin Teague, Disney’s executive vice-president of product management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN, is the “democratisation of creativity.” “Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience,” Teague told media in the closed-door press meeting. “They want to be a part of the story. They want to put themselves in the story. They want interactivity. They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience.”



Disney’s strategy includes a $US1.5 billion investment in Epic Games, which essentially lays down digital bedrock for gamers to engage with Disney IP – Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars and more – inside the Fortnite gameplay environment. In addition to the studio’s suite of next-generation spin-offs, variously about younger versions of known characters (Ariel, Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends) or siblings and offspring (The Lion Guard, Descendants: The Rise of Red), a substantial new slate for Pixar was unveiled at D23. Ginnifer Goodwin and Ke Huy Quan unveil The Bluey Movie at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images That included Incredibles 3, Coco 2 and Frozen 3, on top of original films Gatto, about a street-smart black cat, due out in 2027, and Ghost Market, Pixar’s first supernatural thriller, due out in 2028. There is also, separately, a Bluey movie. There’s a good reason for that. As much as rusted-on fans might not like to hear it, key pieces of the Disney ecosystem are showing their age. Star Wars, the home of Luke Skywalker and Princess Leia, turns 50 next year. Marvel’s Cinematic Universe is in phase six, almost two decades after phase one began. Even Thor is starting to look a little long in the hammer.



Another perspective Disney The A-list stars added to Disney’s hall of fame – and what that means for the studio’s future Along with vertical content, however, all roads ultimately lead back to the central content funnel, Disney+. In the past two years the studio has consolidated its assets under the brand, including Hulu, its US-streamer, which is now tucked inside the Australian Disney+ app, and its sports streaming app, ESPN. Eric Schrier, the president of Disney Television Studios, said the strategy was intended to join dots for new audiences, who have not watched older, institutional content such as The Simpsons, Star Wars or even Disney live-action films, but might sample them via the streamer’s vertical and other content. “It gives us an opportunity to take a generation that is consuming most of this content in short form and introducing them to something like The Simpsons,” Schrier told the D23 press briefing. “They may not watch the traditional Simpsons show. They may see clips online, they may see curation, and then eventually become fans of The Simpsons and watch the whole show completely.” And all of this comes as Hollywood obsesses about vertical dramas, the phone-sized, modestly budgeted soap operas which have effectively turned handbags into home entertainment consoles.



Last month, Atlanta hosted the first vertical film festival, Vertex Micro Fest, which focused on short-form vertical content, “micro-dramas” and “AI-powered” stories, while Los Angeles last week hosted Verticon, a fan convention where fans and vertical drama stars pressed the flesh for three days. Verticon also played host to the Verties, the vertical content world’s answer to the Emmys or Oscars. The best actor and actress awards went to Cayman Cardiff (Seducing My Hockey Rival) and Nicole Mattox (Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas); vertical of the year was the romantic thriller Swipe Left: Dying for Love, from indie studio muVpix. Discussing Disney’s future: Content creator Blake Silva, Disney executives Eric Schrier and Erin Teague, and moderator (and creator) Jon Youshaei. The Walt Disney Company/Image Group L.A. Setting aside the eyebrow-raising titles, the vertical content business is now worth about $US150 billion globally; vertical dramas account for about $US14 billion of that. At Disney, the vertical strategy was initially tested as a sidebar product within the company’s ESPN ecosystem, before being rolled out widely. What testing in sport revealed, Teague said, was that time-challenged consumers were seeking a way of engaging with the major hits.



Editor's pick Film & TV production The palm-of-your-hand soap operas turning viewers away from TV “There’s no replacement for the live sports viewing experience, but ... thinking about the different ways people are busy, there’s a fight for attention,” Teague said. “People are consuming the live content, but they’re also catching up with key plays, with highlights, and all of that content is short, and actually better natively for a mobile consumption experience,” she said. Teague said viewer engagement had doubled since Verts were launched. In the end, however, replacing legacy IP with enduring appeal will be tough. Disney’s vertical content play can map the Star Wars universe infinitely outward, but few characters can match Princess Leia or Darth Vader for audience recognition, engagement and loyalty. “There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content,” Teague said. “But what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips. Similarly, [in sport] there’s no replacement for the live game. But the additional commentary and analysis around the game is just as interesting.



“The ways that we can merge those experiences to give people exactly what they want, when they want it in a split second, is the challenge.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Families lost everything when a bushfire hit town. This club helped them heal
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Families lost everything when a bushfire hit town. This club helped them heal Danny Russell August 30, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It is Thursday night at Harcourt Football Netball Club, and it soon becomes evident that fire has changed the way they view success. The under-12 side is having a scratch match against their parents. Laughter breaks out when a dad slips over and almost pings his hammy. A son sells his mother some candy as he dances around her outstretched arms and delivers the ball neatly to a teammate. Harcourt’s under-12 side plays a scratch match against the parents. Justin McManus President Mark Dorian is busily unravelling cords and plugging a cash machine into the bar before clearing tables for the Thursday night meals – pizzas and a hearty scoop of Neapolitan ice-cream for the kids. There is a buzz around the club as five teams enter a weekend of finals, including their senior team against Navarre at Maryborough’s Princes Park on Sunday.



Related Article Victoria bushfires ‘A damn lot of luck’: How three Victorian towns were spared by unstoppable fires But evidence of January’s devastating bushfire is never far away. Blackened trees, their branches regenerating with sprouting leaves, stand at the edge of the recreation reserve’s elevated car park, revealing just how close the flames came to engulfing the clubrooms. A damp clearing, to the west of the ground, is all that is left of the Harcourt Cooperative Cool Store – a vital storage base for up to 90 local businesses that was razed to the ground. More than 50 houses were lost. As Dorian emerges from the clubrooms, he trades witty quips with parents enjoying an afternoon drink.



Through his guidance Harcourt Football Netball Club has become a crucial focal point for the community. With support from AFL Victoria and Netball Victoria, one of the first things they did was offer free registration, free uniforms and free equipment for families. Then they provided free meals on a Thursday night. Members of Harcourt Football and Netball Club in the recovering bush at the edge of their oval. From left: Harper, Bonnie, Cohen, senior coach Sam Gale, captain Tom Walters, Austin, Judd, Joel and Raf. Justin McManus “We just made a big effort to try and bring normality to people’s lives. I mean, especially for the juniors, it was really about having a place to go,” Dorian says. “People are still going through all sorts of things now, whether they lost everything, or it affects their work, or who knows? It affects people in different ways. But what this does is gives people a place to unwind, and get away from it, even if it’s for an hour or so, and just enjoy being around people.”



Mother-of-two Shelby is one of those people. The junior coach is putting the under-11 netballers through their paces ahead of their weekend final and also plays for the club’s C-grade team. She admits she is still finding her feet after the fire burnt her rental home to the ground. More than 50 homes were lost in the fires in Harcourt and the surrounding area. Justin McManus Shelby, who asks for her surname not to be used for privacy reasons, and her son and her daughter lost all of their possessions. They are living temporarily at her father’s farm where she works part-time and studies social work.



“It’s a very long process [recovering], especially when there’s already a shortage of houses in the country,” she says. “When you lose 53 [houses] in one community, it makes it very challenging to house everybody. But yeah, this has been a place that we can come, we can enjoy ourselves, we can feel supported, and just find that purpose still. And sport is so good for mental health.” Harcourt Football Netball Club president Mark Dorian during Thursday night training. Justin McManus Members of the Harcourt senior football side are filtering into the ground. The Lions are looking to bounce back after last week’s three-point loss to Talbot. But for some, winning their semi-final on Sunday will be a bonus. “We’re a success-driven club. Like we’ve been strong for a long period of time, and that’s our motive,” captain and local farmer Tom Walters says. “But on the other hand, sometimes things are bigger than footy, so sometimes you have just got to enjoy the experience and help each other out.



“We all donated a match payment or a portion of a match payment during the year that went to families at the club who were directly affected. It just enabled us to give back a little bit to people that needed it more than us.” Seven months after the inferno devastated the town, club secretary Di Selwood experiences waves of “survivor guilt”. Junior members of Harcourt Football Netball Club enjoy Thursday night pizza. Justin McManus She and her daughter left their Harcourt home early, her husband evacuated when the fire became too intense, and yet their house was miraculously saved by their neighbours, CFA veterans Peter and May Wilson. “I don’t know how, but with buckets and whatever they had available, and they managed to keep the fire to the periphery. We had some burnt trees and fencing, but they saved our house,” Selwood says.



“I’m very grateful, extremely grateful. A bit of survivor guilt. You know, there are people in our street that lost everything.” Selwood says she and many others were kept busy after the fire. Coach Shelby (right) takes junior netball training at Harcourt. The fire ran to the fence. Justin McManus She explains the football-netball club had cancelled their Bunnings fundraising barbecue because of the disaster, but were able to use the meat to help feed the town. “We set up and cooked barbecues and fed people probably for the first couple of weeks, and that was part of, I suppose, how the club kept a connection to the community,” she says.



“Then when the council and government and other services came in and took that load away, then we just started focusing on our club, our members, and how we were going to get them back to community sport and back to their friends and what they needed.” The club has smashed its record for participation this year across five football teams and seven netball sides, as well as 52 Auskickers and more than 20 taking part in NetSetGo. Members enjoy a Thursday night drink at Harcourt Football Netball Club. Justin McManus “We’ve had more players across football and netball than ever before, and in fact I think we’ve got the most in our league,” Dorian says. “The biggest thing was really making sure that families were able to have somewhere to go.”



Shelby, 31, says the club became a place for families to heal. “We don’t have a pub, things like that, for people to come together, so this has been one of those places,” she says. Harcourt’s senior side prepares for Sunday’s semi-final against Navarre. Justin McManus “Even people that don’t even have kids playing here any more, they’ll still come down to training and catch up, have a drink, and have something to eat. “It has ensured that children still have the opportunity to play sport without that financial pressure on parents.”



Dorian, who has two teenage sons playing with the Lions, Jack and Tom, says some people have found new homes, others are rebuilding, some have left town and some don’t know where they’re going next. “For some, the struggles are still just as deep at the moment,” he says. Harcourt’s under-12 side plays a scratch match against the parents. Justin McManus But the football-netball club has been a constant. “For me, success is measured on participation and the vibe of the club and that’s more important to me than anything that we may win, hopefully, in a few weeks’ time,” he says. “It’s about community and people being together.”



Related Article Victoria residential property Victorian regional towns that boomed most in the past year Selwood agrees. The mother of two netball-playing daughters, Madi and Rhian, says six of the club’s families lost everything, but “they have stayed around”. “It’s not about whether we win the cups or you know what happens in the finals,” she says. “Maybe the senior footballers would disagree with me. In fact, I’m probably sure they would. But I think success for us is bigger. “It’s not all about the wins. It’s about the club culture. It’s about the people being able to come to a community space and be valued, be a valued member, be heard, be seen, be supported, and I think that’s where the success for us this year is.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
