World.title: Kiss’s winning ways continue as Wallabies outlast Argentina
World.content:
Breaking SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Kiss’s winning ways continue as Wallabies outlast Argentina Iain Payten August 30, 2026 — 7:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’s unbeaten run continued as Australia posted a third straight win under the new Wallabies coach with a tense 27-21 win over Argentina in San Salvador de Jujuy. The forwards yet again stood up for the Wallabies, scoring three of the side’s four tries in a gritty performance that included a good share of close-quarter combat. Loading The Wallabies led 19-7 early in the game, but Argentina fought back to trail by just one point with 30 minutes remaining. But a 54th-minute try from Tom Hooper pushed the Wallabies back out to a six-point lead, one they held on to in a see-sawing final 25 minutes. Australia’s mistakes down the stretch allowed the Pumas to stay in the contest. But key turnovers won by flanker Fraser McReight in the dying stages saw the Wallabies stave off disaster and claim the tight victory.



It is the first time the Wallabies have won three straight games since Kiss’ predecessor Joe Schmidt began with the Wallabies in 2024. The victory came with several key players sitting in the stands - with captain Harry Wilson rested and Len Ikitau not used. It did come at a price, however, with in-form halfback Ryan Lonergan taken from the field in the second half with a shoulder injury. Tom Hooper of the Wallabies scores a try while being tackled by Ignacio Ruiz. Getty Images The Wallabies led 22-14 at halftime after an opening half where they had the majority of possession and territory. The Pumas defence had plenty of starch early for the Wallabies’ one-out runners but some attacking space - and the first points - was finally found with some slick handling and running on the left edge.



And it was all performed by forwards, when Josh Canham got free as an extra man after quick hands on the left, before dropping a switch of play to lock partner Jeremy Williams, who also ran left and almost made the line. He offloaded to Brandon Paenga-Amosa just short of the line for a sixth-minute try. The Wallabies marched back downfield straight away, after stealing a lineout and then winning a penalty from a contestable kick. A lineout drive was stopped, but Carter Gordon charged onto a ball from a goal line ruck and scored a second five-pointer for Australia. Carter Gordon of the Wallabies is challenged by Ignacio Mendy and Santiago Carreras. Getty Images At 12-0 after 10 minutes, things were going well, but the Pumas responded quickly. A nice inside pass move near a midfield ruck found a gap and fullback Gerónimo Priscinatelli surged over soon after off quick phase ball.



The Wallabies got the benefit of poor Argentina discipline in the next sequence when they were helped back down to the hosts’ line. Multiple lineout drives were repelled before a Fraser McReight pick-and-drive from loose play gave Australia a third try inside the opening 19th minutes. The Pumas were told they were close to a yellow card, but it was the Wallabies who lost a man. Harry Potter was binned in the 24th minute when he stuck a hand out and knocked down a pass in his own 22. Brandon Paenga-Amosa of the Wallabies celebrates after scoring a try. Getty Images The Wallabies were under pressure in the red zone for most of those 10 minutes but survived without conceding points. But as soon as Potter returned, they conceded a try when a quick tap from a scrum on their line was taken by Pumas No.8 Joaquin Moro. He powered through two low tackles and reached out to score in the 37th minute. Australia grabbed last points in the half, however, when Ryan Lonergan knocked over a penalty goal from 30 out after the siren, for an eight-point lead at the break.



Lonergan was taken from the soon after play resumed when he was injured after making a try-saving cover tackle. An error from his replacement Tate McDermott then saw the Pumas score their next try. After a long-range counter-attack try was denied for a forward pass, McDermott had a box-kick clearance charged down, and with enough pressure on the line, Pumas prop Boris Wenger burrowed over. The Wallabies handling was pressured by good Argentina defence, but nice short passing at the line paid off soon after when Hunter Paisami got through, and after some more hard-line running from the Wallabies, Tom Hooper eventually got over. Ben Donaldson missed a simple conversion, keeping Argentina within six points.

World.title: I want to join all the public transport fare evasion, but just can’t deal with the stress
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPublic transport Opinion I want to join all the public transport fare evasion, but just can’t deal with the stress Claire Heaney Writer August 30, 2026 — 6:00am

August 30, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I trundle up the tram steps, look around for a vacant seat. A few sets of eyes avert from phones to me and back to their phones. The tram eventually empties and I grab a seat. Then, as if making a last-ditch qualification bid for the Aussie sprint squad at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, those same people sprint to the door, furtively looking for the next stop. Watching people, including authorised officers, on public transport is the author’s second favourite sport. Matt Davidson/Wayne Taylor It’s then I clock the ticket inspectors, known in the bureaucracy as authorised officers, moving in packs.



The fare evaders are a mixed bunch. Some appear to be students, others sharp in business attire. After two months of free tram travel across April and May, I realise I’ve missed this regular spectacle. My second Melbourne spectator sport, after AFL, is observing people on public transport. Don’t get me wrong. I get no joy from seeing people interrogated and fined. I have a complicated relationship with public transport fares. I never got over the axing of the Zone 1 short trip fare circa 2003, which robbed inner-city dwellers who rode just a few stops of a cheaper trip. I cycled to work for the best part of two decades in protest. The upside was that I got to childcare faster than by the tram, avoiding the late pick-up fee. But these days I’m back using public transport more than ever. Some days I’ve used the tram, train and bus. Apart from V/Line, I’ve rarely had my Myki checked.



When the two-month free tram travel ended on May 31, replaced by half price fares until the end of the year, I pulled the house apart looking for my two Myki cards I put away for safe keeping. Sure, I’ve been tempted not to pay if I’ve been on a packed tram and it’s a struggle to reach a Myki reader. Free is one of the best words in the English language, but I’m a firm believer in Murphy’s Law. Whatever can go wrong for me will go wrong so I expect the worst, try to plan and tap on. Fare evasion Ben Rushton In any case, these days I just can’t run fast enough to get out the door, and I like to relax and not jump at shadows, looking out for inspectors. For some budget-stretched younger people who I’ve spent time with recently in an education setting, fare evasion is a game of chance. Paying fares is an affront. One was miffed when the Myki saved on his phone paid the fare without him meaning to. He’d been riding buses free for 12 months. “Had my phone in my chest pocket and I brushed past a reader and it tapped on. The only time I ever tapped on getting to TAFE,” he said. Another told me that when approached by inspectors she becomes irrational and loud, so they back off.



While inspectors are doing their job, fines are disproportionate for the harm caused. The fine for failing to produce a valid Myki or concession jumped from $296 to $314 on July 1. One of my kids was fined last year. While the registered Myki was tapped-on, they weren’t carrying a concession card, left at home in the university backpack. PTV told me that the authorised officer can see the concession status attached to the Myki card when they use a hand held scanner. It seems disproportionate to hit a young concession user with a fine for hundreds of dollars when they’ve actually tapped on. Notwithstanding they should carry valid concession proof. (I know my daughter taps on every time as the money comes out of my credit card.) Related Article Opinion

Ageing My friends are permitted only two minutes to talk about their ailments Claire Heaney Writer Yet, I’ve seen a well-dressed middle-aged woman tell inspectors she left her Myki in her other handbag and seemingly get off. And don’t get me started on the politically cynical free Youth Myki for under 18s introduced by the state government from January 1. Sold as a cost-of-living exercise, it must be such a relief for the families of kids on some of the lines I use where parents are shelling upwards of $40,000 a year for private schools. In Queensland, they have a budget-friendly 50¢ fare for most public transport, but reports suggest that it hasn’t stopped fare evasion.



International research has shown there are various behaviours behind fare evasion, including so-called radicals who refuse to pay, strategic travellers who evade if they think they will get away with it, ambivalent evaders who sometimes pay and accidentals who forget or face setbacks trying to pay. A Monash University research paper from 2016, based on a survey of 1561 Melbourne commuters, found that repeat evaders were a small but overrepresented group among fare dodgers. “Deliberate evaders were the smallest cluster but the most frequent transit users,” the paper says. They were described as “sensation seekers” and happy to bend the rules to save money. Half of commuters were deemed “never evaders”. Related Article Opinion

Friendship Who suffers FOMO any more? I’m more likely to have ROMO Claire Heaney Writer In recent developments that will be a relief to confused tourists I encounter and those of us who find ourselves digging into pockets and handbags for errant Myki cards, you can now tap on with a credit or debit card. And, as my hardcore bus riding friend will have recently discovered, tap-and-go contactless payments have been enabled across the bus network since July 26. This is going to make it harder for people like him to get out of fare evasion – it’s surely going to be harder to justify not paying or at least convincing a ticket inspector as to why you haven’t paid. In a perfect world public transport would be free. I will begrudgingly tap on but if you aren’t tapping on, do you mind getting up and letting us fare-paying travellers have a seat?



Claire Heaney is a Melbourne writer. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat Bridget McManus August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Danny Estrin, the lead singer of Perth progressive metal band Voyager, was told he had 12 months to live, soon after the band performed at the 2023 Eurovision Song Contest. Three years and several rounds of chemotherapy later, the father of two daughters, aged five and nine, is still here. “I decided, I’m just going to enjoy the time between chemotherapy sessions as much as I can,” says Estrin, who is also still holding down his day job as an immigration lawyer. “It’s probably diametrically opposed to what a normal terminal cancer patient should be doing but I’m enjoying life as much as I can and filling it with good stuff.” Danny Estrin with a Porsche 928 in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Voyager have just returned from touring the Netherlands and the UK, and Estrin is stoked to be back on home soil feeding his “lifelong addiction” – cars. Having combed the car meets and garages of Western Australia for other enthusiasts, he’s making his television hosting debut with a fresh take on the motoring lifestyle genre, SBS2’s Precious Metal: A Love Story. His first automotive love was a Mercedes-Benz S-Class he spotted as a child in Hamburg, Germany, where he lived until his parents moved to Perth when he was 11. “It was the ultimate luxury,” he says. “It was huge. It was a 5.3-metre Colossus driven by executives. It had the car phone and electric everything, which back in the day was just crazy. It’s like, ‘Oh, someone important must be in that car!’”



Related Article Analysis

Australian TV Is Kitchen Cabinet past its use-by-date? Don’t write it off yet More a “man of letters and music than a man of wrenches and spanners”, Estrin leaves the mechanical side to his qualified mate, metal music fan Will Keogh, who appears on the show. Estrin has lost count of how many cars he has acquired, most of which are sitting in the garages of friends “with big hearts”. His very first, the white 1988 Toyota MR2 AW11 sports car that appeared alongside him on the Eurovision stage, is on display at the Motor Museum of Western Australia. “There’s something about the design and the shape of cars, and the fact that cars are objects of freedom and boundlessness. The steering wheels, the way the interior feels, smells, looks. The design, the headlights,” he says. “And the way that every car has a face: this one looks a bit sad; this one’s smiling, it’s a happy car. For me, styling was always much more important than the engine. I really couldn’t care about it. For me it’s about, ‘Oh, look! This has rear headrests! This has 16 ashtrays’ – as was the case in Germany in the ’80s. As part of this show I’ve explored other people’s reasons for their passion.” Danny Estrin and fellow motoring enthusiast Graeme take a vintage ride in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Throughout the series, Estrin, sporting his signature shiny houndstooth suits, meets people from all walks of life. Their wheels are just as diverse, among them a Morris Mini, a Renault Spider, a Porsche 356, a 1927 Chrysler Silver Wings, two Jaguars, and a Tesla Model 3/Chrysler 300 SRT Custom. There are also a Nissan Cube and two Toyota Landcruisers, one belonging to the series’ sole celebrity guest, former Neighbours actor Dan Paris, featured in the first episode.



Related Article Australian TV It’s been 25 years since Tampa. A documentary aims to show the story behind it isn’t ‘black and white’ “They don’t necessarily need to be the most exciting cars,” says Estrin. “It’s the stories that are the main thing. It could be teacups. It could be anything that’s collectible and has a sentimental value. I really wanted to explore what connects these people to these pieces of metal.” Voyager are off to the US next month to play at the ProgPower USA festival in Atlanta, and will then tour Australia in November, with shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney. “I’m still doing chemotherapy but the brakes are on at the moment. Hey! There’s a good car pun!” he says, laughing. “It’s a pretty aggressive form of cancer, unfortunately. It’ll get me sooner or later but, as statistics go, the longer you are alive, the longer you will be alive, hopefully. It’s quite surreal, actually, to think that this show is about to be released after all the turmoil of the last three years.” Precious Metal: A Love Story premieres on Wednesday, September 2, at 8.30pm on SBS2.

World.title: Leah Purcell is renowned for being tough on screen, but it’s what lies beneath that is the secret to her success
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Laughter might not come easily to the characters Leah Purcell plays: taciturn police sergeant Andie Whitford in High Country; fierce but distraught Molly Johnson in The Drover’s Wife; double-crossed undercover cop, now prisoner, Rita Connors in Wentworth. But asked why she thinks audiences have embraced her High Country character, she erupts in raucous and infectious laughter. “Maybe they just like me … everyone fell in love with me!” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Purcell has forged a remarkably varied and successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women battling adversity and hardship. It’s what lies beneath that hard surface that is key to her appeal. Ariadne Sgouros, Leah Purcell and Brendan Cowell in High Country: What Lies Beneath. What Lies Beneath is also the subtitle of the returning season of the mystery thriller High Country, which sees Whitford back in uniform and investigating dark deeds in a small, close-knit town. For those coming in late – no spoilers – High Country evolves around Purcell’s police officer Andie, who is transferred to a picturesque but insular mountain township of Brokenridge to replace retiring cop Sergeant Sam Dyson (Ian McElhinney, the veteran Northern Ireland actor best known as Barristan Selmy in Game of Thrones). It’s a town filled with grievances, suspicion and vendettas and a handful of missing-person cases. Those disappearances dovetail with the discovery of a far-reaching conspiracy involving many of the town’s residents.



Alongside the mystery-thriller element, High Country also dealt with Andie’s new-found connection to her Indigenous ancestry and relationships with partner Helen (Sara Wiseman), teenage daughter Kirra (Pez Warner) and ageing mother (Melissa Jaffer). Related Article Australian TV ‘Oh Jesus’: When Claudia Karvan agreed to go on Australian Story, she didn’t expect this It was filmed in Victoria’s high country, mainly around the township of Jamieson, which is where John Ridley – who created the show with Marcia Gardner – grew up and continues to live. The dramatic mountain landscape is a key element of the show. It also happens to be a region associated with many real-world events, from missing hikers to the cult known as The Family and most recently the notorious fugitive Dezi Freeman. Purcell wears many hats on High Country. In addition to playing the lead, she is an executive producer, which allows her to have input to the script and key production decisions. She is also the cultural consultant, ensuring all protocols are correctly carried out. That haunting voice on the opening soundtrack is hers as well. Leah Purcell with Aaron Pedersen in the first season of High Country, which was a hit in the UK and US. The new season takes up months after the events of the 2024 debut. It kicks off with a double murder on a houseboat, but there are many continuing storylines and characters, most notably Sam Dyson and Andie’s family. Purcell says that many decisions regarding the new, eight-episode series were based on audience feedback. “Everyone fell in love with their relationship,” she says of Andie and Sam.



“We both thoroughly enjoyed working with one another. So we kept [the storyline] open and everyone’s diaries aligned and away we went,” she says. “He’s a great bloke and phenomenal actor and the story lent itself to opening up that relationship. It’s a thriller, so there’s many threads to the story, and it’s a great thread to have him being a part of.” Related Article Streaming Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since Audiences also felt that Andie’s domestic relationships were authentic. “Pez [Warner] reminded me of myself,” says Purcell. “She had no training, comes from Newcastle, is a little go-getter. We all have a great relationship and I think that comes across clearly in the first season.” Andie has now settled into her job and has begun to understand the lay of the land. But she remains very isolated. Work is her life, her family. We only see her wearing her dark blue uniform. “That was all part of trying to show her isolation and what she’s put herself in at home.” The new cast includes Brendan Cowell as a gnarly, surly and possibly shifty detective who has a contemptuous history with Dyson, as well as a troubling personal connection to the victims of the houseboat murder. Purcell has played opposite Cowell on stage, describing him as deep and very smart. She credits Ridley and Gardner for allowing actors to “mould the words to suit their mouths. Brendan is very clever with that shorthand, which suits his character … the abruptness and poeticness around some of his lines.” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Leah Purcell has forged a successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women. Benny Capp



Season two of High Country has a noticeably different palette and setting to the first, which was dictated by the seasons in which the filming took place. “The lakes were down. So you utilise what you’ve got. He [John Ridley] said it’s a great way for any secrets that are hidden in that man-made lake [to be revealed]. When the water goes down, the secrets will rise and that’s what happens.” Where season one was all lush and damp forests, season two is a baked and receding lake (the actual Lake Eildon), a barren mine and the glare of summer. Related Article Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now “We utilised that in the story, the change of landscape,” says Purcell. “The hardness of a mine, the masculinity in this story. It was all a hardened approach to the various landscapes up there. Turn one way and you’ve got lush mountains. Turn and you’ve got a mine shaft. That was all deliberate, just working with the landscape and the time of year we could shoot.” Purcell believes that the success of High Country in the UK and US, where it aired on BBC and Hulu respectively, was due to it breaking the mould of what Australian stories are normally about. Instead of red-hot desert, viewers saw snow, mountains and greenery. But mostly, she says, it was down to the character. “That’s what you want from your leading lady, that the audience falls in love with the character and what she was going through. And it’s a First Nations story, that was something else that makes this different. A woman trying to work out who she is and there happened to be this First Nations connection to Country. “It wasn’t just the landscape; the landscape was talking. A lot of people thought that was a great addition to our cop story.”



Leah Purcell in The Drover’s Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson, which is being turned into a TV series. Brett Boardmen Purcell recently added librettist to her extensive list of credits, having written the opera adaptation of her play, film and novel The Drover’s Wife, which is also being turned into a TV series. The series “is not what people think. It starts with Molly Johnson’s six-times granddaughter in 2020. We’ve flipped it, coming at it from a different perspective. It’s not just the movie in six episodes. We always try to find a different way into those stories.” There’s nothing accidental about Purcell’s confidence and skill as a TV creator. “People have said, ‘Leah you’re so easy to shoot’. Because I understand what they need, what the camera person needs. It’s experience, and time. It’s a talent to be at one with the camera, just me and it. It’s a talent that you learn if you’re aware of it. Some people can be in the industry forever, and it’s not quite their thing, but I’ve had a couple of DOPs come up to me and say you’re so easy to shoot because you understand what the camera is doing.” Related Article Streaming Why the makers of Netflix’s My Brilliant Career tinkered with a classic She recalls one of her first roles on Police Rescue. “It was my training ground. I would sit and watch and understand when the camera was moving or crept in for a close-up. When Steadicam came in, that was magic, that was like dancing. “I love that challenge. Sometimes you can get caught up for a very long time trying to get the take if you don’t understand what they’re trying to achieve with the camera. So I would ask them, what do you need from me? It’s all very clinical, it’s maths when you break it down. It’s our job to make it look natural. I learned very early that the relationship other than [with] your fellow actor is with the camera.”

World.title: A black Swan event raises the question no one asks
World.content:
I have read tens of thousands of words over the past fortnight about the Sydney Swans’ debacle at Melbourne’s Pullman hotel, which has dismantled their season and left the club in crisis. There have been an extraordinary number of permutations and opinions, but one question seems still untouched.

To their credit, the Swans hierarchy has expressed the right priorities – decency, the wellbeing of the women involved, responsibility to the wider club and players. But while police and AFL investigations go on separately, the “Pullman five” have been suspended for the rest of the season by the club because they “breached club standards”. My question is, what precisely are these standards?

The misdoings of five suspended Sydney footballers at the Pullman Hotel raise questions about what exactly “club standards” are. Simon Schluter

At what point did the players breach these standards? When they went out partying all night? When they requested lap dances? Or only when they (allegedly) crossed the line into sexual assault?

The problem is that such moral codes are often highly amorphous and deliberately general. While I don’t doubt that the Swans are genuine in wanting high standards – particularly as the sense of betrayal within the club seems so powerful – such codes also provide a shelter behind which to hide in crises like this.

World.title: From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit
World.content:
CultureTV & radioDisney From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit Michael Idato August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meet the content stream of the future: movies, TV shows and a raft of next-generation spin-offs, coming to a mobile phone near you. While it’s true that bricks-and-mortar cinemas are going nowhere anytime soon, there is one inescapable truth dawning on Hollywood: the future is vertical. YouTube calls them Shorts, Netflix calls them Clips and on Disney+ they are Verts: a bite-sized, swipe-able TikTok-style feed of short-form content, including trailers, typically aimed at upsizing you to the full movie or episode. Loading But following a new deal with TikTok, Disney’s Verts are expanding into fan-created content and, coupled with a suite of spin-offs pitched at younger audiences, including Ariel, The Lion Guard, Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures and Descendants: The Rise of Red, represent the studio’s most significant shift towards younger viewers in decades. Critics might see this as the TikTok-ification of content, in the midst of the YouTube-ification of platforms: shrinking everything to the mobile phone, both in size and scale of ambition. Indeed, under the new deal, fan-created content would be seen on TikTok and inside the Disney+ app. That’s a substantial step past running trailers and preview clips.



But Shorts, Clips and Verts, and their longer form cousin, the “vertical drama”, may not be the cinematic death knell their critics might fear them to be. The key detail: 2026 has also been an extraordinary year for bricks-and-mortar cinemas. Despite fears streaming would destroy movie houses, global ticket sales are up 15 per cent year-on-year, and five films have crossed the $US1 billion mark this year in global box office receipts. Disney chief executive Josh D’Amaro on the main stage at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images They are Michael, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, from Universal Pictures, and Toy Story 5 and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, from Disney’s Marvel Studios and Sony. Two more films – The Devil Wears Prada 2 (Disney) and Project Hail Mary (Amazon MGM and Sony) – are just shy of the $US700 million mark, and Disney has another monster hit due before the end of the year, Avengers: Doomsday, in December.



The Disney+ Verts screen. So what is going on? And why, when cinema is upsizing to IMAX for The Odyssey, is consumable content in the home downsizing? The answer may be generational, as companies like Disney sharpen their aim at new, younger audiences. Earlier this month, as tens of thousands of fans moved through the D23 convention in Anaheim, California, showing off cosplay costumes, buying merchandise and engaging with the studio’s brand “activations”, behind closed doors its executives were outlining the future of the studio’s content strategy. And central to that strategy, says Erin Teague, Disney’s executive vice-president of product management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN, is the “democratisation of creativity.” “Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience,” Teague told media in the closed-door press meeting. “They want to be a part of the story. They want to put themselves in the story. They want interactivity. They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience.”



Disney’s strategy includes a $US1.5 billion investment in Epic Games, which essentially lays down digital bedrock for gamers to engage with Disney IP – Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars and more – inside the Fortnite gameplay environment. In addition to the studio’s suite of next-generation spin-offs, variously about younger versions of known characters (Ariel, Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends) or siblings and offspring (The Lion Guard, Descendants: The Rise of Red), a substantial new slate for Pixar was unveiled at D23. Ginnifer Goodwin and Ke Huy Quan unveil The Bluey Movie at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images That included Incredibles 3, Coco 2 and Frozen 3, on top of original films Gatto, about a street-smart black cat, due out in 2027, and Ghost Market, Pixar’s first supernatural thriller, due out in 2028. There is also, separately, a Bluey movie. There’s a good reason for that. As much as rusted-on fans might not like to hear it, key pieces of the Disney ecosystem are showing their age. Star Wars, the home of Luke Skywalker and Princess Leia, turns 50 next year. Marvel’s Cinematic Universe is in phase six, almost two decades after phase one began. Even Thor is starting to look a little long in the hammer.



Another perspective Disney The A-list stars added to Disney’s hall of fame – and what that means for the studio’s future Along with vertical content, however, all roads ultimately lead back to the central content funnel, Disney+. In the past two years the studio has consolidated its assets under the brand, including Hulu, its US-streamer, which is now tucked inside the Australian Disney+ app, and its sports streaming app, ESPN. Eric Schrier, the president of Disney Television Studios, said the strategy was intended to join dots for new audiences, who have not watched older, institutional content such as The Simpsons, Star Wars or even Disney live-action films, but might sample them via the streamer’s vertical and other content. “It gives us an opportunity to take a generation that is consuming most of this content in short form and introducing them to something like The Simpsons,” Schrier told the D23 press briefing. “They may not watch the traditional Simpsons show. They may see clips online, they may see curation, and then eventually become fans of The Simpsons and watch the whole show completely.” And all of this comes as Hollywood obsesses about vertical dramas, the phone-sized, modestly budgeted soap operas which have effectively turned handbags into home entertainment consoles.



Last month, Atlanta hosted the first vertical film festival, Vertex Micro Fest, which focused on short-form vertical content, “micro-dramas” and “AI-powered” stories, while Los Angeles last week hosted Verticon, a fan convention where fans and vertical drama stars pressed the flesh for three days. Verticon also played host to the Verties, the vertical content world’s answer to the Emmys or Oscars. The best actor and actress awards went to Cayman Cardiff (Seducing My Hockey Rival) and Nicole Mattox (Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas); vertical of the year was the romantic thriller Swipe Left: Dying for Love, from indie studio muVpix. Discussing Disney’s future: Content creator Blake Silva, Disney executives Eric Schrier and Erin Teague, and moderator (and creator) Jon Youshaei. The Walt Disney Company/Image Group L.A. Setting aside the eyebrow-raising titles, the vertical content business is now worth about $US150 billion globally; vertical dramas account for about $US14 billion of that. At Disney, the vertical strategy was initially tested as a sidebar product within the company’s ESPN ecosystem, before being rolled out widely. What testing in sport revealed, Teague said, was that time-challenged consumers were seeking a way of engaging with the major hits.



Editor's pick Film & TV production The palm-of-your-hand soap operas turning viewers away from TV “There’s no replacement for the live sports viewing experience, but ... thinking about the different ways people are busy, there’s a fight for attention,” Teague said. “People are consuming the live content, but they’re also catching up with key plays, with highlights, and all of that content is short, and actually better natively for a mobile consumption experience,” she said. Teague said viewer engagement had doubled since Verts were launched. In the end, however, replacing legacy IP with enduring appeal will be tough. Disney’s vertical content play can map the Star Wars universe infinitely outward, but few characters can match Princess Leia or Darth Vader for audience recognition, engagement and loyalty. “There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content,” Teague said. “But what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips. Similarly, [in sport] there’s no replacement for the live game. But the additional commentary and analysis around the game is just as interesting.



“The ways that we can merge those experiences to give people exactly what they want, when they want it in a split second, is the challenge.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: National vows to reduce student loan repayment rate if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party is promising to reduce the compulsory student loan repayment rate if re-elected, while cracking down on overseas-based borrowers.

It said it would reduce the repayment rate from 12 percent to 10 percent from April 2027.

The party's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said compulsory student loan repayments were paid at 12 cents on every dollar earned above $24,128.

"It is often one of the biggest weekly expenses for a young graduate," she said.

''Reducing this to 10 cents means an accountant starting out in their career and earning $75,000 per year would keep an extra $39 a fortnight, or around $1000 a year.''

National would also introduce new financial penalties for borrowers who left the country before paying back their student loan.

That included adding to student loan interest, restricting KiwiSaver withdrawals and making it easier for police to issue arrest warrants for "serious, sustained loan defaults".

Willis said it was not fair for graduates to take their skills offshore after receiving a heavily subsidised tertiary education, and not try to repay their loan.

"Overseas-based borrowers currently account for 93 percent of overdue student loan debt. Only around three in 10 meet their repayment obligations in a given year, compared to 95 percent of New Zealand-based borrowers," she said.

World.title: Person critically injured after fight in Lower Hutt
World.content:
One person is in hospital with critical injuries following a fight in Lower Hutt overnight.

Police were called to Waterloo Road just after 2am.

One person was taken to hospital with critical injuries.

Several other people suffered minor injuries during the fracas.

Detective Senior Sergeant Peter Reeves, from Wellington District Investigations, said police were urging anyone with information to come forward.

They could contact police on 105, quoting file number P067465363.

World.title: Springboks bounce back to defeat All Blacks for first loss in Rennie era
World.content:
The Springboks beat the All Blacks 33-26 in the second test in Cape Town to level the four-match series 1-1.

The All Blacks scored four tries to the Springboks' three tries but the hosts kicked several penalty goals to help claim a seven-point victory in front of a sold out crowd of about 60,000.

South Africa came flying out of the blocks and were the first to score with midfielder Jesse Kriel going over near the posts after a strong lineout drive on the right edge of the field.

Wing Cheslin Kolbe kicked the conversion to make it 7-0 to the Springboks in just the third minute of the match.

The All Blacks were having some issues at lineout time but they struck back with a try of their own with a lovely backline move resulting in a break to wing Will Jordan. He fed the ball inside to halfback Cam Roigard who scored under the posts.

Cam Roigard goes in for a try. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

First-five Ruben Love added the extras to tie the game at 7-7 after 16 minutes, though the Springboks kicked a penalty goal soon after to retake the lead 10 points to 7.

The Springboks and the DHL Stadium crowd were fired up and the hosts were next to score a try with midfielder Damian de Allende barging his way over a few phases after another lineout drive in the All Blacks 22.

Kolbe was successful with the conversion to extend South Africa's advantage to 17-7 midway through the first half.

The All Blacks absorbed more pressure before going onto the offensive and captain Ardie Savea made a break down field before the visitors spun the ball wide to fullback Damian McKenzie who scored in the right corner.

Damian McKenzie scores for the All Blacks. BackpagePix/ Samuel Shivambu

Love nailed the tricky conversion to cut South Africa's lead to 17-14 with ten minutes remaining in the first half.

The Springboks were awarded a penalty close to the All Blacks line with just a few minutes left in the first half and chose to take a scrum.

The All Blacks stopped the pushover attempt but South Africa weren't to be denied with captain Siya Kolisi surging over close to line a few phases later.

Kolbe kicked the extra two points to give the Springboks a 24-14 lead going into halftime.

Siya Kolisi celebrates his try with his Springbok teammates. BackpagePix

The Springboks landed the first punch of the second half with Kolbe kicking a penalty goal to extend their advantage to 27-14 in the 49th minute.

The hosts were on a roll and were awarded another penalty close to the All Blacks 22 with the tourists pinged for holding on at a ruck. Kolbe nailed the penalty kick to put the hosts ahead 30-14 with half an hour remaining.

The All Blacks really needed to be next to score to stay in the game and they did just that with wing Leroy Carter outsprinted the cover defence to dive over in the left corner after some nice passing from Fabian Holland and Quinn Tupaea.

Leroy Carter on his way to the tryline. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Love missed the conversion with the score 30-19 to the Springboks with 13 minutes left.

South Africa hit back not long after with Kolbe kicking a penalty goal from 40 metres out to extend the hosts advantage to 33-19 with about nine minutes remaining in the match.

The All Blacks hit back with a try to Savea and Love nailed the conversion to make it a seven point game at 33-26 with just a few minutes remaining.

That's how the score would remain with the Springboks hanging on to claim the win and level the four match series 1-1.

The third test is in Johannesburg next weekend.

World.title: Some patients face 24-hour wait at Wellington Hospital emergency department
World.content:
Patients presenting at Wellington Hospital's emergency department have faced wait times of more than 24 hours to be seen this month.

An ED nurse said, on a recent Monday night shift, one man fell asleep and hit his head, while waiting 12 hours to be seen.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said the current situation in Wellington ED was unacceptable, as it continued to be one of lowest-performing in the country, while Health NZ said the hospital was under extreme winter pressure, and very long waits occurred for complex circumstances and weren't the experience of most patients.

The New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) delegate said she feared speaking out would result in repercussions - RNZ agreed not to name her for this reason.

She said, on the overnight shift on Monday 17 August, the hospital escalated to Code Red several times.

Health NZ said code red in ED referred to the amount of pressure the department was under. It's based on waitingroom congestion, staffing skill mix, changes in care hours and the seriousness of the patient cases.

One man had come to the emergency department in the evening, she said, and wasn't admitted until about 6am.

"The only reason he was brought through then was because of him falling asleep and face-planting, and they were checking him for any injuries."

The nurse said ED wait-times recently were extremely long - at times reaching 24 hours - although the peak was 18 hours more recently.

The six-hour ED treatment and discharge target was only achieved 57.6 percent of the time at Wellington Hospital in January-March. RNZ / REECE BAKER

In internal Health NZ documents RNZ has seen, the agency said in early August that some patients exceeded 24-hour waits in ED, with high numbers of patients waiting more than six hours, due to medical bed shortages.

Hospitals throughout the country have a target that 95 percent of patients are admitted, discharged or transferred from an emergency department within six hours.

Latest results from Health NZ, between January and March 2026, show Capital & Coast hospitals only met that target 57.6 percent of the time.

An ED summary shift report from a staff member from Monday, 17 August said the department that night was operating under "extreme pressure", experiencing "significant and sustained over-crowding".

A mental health patient locked themselves in the bathroom and self-harmed, the nurse said, while a member of the public walked in and threatened to "kill staff", assaulting a security orderly.

Police confirmed to RNZ they attended the hospital at 11.30pm to a report of disorderly behaviour - a person was arrested for breach of conditions, a spokesperson said.

Health NZ said it wouldn't comment or confirm details about the specific patient incidents, without a privacy waiver.

File photo 123RF

'Lots of pressure'

The nurse said the hospital was full and bed-blocked that night, with at least 11 patients needing to be treated in corridors, although this was normal.

"It's just a sh**show to work in at the moment. Lots of pressure.

"We're getting high presentations, but the pressure's coming from where we can't get patients off to wards to free up our ED space, so that we can continue to see the new ones coming in."

She said there could be up to 24 patients in corridors on other days.

"It's awful, you know, and every day you're seeing your corridors full and we're all walking past these corridors.

"There's no privacy for any of these patients."

Twenty-seven nurse vacancies at Wellington ED

A Health NZ spokesperson said there were 27.1 full-time nurse vacancies at in the ED.

In the coming months, 18 new nurses would come on board, leaving 8.8 full-time nurse vacancies, which were being recruited.

Michelle Sutherland, interim group director of operations for the region, said the hospital had 212 ED patients on 17 August, following several days of high demand.

Winter was an extremely busy time for health services, so more patients were expected.

She said 66 percent percent of patients on 17 August were discharged from the ED within six hours.

"We acknowledge that a number of patients experienced very long waits. The longest waits tend to reflect particularly complex circumstances, rather than the experience of most people in the department."

Health Minister Simeon Brown RNZ / Mark Papalii

Wellington ED wait-times 'not acceptable' - minister

Brown said the current situation at Wellington Regional Hospital's emergency department was not acceptable.

"It continues to be one of the lowest-performing in the country, and that is not good enough for patients or for staff.

"Our doctors, nurses and healthcare workers work incredibly hard every day, but they are operating in a facility that does not support safe patient flow or timely treatment."

Brown said the government had prioritised a redevelopment of ED in the Health Infrastructure Plan and work was underway across the hospital campus.

His office said additional beds had been provided, among other planning measures made for the winter season.

Space in the hospital has been a long-standing issue, with the redevelopment likely to be complete by 2029.

He said wait times at Wellington Hospital had come down under the current government, compared to the previous Labour government, and the ED now met the wait-time target 57.6 percent of the time, increasing from 43.8 percent in 2023.

Code Red instances had also fallen, he said, with his office providing a table that showed 729 Code Reds in 2023, compared to 567 in 2025.

"However, there is still a long way to go before Wellingtonians can access emergency care as quickly as they deserve."

World.title: One dead after Auckland house fire
World.content:
One person has been located dead by police following a house fire in Henderson.

Emergency services were called to Forest Hill Road about 8.40pm on Saturday.

On Sunday police confirmed one person has died.

Acting Detective Senior Sergeant James Kim said a scene guard was put in place at the property overnight.

"The cause of the fire remains unexplained at this early stage."

Police will be carrying out a scene examination at the house today, including working with fire investigators.

Members of the community may see an increased presence while enquiries continue, he said.

The house in Henderson Valley was well ablaze when crews arrived at the scene last night.

At its peak up to 35 firefighters were fighting the blaze, which broke out at around 8.30pm last night.

Shift manager Garreth Lewis said the house was totally ablaze when crews arrived.

Six trucks, as well as one command unit and one hazardous materials unit, were sent to the scene.

Lewis said crews were searching for the person, along with fighting the fire.

World.title: Roads closed due to flooding in Whangārei, strong winds for Hawke's Bay, Southland
World.content:
Several roads are closed in Whangārei after heavy rain caused flooding.

However, the region is in for a reprieve on Sunday.

MetService meterologist Braydon White says it's lifted its rain warning for the region and that yesterday's heavy downpours have eased.

He says up to 120 millimetres of rain fell in an hour in some parts, while there was up to 90mm in an hour in Kerikeri.

The closed roads include Russell Road, Ngunguru Road North, Otonga-marua Road, Marua Road, and Kaiikanui Road.

Several other roads were down to a single lane because of surface flooding.

Fire and Emergency said a slip occurred at a house on Queen Street in Russell last night.

Crews were attending another incident when they became aware of the slip.

A spokesperson said the people in the house chose to stay there overnight.

Wind watches in place

MetService says the heavy rain for northern New Zealand will move away to the east early today.

It is warning people in Hawke's Bay, Tararua and parts of the South Island to brace for heavy winds.

It's issued an orange strong wind warning for Hawke's Bay south of Hastings, and the Tararua District from 7pm on Sunday until tomorrow evening.

It says severe gale westerlies could gust up to 120km/h in exposed places.

It's also issued a strong wind watch for Tasman and southern areas of Southland, Clutha and Dunedin.

World.title: Firefighters search for one missing in Henderson housefire
World.content:
One person remains unaccounted for, following a large housefire in Henderson Valley in Auckland.

Thirty-five firefighters were at the scene of the fire.

Fire and Emergency says it received calls about the incident just after 8.30pm Saturday.

Shift manager Garreth Lewis said the house was totally ablaze when crews arrived.

Six trucks, as well as one command unit and one hazardous materials unit, were sent to the scene.

Lewis said crews were searching for the person, along with fighting the fire.

World.title: Thousands of youths to lose access to unemployment benefits after welfare law change
World.content:
Thousands of youths across the country are set to lose access to unemployment benefits, after a welfare bill passed into law under urgency on Friday night.

From November 2026, the government will end Jobseeker payments to 18-19-year-olds whose parents earn more than $67,225.

The limit was originally just over $65,000 when the policy was announced, but has since been adjusted.

In October last year, it was estimated that about 4300 young people would become ineligible for support as a result.

Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston said the legislation reflected the government's commitment to reduce benefit dependency and encourage people into work.

"This legislation reinforces the expectation that young people who are not in employment, education or training should be financially supported by their parents, not by taxpayers through the welfare system," she said.

"New Zealanders deserve a welfare system that is firm, fair and simple."

The bill also makes changes to how accommodation supplements are calculated.

Upston said the changes would "better target that support to those who need it most".

"Importantly, it does not apply to homeowners who are receiving New Zealand superannuation, veteran's pension, supported living payment, or the emergency benefit that is the equivalent to the supported living payment.

World.title: Marshall fires up over 'outrageous' refereeing in loss to Cowboys
World.content:
A fired-up Benji Marshall says he will issue a "please explain" to the NRL after a series of "outrageous" calls went against Wests Tigers in their loss to North Queensland.

The Cowboys punched their ticket to the finals for a second time in three years with a 24-10 win at Townsville Stadium on Saturday night, but the victory wasn't without controversy.

NRL live Roosters halfback Sam Walker will go for scans after sustaining a concerning ankle injury in his side's 26-12 loss to the Dolphins, while North Queensland lock in a finals spot with a 24-10 victory over Wests.

Tigers five-eighth Jarome Luai had his length-of-the-field try chalked off in the first half because of a rake in the lead-up, and prop Terrell May's was also denied by the bunker after Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater was impeded, despite standing metres away from the ball.

"The level of some of the refereeing decisions today was honestly outrageous, and I thought we copped the raw end of the stick all night," Tigers coach Marshall said.

"We'll be sending in a few questions and asking for a please explain.

"We get penalised for contesting. They go down, take Jock Madden out [the] same thing. We get no penalty. They score.

"I feel like I need to stand up for my players because the way they're fighting, it's just not right."

To make matters worse, the joint venture (8-15) will sweat on Luai, who hobbled off the field in the second half and was also placed on report in his penultimate game for the club.

North Queensland (13-10) will not worry about the contentious calls after becoming the last team to seal their top-eight spot, after South Sydney secured their finals place with a 42-22 victory over Gold Coast earlier on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Tadej Pogačar crashes out of La Vuelta a España
World.content:
Five-time Tour de France champion and overwhelming favourite Tadej Pogačar has pulled out of the Vuelta a España after crashing during the eighth stage of the race.

The Slovenian held a big lead in the race but got caught in a crash about 33 kilometres from the finish on Saturday, local time.

He tried to get back on his bike but could not carry on and walked to an ambulance. Race organisers confirmed he pulled out of the race.

The UAE Team Emirates leader was trying to become the ninth male rider to win all three grand tour races.

Pogacar won the Tour de France for a third straight time and a record-tying fifth overall in July, and he claimed the Giro d'Italia win in 2024. He had not raced in the Vuelta since making his grand tour debut at the event in 2019.

Footage showed Pogačar with cuts on his head as well as his left arm and shoulder. Pogačar veered to his right, into other cyclists, as he appeared to try to either hit or avoid something in the road.

He lost control and flew over his handlebars, hitting his head and shoulder.

UAE Team Emirates sports manager Matxin Joxean Fernandez said after the stage that Pogačar had needed stitches in his eyebrow and elsewhere.

"It's no-one's responsibility … It's simply one of those things that happens in cycling, unfortunately," Fernandez said.

"He initially wanted to keep going, but we saw he was in a lot of pain in his shoulder and decided he couldn't continue. There isn't much else to say.

"After seven days Tadej was happy and it's a very big shame for him, cycling is about good and bad and [we hope] Tadej recovers as soon as possible because hopefully it's not something too bad, we're not going to think about that right now but we'll see what the doctor says."

Pogačar — who had led since winning the opening stage — had an advantage of 3 minutes, 50 seconds over Enric Mas of Movistar before Saturday's stage, which did not feature any major difficulty and offered sprinters a chance to shine along a flat 171-kilometre route from Puçol to Xeraco. Bryan Coquard, from the Cofidis team, claimed the stage win ahead of Mads Pedersen and Jordi Meeus.

Pogačar wins Vuelta stage four Tadej Pogačar has taken a dominant lead in the Vuelta a España, winning his second stage with a phenomenal 50km solo attack in Andorra.

Mas took the race leader's jersey from Pogačar, becoming the first Spanish rider to lead the race since Jesus Herrada in 2018. Felix Gall stood second overall, 1:11 off the pace, with Primoz Roglic in third.

The 31-year-old Mas did not put on the leader's red jersey when he was presented with it in the post-race ceremony, instead just holding it up. He was also not wearing it in television interviews after the stage.

"To get the red jersey thanks to a crash, it's not a good feeling," he told Eurosport in translated comments.

"We'll try to defend it tomorrow but tonight we need to assimilate what happened and give Tadej all our support and hopefully he will recover soon. We decided with the team that I was not going to wear the red jersey [today] and then if I deserve it tomorrow, I will wear it."

Pogačar's main rival, Jonas Vingegaard, is not competing in the Vuelta after crashing during this year's Tour de France.

This was Pogačar's 10th Grand Tour and the first he has ever abandoned. He had never finished lower than third place.

The three-week race concludes in Granada.

AP

World.title: Sprinter Ellie Beer reveals emotional toll of being elite athlete at 16
World.content:
At age 16, 400 metre runner Ellie Beer was exceeding expectations.

She was the new kid on the block in Australian sprinting, smashing her personal best (PB) time and making history.

But maintaining that level of performance was all-consuming.

"It was just spotlight moment after spotlight moment," Beer tells ABC Sport.

"I remember feeling the pressure of what others were thinking.

"I felt like I had to rise to the occasion, like every race I had to run a PB and that it would be good enough."

It took another five agonising years for Beer to beat her 2019 PB of 52.53 seconds.

"There were moments where I was like, 'Will I ever get better?' I [felt] like maybe I peaked at 16," Beer says.

"I had thoughts of wanting to give up and not pursue it anymore."

Ellie Beer competed for five years without running a personal best. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

The transition from a junior to a senior athlete, from about 17 to 19 years of age, was particularly hard.

"I had set my standards so high that I had to run consecutive 52 second runs, but I wasn't getting close to that time due to the pressure," Beer says.

She started overthinking her races, predicting what would happen before they had even begun.

"I would be worrying about the lactic [acid] hitting the last hundred. 'How am I going to run down that back straight?'

"I went out and pretty much just ran stressed and nervous."

Ellie Beer started to overthink races and then tied her identity to her results. (ABC Sport: Glenn Mullane)

Beer credits her coach and support team with getting her on the start line during that time.

"The back of my head [was saying] 'I don't want to give up the sport,' but the front of my head was telling me, 'No, [I] want to be done.'"

"I knew in my heart that I didn't want to give up," she says.

But moving forward wasn't easy.

When passion turns to pain

Beer stands out. She's more than 1.8m tall, with long, bouncy blonde locks and an infectious smile.

You can't miss her on the track thanks to her trademark arm sleeves, which help her to get in the zone.

Ellie Beer says wearing arm sleeves helps her to get in the zone. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"My coach always says, 'Wear your arm sleeves, Ellie, because you feel fierce,'" she says.

"[They] make me feel like I'm ready to go out there and perform."

Now 23, Beer is a different person to the 16-year-old who stormed onto the world stage. But it's only because of where she's been.

Beer's big break came at the Queensland Track Classic in 2019 when she won the 400m in a PB of 52.53.

It earned her a spot in the Australian 4 x 400m relay team for the 2019 IAAF World Athletics Championships, and the title of the youngest-ever Australian selected.

A young Ellie Beer competes at the IAAF World Athletics Championships in 2019. (Getty Images: Christian Petersen)

She then ran a flying time, which helped Australia qualify for the Tokyo Olympics.

Beer was selected for that 4x400m relay team for Tokyo, and at 18 her Olympic dream was realised.

Ellie Beer (right) realised her dream to compete at an Olympics in Tokyo. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

After Tokyo, Beer won the 2022 national senior 400m title and placed seventh in the 400m final at the World Under 20 Championships. But still no breakthrough runs, no personal bests. That pressure to rise to every occasion was weighing heavily.

"I was just really worrying about trying to perform a perfect race, sometimes for others," Beer says.

Ellie Beer was constantly worrying about the race, before it even began. (Getty Images: Pedro Vilela)

"I used to be, after bad races, quite down on myself.

"And then [I] would kind of dwell into the rest of my season."

The power of pushing through

At 21 years old, already having graced the international stage for five years, Beer knew something had to change.

It was 2024, leading into the Paris Olympics, when her mindset switched thanks to a supportive team.

A mindset change in the year leading up to the Paris Olympics helped Ellie Beer make a breakthrough. (Getty Images: Christian Petersen)

She now has a wellbeing coach, a psychologist, and Brett Robinson, who has been her running coach since she was 11.

"He [Robinson] has helped me so much along the way," Beer says.

"Particularly during times when I didn't believe in myself, he would always believe in me more.

"I don't even want to call him a coach; I want to call him family."

What they did together seems so simple, but it worked.

"Nerves, they never go away, [but] I've changed my mindset around them," Beer says.

"I channel them and [have learned to] embrace them.

Ellie Beer now embraces the nerves and leans into them, rather than letting them consume her. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"It's a word that Robbo and I have used quite often.

"Embrace the hurt, [because] the 400 [is] a very tactical event, but learning to embrace that lactic acid, embrace where you are and being grateful to go out there and perform."

With that, Beer stopped worrying about the uncontrollable and she wasn't so driven by the outcome.

She also stopped tying her identity to her race results.

"I'm learning, yes, I'm Ellie Beer the athlete, but I'm also Ellie Beer the daughter, coffee enthusiast, social girl, the friend," she says.

Loading Instagram content

"I've just learned that you [might have] one bad race, [and] yes, it sucks at the time, but it's just one race. We move forward and we focus on the next."

Mind over matter

That change has seen results.

2024 was a good year for Beer. She broke the personal best drought at the Adelaide Invitational, took the national 400m title, the Oceania 400m title, and then produced another PB at the Paris Olympics.

In 2025, she won her third national title and got her PB down to its current form of 51.3 seconds. She also won a bronze relay medal at the World Indoor Championships.

Loading Instagram content

This year, she secured her fourth national title, was crowned Oceania Champion again, and recently helped the mixed and women's relay teams qualify for the 2027 World Athletics Championships.

Her biggest goal now is running the 400m in under 51 seconds.

"I've had that goal for the last couple of years and we just haven't quite got it yet," Beer says.

"We've got PBs which I'm happy with, but our standard for Australia to get into most major teams is to run a 50.7.

"To run a sub-50, oh my gosh, I'm going to be ecstatic.

"But I've learned [that with] running, even just a PB is amazing [and] I'll be happy with that."

Ellie Beer's goal now is to run the 400 metres in under 51 seconds. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Beer stresses the nerves are still there and probably always will be.

When asked what her greatest challenge is in getting that sub-51 mark, her answer is not a surprise.

"Probably my own self," Beer says.

"I'm a different athlete compared to when I was a junior, [but I] still struggle with the self-doubt and the what if."

The Gold Coast local is now an ambassador for the Australian Institute of Sport's mental fitness program, and says she is happy to share her experiences of vulnerability to help other athletes.

"Having that experience of not running a PB for five years, that's the reason as to why at this age now I want to share better ways to deal with it," she says.

"As part of my training, I speak with my sports psychologist, I speak to my wellbeing officer, I speak with my coaches to help rewire my mindset leading into races.

"There's a major percentage physically, [but] mental plays a massive part as well."

It is possibly a contradiction, but mentally, Beer likes to switch off with coffee.

Loading Instagram content

She just can't survive without her two iced long blacks a day, on top of an espresso shot with eggs on toast in the morning.

"I love coffee," Beer says.

"My favourite thing to do outside of training is search for the best cafes and try all of them."

The focus is just one part of rebuilding her identity outside of running.

In the long term, Beer has her sights set on being selected for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

"I would love to perform in front of a home crowd," she says.

But for now, there's always coffee.

World.title: Wallabies win tense Test in Argentina as coach Kiss remains unbeaten
World.content:
The Wallabies have won a gritty and tense Test match described by two separate players as "bloody hard", securing a 27-21 win over Argentina.

Australia scored four tries to three in Sunday morning's clash in the mountain town of San Salvador de Jujuy, where the stadium sits more than 1,200 metres above sea level.

The Wallabies made a hot start with three tries in the opening 20 minutes, but had to show plenty of determination to hold off an Argentine fightback to secure the team's fourth Test win in a row.

The Australian forwards were excellent for much of the match, especially disrupting the Los Pumas' line-out in the second half.

Australia's forwards were very good in the set piece against Argentina. (AP: Gustavo Garello)

Wallabies flanker Fraser McReight was named player of the match after an effort where he was a constant feature around the ball, including a crucial penalty won late in the contest with Argentina attacking inside the 22m.

"It was a back-and-forth sort of match," McReight told the host broadcaster.

"Argentina were very good. I felt like we were pretty poor in some areas, but [I'm] just really proud of the group and I'm happy we got the win over here."

The Wallabies were by no means perfect in Jujuy, with winger Max Jorgensen and flanker Tom Hooper each describing the match and conditions as "bloody hard" in separate interviews.

The Wallabies made a hot start with the opening two tries of the match. Hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa finished off a lovely passage of passing between forwards to score in the seventh minute, then fly half Carter Gordon touched down four minutes later from close range after the Wallabies forwards pounded their way to the goal line.

Argentina struck back through fullback Geronimo Prisciantelli after a lovely backline move, but when McReight scored in the 20th minute, the Wallabies were in control at 19-7.

But Los Pumas wrestled back the momentum, and a sin bin with Wallabies winger Harry Potter for deliberately knocking the ball down in the 25th minute put the home side in the ascendancy.

Argentina number eight Joaquin Moro took a quick tap from close range and powered over the line to reduce the deficit to five points, but a penalty goal from Wallabies scrumhalf Ryan Lonergan gave Australia a 22-14 lead at the break.

Lonergan came off after just five minutes in the second half after making a desperate cover tackle to deny Prisciantelli a second try.

Los Pumas were denied a try due to a forward pass picked up by the TMO in the 48th minute, but loosehead prop Boris Wenger dove over three minutes later to reduce Australia's lead to one point.

But the Wallabies responded quickly, with a line break from centre Hunter Paisami putting Australia into the attacking 22m, and leading to Hooper reaching out a few plays later to give the Wallabies a 27-21 lead.

The Wallabies were on top as the second half wore on, but could not get the try to seal the game. Jeremy Williams knocked on while trying to score, then reserve scrumhalf Tate McDermott was held up over the line.

It kept Los Pumas in the contest, but the Wallabies' defence held firm in the final five minutes to secure the win.

"It was a very tough game. Everyone knows that coming over to Argentina is a bloody hard place to win. It's you against them, plus the whole stadium," Jorgensen told Stan Sport.

"It wasn't near perfect, we've still got a lot of work to do, but to come away with a win in Argentina is very good."

The win is Australia's fourth in a row, and maintains coach Les Kiss's perfect record after three Tests in charge.

Australia has leapfrogged Argentina into seventh on the World Rugby rankings, with both sides to meet next week in the second Test at Mendoza.

Follow all the live action from the first Test between the Wallabies and Argentina in the blog below.

World.title: Blues' resurgence continues with stirring wildcard win over Demons
World.content:
Carlton will play an elimination final against Geelong after winning a wildcard clash against Melbourne at the MCG.

Despite conceding the first four goals of the game, the Blues improved steadily throughout the game to grind the Demons down, before finally emerging 19-point winners.

Ben Ainsworth kicked three goals for Carlton, while Sam Walsh and rising star Jagga Smith were sensational in the midfield.

The Blues had multiple opportunities to put the game to bed in the last quarter, but it wasn't until Smith converted a set shot for his second of the evening when the result was put to bed.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional return for South Sydney
World.content:
Jai Arrow has made an emotional return for South Sydney, leading the side out and officially playing his 99th match for the club against Gold Coast.

Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year, has received special dispensation from the NRL to play the opening seconds of the Rabbitohs' final two matches for the year.

He was substituted before kick-off for Cameron Murray and left the field at Skilled Park to a standing ovation.

Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett and former stalwart Jason Clark helped Arrow put his boots on before the match.

The Titans wore a commemorative jersey with Arrow's face on the front.

He played 56 matches for the club from 2018 to 2020.

Arrow will lead South Sydney out again next week in their final game of the regular season against the Sydney Roosters.

Arrow was in tears as he left the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It will mark his 100th game for the club and the 180th and final match of his career.

Arrow was in the room when elated Souths players were told about the plan during their team review session on Monday morning.

"We all play a tough sport and we all mean so much to so many people, but it's so special to see what players mean to other players when things are going tough," said Rabbitohs fullback Matt Dufty.

"[Jai] brings a smile to everyone's face. Whatever we can do to give back to him, even if it's a little bit, it's just what we need to do. We're all behind him."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

Murray replaced Arrow before kick off. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of his jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs showed their support by marking tries with 'arrow' celebrations during July.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Walker's season in jeopardy, Cowboys lock in top eight with Tigers win
World.content:
An inspired defensive effort has seen the Dolphins hold on for a 26-12 victory over the Roosters, who lost star halfback Sam Walker to an ankle injury early in the second half.

Walker will go for scans for a suspected syndesmosis injury.

In Townsville, the Cowboys became the eighth and final team to lock in a finals berth with a 24-10 victory over Wests.

Earlier, South Sydney beat the Titans 42-22 to lock in a finals spot after a pre-game tribute to retiring Jai Arrow.

World.title: Magpies legend Pendlebury set to join Gold Coast Suns for 2027 season
World.content:
Collingwood legend and AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury will move to the Gold Coast Suns in 2027.

Pendlebury, who has played 442 games for the Magpies, will move to the Suns as an unrestricted free agent.

The contract is believed to be a multi-year agreement, where the 38-year-old will play a hybrid coaching and on-field role for two seasons, before moving into an assistant coach role for another two years.

Pendlebury was not offered a new contract to continue his career at Collingwood.

"For the past 21 years, it's been an incredible privilege to be a Collingwood footballer. From walking in the doors as a 17-year-old, to seeing the way everyone at the club has welcomed and embraced my family over all these years is something that is truly special," Pendlebury said in a statement.

"I've spent the majority of my life here and so many of my best memories have come through being part of Collingwood. The friendships, the challenges, the successes and even the tough times have all shaped who I am.

"The privilege of pulling on the Collingwood jumper has never been lost on me. I understand what this club means to so many people and I've always tried to represent it in a way that makes our Magpie Army proud.

"This decision has not come lightly but I know this is the best thing for me and my family as I transition into the next phase of my football journey."

The midfielder will leave the Magpies as one of the club's greatest-ever players, having won two premierships, a Norm Smith medal and six All-Australian nods.

His role at the Suns is set to mimic former Hawthorn legend Luke Hodge's 2018 move to the Brisbane Lions, where Hodge played two seasons as an on-field coach for a young Lions squad that has gone on to win two premierships from three grand final appearances.

The deal will be officially ticked off when the AFL's free agency period begins on October 2.

Pendlebury was denied a finals farewell game in Collingwood's wildcard loss to the Western Bulldogs on Friday night after straining his hamstring in the final game of the regular season.

Tech.title: Vicariously hike the Appalachian in the gorgeous A Trail Tale
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I used to be an avid hiker and would try to go backpacking a few times a year. I always dreamed of thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail, but life kind of got in the way. (Turns out jobs, wives, and children aren’t thrilled with the idea of you disappearing for three months.) But I’ve been longing to reconnect with my love of the outdoors and just recently took my kids on their first camping trip. So I discovered A Trail Tale at a really opportune time. It’s an interactive trail journal created by Andy Moliski with help from his brothers Adam and Alex.

The various segments of the trail are rendered in beautiful pixel art reminiscent of a ‘90s Sierra point-and-click adventure. Alex recorded an equally gorgeous original score that combines nature sounds, acoustic guitar, strings, and even what sounds like clarinet.

As you click through each day, you’re greeted with information about landmarks and a game-like UI that is partially inspired by titles like Oregon Trail. (Spoiler: nobody dies of dysentery in this one.) Clicking on Andy unfurls a menu of icons that offer details about the journey, his mental state, and even bits of poetry. There are even little icons for things that impact his fortitude and morale meters, like inclement weather or picturesque scenery.

It’s insanely easy to just get lost in Andy’s journey for hours. And it’s making me wonder if I should get back out there and start tackling some more of the AT myself.

Tech.title: Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday, and today the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Reuters and the Washington Post that he had been deported to the UK. Yiannopoulos came to the US legally in 2019, but overstayed his visa. After he failed to appear in court for an immigration hearing, a final order of removal was issued ​on July 22.

The British national made a name for himself as an editor at Steve Bannon’s Breitbart and an early supporter of Donald Trump’s. He has had a long history of controversial statements and associations, including reportedly helping arrange Trump’s dinner with Kanye West and white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and he was a key figure in the online harassment campaign Gamergate.

In recent years, however, his antics have led to a falling out with most significant figures on the right, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. He has denied condoning statutory rape or pedophilia, but he has suggested it’s acceptable for an adult to have a sexual relationship with a 13-year-old.

There’s no word if the 44 interns in a trenchcoat who also constitute the entity known as Milo Yiannopoulos have also been deported.

Tech.title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking damages for “tens of thousands” copyrighted works. The companies are asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance when identifiable copyright data was stripped. In total, the damages could amount to several billion dollars if a court finds in Sony and Warner’s favor and awards the maximum amount.

In addition to suing Anthropic as an entity, the complaint names Co-Founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann as individual defendants. The suit alleges that Mann used BitTorrent to download over five million pirated books, and that employees downloaded at least two million more from Pirate Library Mirror. It also claims that Anthropic scraped lyrics from sites like MusixMatch and LyricFind, which paid to license content from the labels.

According to the filing:

Plaintiff Music Publishers, a group of the world’s leading music publishers, bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history. Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic’s “Claude” series of artificial intelligence (“AI”) models.

Specific songs named as being found in Anthropic’s training data include Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Bon Jovi’s “Livin’ On a Prayer,” Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” and TaylorSwift’s “Paper Rings.” Antrhopic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Distraction-free writing gadget BYOK is adding custom extensions
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

BYOK is a no-frills, single-purpose gadget that 90 percent of people will find absolutely frivolous. But for those who spend a significant chunk of their lives putting words to virtual paper, there is an obvious allure. Personally, I think it’s at its best when you just stick to the bare minimum, focusing on pure text drafting. Certain users, though, need more. They want BYOK to take notes, they want to use it for writing screenplays, or maybe they want to organize a sprawling novel.
